World.title: South Africa: Fired for Being Foreign - How Employers Gave in to March and March Threats
World.content:
The Casual Workers Advice Office has recorded a sharp rise in reports of xenophobic labour practices in Gauteng

The Casual Workers Advice Office has noted a sharp rise in reports of unlawful treatment of immigrant workers by employers in Gauteng.

Reports include payments withheld, exploitation, exclusion from UIF and unfair dismissals.

People we spoke to who have lived in South Africa for years believe that "there is much more hatred" against immigrants in recent months.

"They used us and threw us away when they were done," Raphike Bado, a Malawian immigrant who had worked in South Africa for many years, told GroundUp at the Casual Workers Advice Office (CWAO) in Germiston.

The CWAO says it is dealing with a wave of cases targeting immigrant workers in Gauteng. Many have been unable to work since the run-up to the 30 June "deadline". Many have now completely exhausted their savings and cannot afford the travel costs to leave South Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Gugu Moyo, the CWAO's immigrant liaison officer, said immigrant workers "are being treated as less than human" and are being exploited.

She worries that there "is no end in sight" as politicians and anti-immigration "activists" continue to scapegoat immigrants and spread hatred.

The workers are "ordinary people just trying to create a life here like all of us", she said.

The CWAO said it has, since June, taken on over 100 cases of Gauteng workers being fired, suspended or shut out of their jobs. Many of them have valid papers.

None of the immigrant workers it has assisted has successfully claimed UIF, despite contributing to the fund, because their employers have refused to co-operate. CWAO is trying to assist with CCMA cases.

The workers CWAO is assisting described cases of exploitation, including low wages, unpaid overtime and unsafe working conditions.

CWAO said it has also helped hundreds of immigrants who wanted to contact embassies, sort out documents or arrange repatriation.

The workers

"We can no longer trust anybody. If you are a foreigner, whether you have documents or not, you fear for your life," an emotional Rejoice Moyo told GroundUp.

Moyo's is one of two dozen stories related to GroundUp by immigrant workers who had approached the CWAO Germiston office for assistance.

Originally from Zimbabwe, she has lived in South Africa for 17 years. But she was dismissed after the anti-immigrant group March and March turned up on 10 June at the shop where she worked as a sales consultant.

"These foreigners you are hiring must be gone," a March and March supporter told her employer and informed him of their 30 June "deadline" for undocumented immigrants to leave South Africa.

Moyo is documented and living and working legally in the country, but her employer "didn't care" she said. He dismissed her and a colleague and tried to coerce them into writing a resignation letter stating they had resigned "because we were scared of March and March".

She said she was only paid for the days she worked in June. She was not given notice pay or accrued annual leave.

Mbombo Nana and Sylvia (who preferred not to give her last name) fled war in the Democratic Republic of Congo and have lived in South Africa for over a decade.

"Now I face violence here," said Nana. "What do I do? I have nowhere else to go."

Nana and Sylvia have refugee papers and are legally allowed to work. But they were both dismissed after people turned up at their workplaces demanding that "only South Africans" be hired.

"We are working very hard, but they treat us like nothing because we are foreigners," said Sylvia. She said she was chased by a mob yelling, "Abahambe!" (They must go, a Zulu catchphrase adopted by anti-immigrant groups).

Monica Chifamba, who came from Zimbabwe in 2010, was also recently dismissed without payment. A single mother with two children, she is struggling to feed her family and pay rent and school fees.

Close 

She said she is often told to "go back to Zimbabwe".

She said she has experienced xenophobia during previous election periods, "but 2026 is different". She and her children are "living in fear", too afraid to answer the phone or speak in public.

She is an orphan and has nothing to return to in Zimbabwe, she said.

Raphike Bado has worked in plastic manufacturing since he came from Malawi in 2013. He said that the company he worked for hired "many foreigners" as they were "cheaper" and "could work longer".

On 15 June, he and fellow employees were told not to come to work the following day, "because March and March" were coming.

Bado was subsequently dismissed without compensation.

CWAO organiser Andile Nyembezi said that "xenophobic forces are mobilising based on ethnicity and tribalism which only divides" and does not create jobs or improve working conditions.

Out of fear, none of the workers we spoke to agreed to be photographed.

World.title: Smithsonian-linked museum in El-Sayed’s backyard puts America’s post-9/11 response on trial
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

DEARBORN, MI – Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a Smithsonian affiliate in Michigan continues to use its 9/11 exhibits and anniversary programming to focus on discrimination and government actions in the attacks' aftermath, while giving less attention to the nearly 3,000 people killed that day, Fox News Digital found.

The Arab American National Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, features an exhibit arguing that Arab Americans "suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th," both from the attacks themselves and from what the museum describes as unfair treatment by the U.S. government afterward. Since its founding, the museum has repeatedly hosted programs examining what it describes as discriminatory consequences of the U.S. response to 9/11.

Fox News Digital visited the museum earlier this month, reviewed its exhibits and gift shop, and examined years of anniversary programming and federal funding records.

The AANM has received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and is also an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution. The Smithsonian has been under intense scrutiny from conservative lawmakers in recent months for allegedly allowing political bias to influence its presentation of history.

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

One placard criticizes the government’s post-9/11 detention of immigrants investigated for possible terrorist links, noting that "virtually none were charged" in connection with terrorism.

"The Arab American community suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th. As with all Americans, they suffered the horror and grief. However, Arab Americans were unfairly held responsible, yet not a single Arab American was found guilty of any connection to September 11th," it reads.

On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, crashing two into the World Trade Center, and one into the Pentagon. Passengers and crew fought back aboard United Flight 93, the fourth plane, prompting the hijackers to crash the plane in Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the largest investigation in FBI history.

The museum placard also argues that Arabs faced harsher immigration enforcement after the attacks, saying some were "deported for minor visa violations or petty offenses which previously would have been overlooked."

HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE'

In the 11 months after the attacks, immigration authorities detained 762 noncitizens on immigration charges in connection with the FBI’s terrorism investigation, including for overstaying visas or entering the country illegally, according to a Justice Department inspector general report. The watchdog found that some detainees with no terrorism ties were treated harshly and held under unnecessarily restrictive conditions.

Public opinion also showed a more complicated picture of the post-9/11 backlash. President George W. Bush publicly urged Americans not to blame Muslims for the attacks, and polling later suggested attitudes toward Muslim Americans actually improved in the immediate aftermath. The share of Americans who viewed Muslim Americans favorably rose from 45% in March 2001 to 59% in November, two months after the attacks, according to the Pew Research Center.

Beyond its permanent exhibit, AANM has repeatedly used programming around the 9/11 anniversary to examine discrimination and law-enforcement policies affecting Arab and Muslim communities.

The museum holds a "solidarity" town hall each year, where criticism of the American reaction to 9/11 is often the focus. The online description of the event does not mention the deaths connected to the attacks themselves, but rather "offers a safe space for communities to reflect and engage in dialogue about the harmful prejudices that Arab and Muslim (and anyone perceived to be Arab or Muslim) individuals face on both an individual and systemic level."

One such town hall in 2018 examined "how communities of color have been targeted through the frame of national security and profiled as violent threats."

A year later, the AANM’s annual town, which received support from the National Endowment for the Arts, criticized how "institutions and communities of color have been infiltrated" by law enforcement as well as how leaders of those groups have been "targeted" following 9/11.

SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES

The AANM was founded in 2005, partially in response to the increased scrutiny directed at the Arab American community following the attack on the World Trade Center. In addition to receiving well over half a million dollars in funding from the NEH over its lifetime to support its exhibits and educational programming, the museum also benefited from a $385,000 grant from the Department of Housing and Urban Development which helped it expand its physical footprint in 2013. It received further HUD funding, over half a million dollars, between 2017 and 2019 as well as at least $50,000 from the State Department between 2016 and 2017, according to annual reports published by the museum.

Dearborn, where about 54.5% of residents are of Middle Eastern or North African descent, is a key political center in Michigan ahead of one of the country’s most competitive Senate races this year. Socialist-aligned Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the Senate, drew strong support from the city earlier this month.

The museum’s focus extends beyond its criticism of the U.S. response to 9/11.

On Sept. 10 — the eve of the 25th anniversary of the attacks — the AANM is scheduled to host a screening of "Seeds for Liberation," a film that portrays Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack as part of a decades-long Palestinian "struggle" and places it within a broader history of "anti-imperialist and decolonial movements."

During Fox News Digital’s visit earlier this month, a section of the museum was dedicated to art criticizing Israel's alleged "occupation" of Palestinian land. One piece of art, the word "wall" presented in a stylized print, accuses the Israeli government of perpetuating a system of "apartheid."

The art installation broadly accuses Israel of targeting civilians in military operations, denying basic necessities to Palestinians and unjustly occupying land.

FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM

One placard accompanying a sculpture states that Israel has killed more than 2,000 Palestinian children since Sept. 29, 2000, citing If Americans Knew (IAK).

The placard’s sourcing is itself controversial. Some pro-Palestinian organizations have distanced themselves from IAK over allegations of antisemitism and ties to white supremacists, allegations the group has disputed. IAK also operates a news site that has published articles rejecting the designation of Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Another placard attached to a sculpture pulls a quote from Defense of Children International Palestine, which the Israeli government designated as a terrorist organization in 2021. DCIP and human rights groups have disputed the designation.

The museum gift shop also sells Palestinian-themed merchandise, including map-shaped magnets and key chains, coloring books promising to help children "explore Palestinian heritage" and keffiyehs.

IN CHARTS: A VISUAL BREAKDOWN OF THE SMITHSONIAN'S BILLION-DOLLAR TAXPAYER-FUNDED BUDGET

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The AANM, Smithsonian, NEA and NEH did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital on Friday.

Smithsonian affiliates, like the AANM, are independently operated museums that maintain formal partnerships with the Smithsonian, providing them with access to artifact loans, educational resources and consultations from institutional experts.

In recent months, the Smithsonian has faced mounting pressure from Republican lawmakers and the president over allegations that its museums advance left-of-center ideological causes through their exhibits. Officials have threatened funding cuts against the institution if it does not root out what the Trump administration characterizes as anti-American bias.

World.title: GLP-1 boom could reshape restaurant bars as diners cut back on alcohol
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could be changing more than what Americans put on their plates, as restaurants increasingly look to wellness drinks and other alternatives to traditional alcoholic beverages.

The National Restaurant Association's new 2026 Restaurant Beverage Trends report found growing interest in a wider range of drink choices, particularly among younger consumers, as restaurants experiment with everything from wellness and energy drinks to smoothies, lemonades and alcohol-free cocktails.

Chad Moutray, chief economist at the Washington, D.C.-based National Restaurant Association, told Fox News Digital that the growing use of GLP-1 medications is one of several health trends restaurant operators are watching.

MOVER OVER, APEROL: VIRAL ITALIAN SPRITZ ARRIVES IN US WITH EYE-CATCHING TWIST

The report, which was conducted by the National Restaurant Association and is based on surveys of consumers and restaurant operators across the country, found that health is already influencing some Americans' decisions about alcohol.

Among adults surveyed who said they don't drink alcohol, 25% cited health reasons. That figure climbed to 34% among Gen Z nondrinkers.

Several trends are converging as younger consumers become more health-conscious and GLP-1 medications become more widely used, Moutray said.

"I think you're seeing a lot younger folks who are, in general, wanting to be healthier. You have the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is also driving some of this trend," he said.

PROTEIN COFFEE IS EXPLODING IN POPULARITY AMONG ADULTS WORRIED ABOUT MUSCLE LOSS

"You have people drinking energy drinks and health drinks and all those things. And then you add to that the GLP-1 notion, where if you're taking one of those drugs and your appetite is more suppressed, you're not going to drink as much alcohol."

Restaurants are already preparing to broaden their drink selections.

Among limited-service restaurant operators, 24% said they planned to add new wellness drinks in 2026, while 26% planned to add energy drinks, 29% smoothies and 27% lemonades.

Just under half, 46%, planned to add new coffee offerings.

"I think as GLP-1s become less expensive as this year goes on and as we move into 2027, you're going to see restaurant operators continuing to look for alternatives that can be good menu options for consumers that might be taking those drugs," Moutray said.

CLICK HERE TO 

Derek Brown, a hospitality consultant and founder of Drink Company, said he's also seeing GLP-1s contribute to a broader shift toward moderation.

"Yeah, there's no doubt that GLP-1s are having an effect on the way that people consume," Brown told Fox News Digital. "And it's part of a basket of things that's contributing to people moderating more often."

The drugs can affect people's appetites for both food and drinks, Brown said, potentially leading some customers to consume less alcohol or choose nonalcoholic alternatives.

"I think that's clearly part of this entire moderation trend that we're seeing that's just a part of it, but it's significant enough, so I think that's certainly a real thing," Brown said. "And I definitely think that bars and restaurants are starting to feel that."

The changing beverage landscape, however, doesn't necessarily mean younger Americans are abandoning alcohol.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Per the report, 71% of Gen Z adults and 74% of millennials surveyed said they drink alcohol either at home or at restaurants. Sixty percent of Gen Z adults and 68% of millennials said they drink alcohol at restaurants.

Moutray believes younger consumers are instead choosing from a broader portfolio of drinks.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

That broader selection could be increasingly important for restaurants. The report found that 87% of full-service operators and 80% of limited-service operators said beverages can be an important driver of customer traffic.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's driving traffic, it's getting people excited and it's, hopefully, also helping to improve overall profit margins," Moutray said.

World.title: Blue state's water failures could threaten food supplies across US, lawmaker warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

California's aging infrastructure is helping fuel a clean water crisis that could have ramifications across the country, a key House Republican warned.

Rep. Harriet Hageman, R-Wyo., accused California Gov. Gavin Newsom of playing politics with the management of the Colorado River, a major body of water that millions of people in the Western United States depend on. She's arguing that the Golden State's bloated bureaucracy and environmental regulations are making it more reliant on the Colorado River, thus stressing its supply and affecting the other six states through which it runs.

"The system is now becoming very, very stressed because California has not kept up with the infrastructure demands and needs of its citizens," Hageman told Fox News Digital. "Pinedale, Wyoming, may be a long way removed from Southern California, but when there are calls on the river and when there are demands that we reduce the amount of water that we are able to use in order to meet a demand downstream, that isn't fair."

California's water infrastructure has largely remained unchanged since the late 20th century, despite a ballooning population.

COLORADO SMALL TOWN ABANDONED AFTER ALL ELECTED OFFICIALS RESIGN, WATER CONCERNS GROW

Hageman argued that California's growing need paired with a lack of new infrastructure is hurting the agricultural sector in areas that rely on the Colorado River — which could have ripple effects beyond the West.

TRUMP CAN PROTECT CALIFORNIA AVOCADO FARMERS AND TAKE A BITE OUT OF MEXICAN CARTELS, TOO

"California could grow almost all the food we need in the United States, but they've really decimated their Ag industry because they've taken irrigation water away from their Ag industry to try to meet municipal demand and industrial demand elsewhere. So really it's just, it's a whole parade of bad decisions that are being made," she said.

"Food independence is a national security issue. We do not want to become food dependent on Mexico or Central America or bringing all of our food in from other countries. We have the resources to grow healthy, high-quality food right here while also protecting our environment."

Environmental groups like Tell the Dam Truth have opposed new dam builds in California, arguing they contribute to climate change while harming biodiversity.

"With its strong environmental laws, regulations, and policies, California has the opportunity to not only stop new dam construction, but also decommission dams to restore the biodiversity and carbon sequestration currently inundated in river valleys across the state," the group's website states.

Groups like the Sierra Club have also opposed desalination, an alternative water source that would require California to convert its abundant saltwater into a usable product.

But Hageman said that opposition was misguided.

"They're very backwards people. I kind of look at them like flat-Earthers. They're very backwards people in the way that they approach things. They ignore the fact that humans are also part of the natural environment, and they ignore the benefits of what we can create by building this much-needed infrastructure," she said.

The Colorado River's Upper Basin runs through Colorado, Wyoming, New Mexico and Utah. The Lower Basin runs through California, Arizona and Nevada.

TRUMP TO SHRINK 2 UTAH NATIONAL MONUMENTS BY 90%

It has faced growing problems, in part due to climate change and increased dependence, prompting discussions about whether the seven aforementioned states could update their existing water-sharing agreement.

A failure to do so thus far has prompted the Trump administration to step in and force steep cuts to the Lower Basin states for the next two years.

NEWSOM, WALZ URGE CONGRESS TO BLOCK ANTI-CLIMATE BILL IN THEIR ‘WOKE’ CRUSADE

Newsom praised the plan while pointing out California has reduced its use in recent years, but said it was only a "short-term" solution.

"This is a necessary step to protect a river that 40 million Americans depend on, at a time when climate change is driving a regional water crisis that makes every drop of water count. California continues to lead the way forward, growing our economy while cutting our Colorado River water use to the lowest level since 1949," he said of the Trump administration order. "Any long-term solution must share responsibility fairly across all seven states in recognition of the new reality of the Colorado River."

California also recently made plans for a new reservoir project, projected to cost $6.8 billion, which is expected to be completed in the mid-2030s. The state is also investing in new groundwater infrastructure and other initiatives to expand availability of the critical resource.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A spokesperson for the California Natural Resources Agency re-emphasized the state's reduced dependency on the Colorado River when reached by Fox News Digital.

"California’s Colorado River use is at its lowest since 1949 – and our urban water agencies have reduced their demand for imports by 50% since 2000. Even with that, we continue to invest billions of dollars to increase water supply as we face changing conditions driven by climate change," the spokesperson said.

"Suggesting we move the world’s fourth largest economy entirely to desalinated water is a deeply unserious proposal that ignores the underlying issues facing all users of the Colorado River. All Basin states must share the responsibility of caring for the Colorado River for generations to come – and that means real conservation from all seven states."

World.title: Newsom's attack dog taunts Buttigieg over South Carolina visit as 2028 fight heats up
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The battle for the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential nomination is already spilling into public view, with a top aide to California Gov. Gavin Newsom taking a swipe at fellow White House hopeful Pete Buttigieg over his effort to build support with Black voters in the South.

Newsom communications director Izzy Gardon mocked Buttigieg's recent visit to South Carolina, which his representative Aida Ross highlighted with a post on X over the weekend that included a photo of the former Transportation Secretary with members of the Orangeburg branch of the NAACP.

"Pete returned to Orangeburg, SC! Great night with the Orangeburg Branch of the NAACP," Ross said alongside the photo.

Meanwhile, Gardon responded to the post: "First time in SC in 3 years? Nice!"

JENNIFER SIEBEL NEWSOM DODGES QUESTION ON HUSBAND GAVIN'S PRESIDENTIAL ASPIRATIONS

The exchange garnered buzz online, as it placed two of the Democratic Party's most closely watched potential presidential contenders at the center of a growing fight over Black voter outreach—an issue likely to be central in 2028 as South Carolina again prepares to hold the party’s first nominating contest.

It also comes amid wider Democratic tensions over whether the party is doing enough to engage Black voters and the South, with Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens accusing the DNC of "abandoning the South" and "abandoning Black voters" after Atlanta was eliminated from 2028 convention contention last week.

Meanwhile, South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain declared last month, amid debate over the party’s presidential primary calendar, that "the South is not the past, it is the future," while Democratic chairs from five other southern states also previously warned the DNC against sending Black voters the message that their loyalty is "taken for granted," according to the Associated Press.

When reached for comment, Gardon told Fox News Digital that the post was made from his personal account and in his "personal capacity," calling it "simply my own observation." He stressed that he was "NOT speaking for the Governor or anyone else."

Ross did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

JASMINE CROCKETT WARNS DEMOCRATS ARE TOO FOCUSED ON WHITE VOTERS, IGNORING BLACK VOTERS

"Love to watch Gavin Newsom staffers dunk on Pete Buttigieg staffers as they all jostle to catch up to AOC in the 2028 Dem primaries," Republican strategist Matt Whitlock wrote on X.

"We’re just dropping all pretenses huh," quipped political polling executive Adam Carlson.

Democrat strategists also weighed in on the in-fighting.

"Staffers of potential 2028ers who denigrate other potential 2028ers at this juncture should be embarrassed. They reflect extremely poorly on their principals," Democrat strategist Jennifer Holdsworth said in response to Gardon's jab.

"Weird tweet to send rn - bad look," Democratic consultant Eric Koch said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Potential 2028 staffers, huddle up: you do not want to start the fighting now or on this platform," added the Head of Digital Engagement at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Stefan Smith. "It’s too early in the cycle. The longer we play nice (and encourage the principals to play nice) the better it is for everyone."

World.title: Prince William ‘blindsided’ by Harry, Meghan return as Kate fears new turmoil from royal feud: experts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s surprise decision to return to the U.K. with their children.

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales are "concerned" about the Duke and Duchess of Sussex returning for an extended period beginning this month. Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are set to begin school there in September, People magazine reported.

"Prince William was blindsided," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

"He had found Harry’s recent eagerness to publicly signal that he wanted to spend more time in Britain unusual, but that is very different from anticipating a full return. William now has to navigate a situation he did not create, did not ask for and, given the state of their relationship, almost certainly would not have chosen."

Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment.

In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."

The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that the Waleses are "feeling uneasy" about facing another chapter in the "endless Sussex soap opera."

WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

"It’s about broken trust," Chard explained. "Prince William is said to feel that Harry and Meghan have spent years attacking the institution, then monetizing their grievances through a very lucrative media operation. From his view, it’s an ongoing campaign for maximum impact and self-gain. He’s not going to fuel it, and he’s not going to endorse behavior he sees as damaging."

William and Kate were seen arriving in Scotland on Thursday, where they’ll spend time with King Charles at Balmoral Castle. The royal family has spent summers at the Scottish estate since the reign of Queen Victoria, with family members traditionally hunting, fishing and horseback riding there.

The king learned about Harry and Meghan’s move three days before it was made public, according to reports.

"Prince William, along with Catherine, is currently at Balmoral Castle visiting the king," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "Harry and Meghan have, so far, not been invited to visit the king privately while on a holiday. This will not happen while William is there. I’ve been told he has no desire to connect on any level with his younger brother and simply has no time for [Meghan]."

Fox News Digital reached out to Archewell, which handles the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, for comment.

The Daily Mail reported that the king and his heir held a "Sussex Summit" following the announcement. A source told the outlet that the Prince and Princess of Wales "have no interest in engaging with anything Harry and Meghan do or say."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Things are projected to be tense at Balmoral," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "... Princess Catherine is particularly guarded given how deeply hurt she was by both of them. Both she and Prince William are very determined to maintain their own family stability and remain focused on duty with their royal roles paramount."

Several royal experts previously told Fox News Digital that William and Harry haven’t been on speaking terms since at least 2022.

"My sources have described genuine concern within the Wales camp," Schofield said. "I don’t think Prince William and Princess Catherine are sitting at Balmoral panicking about Harry and Meghan returning, but they are understandably apprehensive about what their return could bring. The last several years have taught them that private family tensions have a habit of becoming very public."

"The concern isn’t simply that Harry and Meghan will be geographically closer," Schofield continued. "It’s the unpredictability that comes with the Sussexes. There have been interviews, books, documentaries and very personal allegations about members of the royal family. … My sources tell me the Wales camp has not forgotten the hostility directed at them after some of Harry and Meghan’s previous public accusations."

Schofield said unnamed sources told her Kate is also unsettled by the news.

"My sources tell me that Catherine does not want to revisit that chapter of her life," Schofield explained. "She has endured very personal allegations, an enormous amount of public scrutiny and a difficult few years. My understanding has always been that her priority is Prince William, their children and the future."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Meghan returning to Britain doesn’t mean Catherine suddenly has an obligation to reopen a relationship that has caused considerable hurt," she said. "Catherine can wish Harry and Meghan well without wanting them back inside her private life. ... The idea of resurrecting the ‘Fab Four’ is fantasy. Too much has happened, and too much has been lost."

The Sussexes are expected to live at a private, nonroyal residence outside London, The Associated Press reported. They won’t resume their royal duties, which they gave up in 2020.

The couple’s return to the U.K. comes as the king continues treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer diagnosed in 2024. In 2025, Harry said he didn’t know "how much longer my father has" and expressed a desire for his children to get to know their grandfather.

Last month, the king met with Harry, Meghan and their children at Highgrove House.

Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported at the time that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place."

"The Sussexes played a blinder with the king welcoming them, having not told him last month of a plan they have had for ages as their children will soon be in school," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital.

The move is understood to have come together relatively quickly, as Harry and Meghan waited to learn whether their children had been accepted to the private school they applied to.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Since the brothers haven’t spoken in years, the imminent arrival of the Sussexes places William and Catherine in a pressured and difficult situation," said Fitzwilliams. "William is reportedly furious. But what is essential is that the king accepts that the Waleses and their children are the future of the monarchy."

Schofield doesn’t believe reconciliation between the brothers is likely, at least anytime soon.

"Geography cannot repair a relationship where trust has been so badly damaged," she said. "Harry’s return could make that estrangement more obvious because people will inevitably ask why two brothers living in the same country still aren’t seeing one another. ... William and Catherine could suddenly find themselves under public pressure to perform a reconciliation that probably doesn’t exist behind closed doors."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"... William may have reached the conclusion that distance is healthier than reconciliation, and he is entitled to make that decision," Schofield said. "The realistic goal at this stage probably isn’t friendship [with Harry]. I would argue it’s peaceful coexistence for the sake of their father. ... Harry and Meghan moving back to Britain creates proximity, not reconciliation. They can buy a house near London. They cannot buy back trust."

World.title: Charlotte man accused of mass shooting threats at 5 schools released days before classes begin
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Charlotte man indicted on five felony counts accusing him of threatening mass shootings against five area public schools was released from jail just three days before students were scheduled to return to class.

Drew Andres Owens, 33, was released from the Mecklenburg County Jail at 11:30 a.m. on Aug. 22, according to jail records. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools students were scheduled to return on Aug. 25.

A Mecklenburg County grand jury indicted Owens in March 2025 on five counts of communicating threats of mass violence on educational property. He has pleaded not guilty, and the cases remain pending.

THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN

Four counts allege Owens sent emails on Feb. 15, 2025, threatening West Charlotte High School, Ardrey Kell High School, Community House Middle School and Hawk Ridge Elementary School.

According to court documents reviewed by Fox News Digital, Owens allegedly sent messages threatening to "slaughter staff and students."

World.title: BRUCE PEARL: Conservatives are attacking the very college sports bill that protects women
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Men don’t belong in women’s sports. That isn’t complicated, but some conservative influencers and interest groups are allowing it to become complicated through careless claims about legislation designed to protect college athletics.

I spent nearly five decades coaching college basketball. I know the difference between winning a possession and winning the game. Conservatives now face a similar choice: We can chase applause by attacking allies and mischaracterizing the bill, or we can unite around the facts and win the larger fight for women, fairness and the future of college sports.

Some organizations and women’s-sports advocates claim the Protect College Sports Act would "gut" Title IX or invalidate state laws that reserve women’s teams for women. They are wrong. The text says the opposite.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: COLLEGE SPORTS BILL ENTERS LEGISLATIVE 'RED ZONE' AS SEASON KICKS OFF

Section 127 explicitly states that nothing in the bill will "override, modify, or amend" Title IX. Female athletes would retain their current legal protections and ability to bring sex-discrimination claims. Section 120 also protects athletes, employees and others from retaliation for reporting discrimination or participating in Title IX proceedings.

I spent nearly five decades coaching college basketball. I know the difference between winning a possession and winning the game. Conservatives now face a similar choice: We can chase applause by attacking allies and mischaracterizing the bill, or we can unite around the facts.

Critics also claim the bill would erase state laws keeping men out of women’s sports. It would not. The legislation establishes national standards for Division I and Division II competition on limited eligibility questions, including academics, professional status, legal violations, age and years of eligibility. It neither creates a federal right for men to enter women’s competitions nor pre-empts state laws establishing sex-based athletic categories.

REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS

The bill does not expressly create a federal right for biological males to compete in women’s sports, and Section 127 states that nothing in the bill overrides, modifies or amends Title IX. Critics seem to be grasping at anything and eager to disregard the Title IX provisions here. Especially since the Supreme Court ruled in June that schools may keep men out of women’s sports.

It also requires governing bodies to enforce rules related to state and federal law and allows individuals to sue when the law is violated.

CONGRESS MUST FIX THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE GIRLS PAY THE PRICE

The bill also gives schools a powerful incentive to invest in women’s and Olympic sports. It creates a $22.5 million athlete-retention fund and allows schools to unlock up to an additional $5 million through eligible NIL investments in women’s, Olympic and non-revenue sports. A school seeking the full $27.5 million retention allowance would first need to invest $5 million in those sports. That is an ingenious way to ensure continued investment in programs that might otherwise be left behind.

And every year Congress waits, the financial pressure on college athletics grows, and the programs with the fewest resources become even more vulnerable. My 2025 Final Four team had a total NIL budget of approximately $4 million. By the 2027 Final Four, some teams could be operating with budgets approaching $30 million.

Conservatives should debate legislation, demand improvements and scrutinize every line. But facts must guide us. Too many Washington organizations would rather score points against perceived rivals than secure lasting victories for women and college athletes.

CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION

Outrage is easy; turning shared principles into law is harder. Infighting only helps the left, which has spent years undermining Title IX while conservatives battle over legislation that expressly preserves it. If we can’t unite and get this done, we will lose college sports as we know them, and women’s and Olympic sports will continue to be among the first casualties.

The stakes extend beyond Title IX, and the crisis is no longer theoretical. Thirty-two Division I Olympic-sports programs were cut between the announcement of the House settlement and May 2025. WRAL reported that more than 40 Division I Olympic-sports programs were cut between May 2024 and July 2025, even though 75% of American Olympians in 2024 competed in collegiate athletics. NCAA data

Even the University of Arkansas, backed by SEC resources, announced plans to eliminate its tennis programs before donors intervened to save them. If programs at schools like Arkansas are vulnerable, imagine the danger facing smaller schools, women’s teams and non-revenue sports nationwide.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Credit where credit is due: Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., and others have stepped up to move this legislation forward. President Trump has also led from the front by restoring the biological meaning of sex in federal policy, taking action to save college sports and backing this bill. Now, those who claim to support the America First movement should get in the game, help Congress finish the job and deliver this win for women and college athletes.

Congress now has the opportunity to take important steps to stabilize college sports, support educational opportunities for young women and men, and provide protections for the uniquely American experience of intercollegiate athletics.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There is broad agreement that college sports cannot go on with no meaningful guardrails around eligibility, transfer policy and NIL oversight. The Protect College Sports Act is an important step in the right direction, and Congress needs to keep the positive momentum moving forward.

Winning the point may feel good. Winning the war matters more.

World.title: ‘Perfectly fine with my body’: Danish PM blasts plastic surgeon’s beauty advice
World.content:
COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is fed up with getting unsolicited beauty advice.

The 48-year-old wrote Monday on Instagram that she had just returned back home from a trip to Ukraine, where she was exposed to air raid sirens in the ongoing war, only to find a message by a plastic surgeon offering her to “fix that little spot on your nose.”

“I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” Frederiksen wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.”

The prime minister of the Nordic country posted a screen shot of the plastic surgeon’s offer on Instagram but without identifying him.

She also posted her response: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body — I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!”

Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, is now in her third term, making her one of Europe’s longest-serving and most experienced leaders. She has led the European Union and NATO member country since mid-2019.

She has pledged to maintain a firm stance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions for Greenland, the kingdom’s semiautonomous territory, and continue supporting Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression.

On Instagram, Frederiksen stressed that she does not interfere with other people’s looks and that “I’m perfectly fine with my body — as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.”

She added that “if you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful. Not my nose.”

The prime minister also said that those unsolicited beauty tips and suggestions made her feel “indignant” and that “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”

World.title: Multiple dead, including children, in Montana shooting and house fire
World.content:
Multiple people, including children, died when a gunman opened fire at a Billings, Montana, home that was then set alight, authorities said Monday.

Police characterized the incident Sunday evening near the city’s West End neighborhood as a family disturbance. The gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot, NBC affiliate KULR of Billings reported.

Interim Yellowstone County Sheriff Kent O’Donnell said at a news conference Monday that “multiple adults and multiple juveniles” died at the residence.

The dead have been identified, he said, but the number of those killed, their names and their ages will not be released for now.

“Because of the fire and obviously water that goes to suppress that fire, it’s going to slow our investigation of the crime scene recovery of evidence,” he said. “So we ask for patience as we complete this investigation.”

A possible motive was not available Monday.

Billings police and county sheriff’s deputies were dispatched to the shooting in the 300 block of White Star Circle at 6:01 p.m. Sunday, Billings police said on Facebook. O’Donnell said gunshots could be heard during the 911 call.

Officers and deputies reached the scene in roughly 10 minutes and at that point heard gunfire from the back of the residence, the police department said.

Three minutes later, the home was fully engulfed in flames, it said.

Video from the scene showed law enforcement officers taking cover behind patrol SUVs on the street near the home as a small tactical team behind a handheld shield moved toward the structure.

Firefighters were dispatched but may have faced water access issues and fewer fire hydrants than might be ideal, officials said.

“The delay in limited access presented significant challenges, fire conditions continued to worsen, and the residents ultimately became ... consumed by fire,” Billings Fire Chief Matt Hoppel said at Monday’s news conference.

The origin of the blaze was also under investigation.

Billings Police Sgt. Jeff Stovall said in a statement Monday that some information was being withheld “to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation.”

“There are details we simply cannot release at this time,” he said.

World.title: ‘Getting no help’: Thousands in Gary, Indiana, still without power nearly 2 weeks after storms
World.content:
GARY, Ind. — The power outages caused by storms that roared through the region nearly two weeks ago have one resident of this Rust Belt city literally gasping for air.

Joetta Walker, who is 73 and has asthma, uses a nebulizer to help her breathe. But right now it’s a useless piece of machinery, and she has had to rely on an inhaler to survive.

“I have a nebulizer where I need to take breathing treatments,” Walker said in an interview at her sweltering home. “I can’t do that without the electricity.”

Lifelong Gary, Ind., resident Joetta Walker, 73, holds her nebulizer. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Walker said the inhaler doesn’t give her the same level of relief.

“I wheeze,” Walker said and demonstrated. “You hear it now because I get too hot.”

No other place in Indiana has suffered more as a result of those Aug. 11 storms than this mostly Black city on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, best known as the hometown of Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5.

As of Monday, more than 8,600 customers were still waiting for their power to be restored, most of them in Gary, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) reported on its website.

Mayor Eddie Melton said he spoke with President Donald Trump and told him “explicitly that we needed help, that we needed resources.”

Melton said he asked Trump to sign an executive order “and move this thing forward so folks can start getting back to work and we start restoring Gary back to normal.”

“He said that he was going to do all that he can,” Melton said.

Melton said he also met with Republican Sen. Jim Banks. He hopes power for residents will be fully restored by Tuesday.

“I believe a good chunk of that will be restored today, and hopefully 100% will be restored tomorrow,” he said.

Melton’s hopeful forecast came a day after he ripped NIPSCO for failing to completely restore electricity to his city.

“Twelve days is too long for families to be without power,” he said Sunday in an address posted on the city’s Facebook page. “I have made it clear the current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

Tree Care workers from Michigan remove a tree from the front of a home in Gary on Thursday after it was toppled during a recent storm. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In an email Monday, NIPSCO, the Merrillville, Indiana-based utility provider that supplies natural gas and electricity to over 1.3 million residential and commercial customers across the northern third of the state, said it’s “focused on safely restoring power to all customers in every affected community.”

On its website, it said it expects to restore power to all of its customers in Gary by Tuesday.

Walker said that can’t happen too soon. She said she has been relying on her nieces to bring her food and charge up her cellphone twice a day. She said she has $750 worth of pork chops, spiral hams and other foods rotting in her nonfunctioning freezer and refrigerator.

“All gone, gone,” she said.

At night, Walker said, she gets around the house by candlelight.

Walker stands in front of her empty fridge, where, she says, more than $700 worth of food has spoiled. Selina Guevara / NBC News

“I feel hurt ... because I feel like they can do better than this,” she said of the power company. “But I also understand how much damage was done, and I also understand the workers have to be tired.”

Another Gary resident, Dion Thomas, 40, said Monday was the first time he’d seen power crews in his neighborhood. But they seemed to be struggling to turn the electricity back on.

“Some people’s stuff was coming on, then it went back out,” he said.

In the meantime, people have been heading to parks to cook whatever food they have left over charcoal and eat it before it spoils, said Thomas, a father of three.

“It’s been crazy,” he said.

Since the power went out, there has been a spate of generator thefts in his neighborhood, said Calvin Boone, 44, a father of four.

“The kids running around, they stealing people’s generators right now,” Boone said. “I think about the older people, the health for them.”

Boone said that everybody has been feeling hot and miserable and that some have taken to sleeping in their cars with the engines on and the air conditioners blasting.

“We ain’t getting no help,” he said.

Channie Weaver got her power back overnight. But it was too late to save the food in her fridge. She said she’d gone shopping right before the storms hit and estimates she lost $300 worth of provisions.

“All the food is gone. We about to go out and get something out to eat,” said Weaver, 50.

Channie Weaver, 50, of Gary. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Weaver said she lives with her 22-year-old daughter, Desaray Weaver, and her granddaughters, Raelynn, 2, and Riley, 1.

“Man, it’s been rough,” Weaver said. “Being hot in the house, no air conditioning, plus my daughter — she’s pregnant. But it’s definitely been rough.”

Weaver and other Gary residents said in interviews that they can’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power is getting restored last is that it’s a mostly Black city.

“I feel like we at the bottom before everybody else,” she said.

Shaquille Brewster and Selina Guevara reported from Gary and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

World.title: Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into a key challenge for Sen. Darline Graham ahead of the South Carolina runoff. Plus, Allan Smith breaks down the shifting political landscape around data centers.

— Adam Wollner

Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. — On Friday, a South Carolina Republican voter named Roger showed up to a Donald Trump and Darline Graham rally wearing a “DARK MAGA” T-shirt. He arrived early and waited hours to see the president speak.

But Trump’s endorsement wasn’t enough to convince him to vote for Graham in Tuesday’s high-stakes GOP runoff. Graham’s recent debate performance affected his perceptions after she said that “national security is not my thing” when asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are U.S. national security issues.

“Her people should have briefed her a little bit more,” he said. “Foreign policy is something that — you’re going to come in as a new senator, as a rookie, you’re gonna have to learn that.”

Glenda Clinkscales, who said she “loves Trump” and was “excited” to see him, didn’t harbor the same feelings for Graham. Like Roger, she was undecided.

“Some good answers and some not so good answers,” she said when asked what she made of Graham’s debate performance. “I’m not so sure about her right now.”

The hesitation by the two Trump supporters casts a cloud over Graham’s prospects for a six-year term as she faces five-term Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C.

Another voter, Daniel Musick of Myrtle Beach, labeled Trump “the best president we’ve ever had.” He had made up his mind for Norman even before watching Trump and Graham at the rally.

“It’s just that she’s untested. I don’t know enough about her,” he said, adding that “part of the reason” for his opposition to Graham is her debate moment. “Her answer on foreign affairs, when it came to China and Taiwan — it was really unclear that she knew her foreign policy, and to me that was the biggest issue.”

Norman has sought to capitalize on her debate blunder, but it’s not clear he is on the path to victory. Norman is 73, at a time when age is an issue for voters, and has been accused by Graham’s team of being insufficiently loyal to Trump as a member of the House Freedom Caucus that seeks to push his agenda to the right.

Graham, 62, has defended her debate moment by saying voters in South Carolina aren’t asking her about China and Taiwan.

“Now the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said at Friday’s rally with Trump. “And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job.”

Trump, for his part, said Graham was just “being honest” in the debate.

“I mean, she’s going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump told reporters Friday before the rally.

To other GOP voters who attended Friday’s event, Trump’s support was enough.

“Honestly, I don’t know as much about the platforms there, but if Trump supports her, I do too,” said Lynn Spivey, who was wearing a Darline Graham sticker.

Patrick Maguire contributed.

📱Related: MAGA Inc., the super PAC tied to Trump, has spent $830,000 on text messages and voter phone calls to boost Graham, Bridget Bowman reports.

Republicans wrestle with data center backlash as Trump promotes the benefits

By Allan Smith

As recently as last month, Republicans in some of this fall’s biggest races publicly expressed skepticism about the growing backlash to data center development.

A lot has changed since then. On Thursday, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, announced support for a one-year moratorium on data center development. In Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, Republican nominees for governor cut ads hitting their Democratic rivals for being too open to the projects.

Earlier this month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who had welcomed the developments to his state and faces re-election this fall, ordered an audit of data center projects in the state before any more can advance. And in Ohio, GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy released a plan stating that any future data center built in the state must pay the electricity bills and property taxes for nearby residents, adding that he will sign an executive order pausing development until such a plan is enacted into law.

Meanwhile, the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote a memo last week for data center industry leaders detailing how in Ohio’s Senate race, the issue is single-handedly tearing down Republican Sen. Jon Husted as his Democratic rival, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, spends millions on anti-data center ads.

Data centers are one of the few issues in American politics that don’t fall along neat ideological lines. Both parties are rapidly trying to figure out what approach works best for them at the national, state and local levels. Democrats, including some who previously offered the industry a warm embrace, are similarly positioning to be seen as champions for data center accountability and tightly regulated growth as progressives angle for state and federal moratoriums on their development.

But the challenge is equally, if not more, daunting for Republicans, who have worked to build stronger relationships with tech leaders after they gravitated to President Donald Trump during his last presidential bid. And they’re campaigning as Trump himself has promoted the benefits of data center development needed to power the growth of AI.

World.title: Supreme Court hands preliminary win to Trump on mail-in ballots executive order
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration Monday in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

At issue are provisions that seek to create a federal list of eligible voters and order the U.S. Postal Service to deliver ballots only to those people.

The justices, divided 6-3 along ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, lifted an injunction a Massachusetts-based judge imposed in June that prevented key aspects of the executive order from going into effect this year in California and 22 other states that had challenged it.

The court also granted a similar application filed by Alabama and 11 other states.

The White House praised the court’s ruling, calling the executive order’s provisions “commonsense measures.”

“This Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement.

U.S. Postal Service headquarters in Washington. Erin Scott / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

Parts of the same executive order are blocked nationwide because of a ruling the same judge issued later in a different case, but the Supreme Court decision is likely to apply to that ruling, too.

That means the administration may, at least in the short term, be able to implement the executive order, but the legal battle is far from over.

“This decision is a painful setback, but it will not be the final word,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was among those who challenged the proposal, said in a statement.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, said Monday night that his state will launch a new challenge to the Trump administration’s policy on mail-in voting.

“Following today’s SCOTUS ruling, California WILL SUE again to BLOCK Trump’s attack on mail-in voting!” Newsom said on X. “Every eligible voter gets a mail-in ballot here — and we’ll fight to keep it that way.”

President Donald Trump has frequently railed against the widespread use of mail-in ballots as part of his broader complaints, offered without evidence, that the election system is plagued with fraud.

His efforts to encourage Congress to pass his SAVE America Act legislation that would impose new voting restrictions nationwide, including proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter ID, have so far failed.

Election workers process mail-in ballots at San Francisco County's election operations facility at City Hall in San Francisco in June. David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

The Supreme Court decision is provisional, focusing only on the argument that U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani acted prematurely in preventing the provisions from being implemented in the 23 states before federal agencies had even drawn up plans for how to implement the executive order.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned ruling.

The decision leaves the door open to judges’ intervening later, especially with regard to any restrictions imposed for the coming midterm elections. On Friday, while the case was pending, the Postal Service issued its final regulation that would enforce parts of the executive order.

The dissenters were the three liberal justices on the conservative-majority court.

“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with states’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful. Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives. Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote.

In a separate dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson accused the majority of “taking its eye off the ball” by focusing on a technical legal argument instead of what she views as the larger goal of the Trump administration: “to secure our imprimatur for its effort to foment chaos ahead of the November elections.”

The Trump administration told the Supreme Court the new regulations did not go as far as the executive order anticipated, saying the Postal Service “will not refuse to transmit ballots” even if senders are not on a state list of registered voters.

The Supreme Court decision is in line with one in a related case by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that rejected a separate attempt by Democrats to block the executive order.

Lower courts declined to put the Massachusetts ruling on hold, leading the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the filing that it was premature for courts to rule on the issue, as neither the Postal Service nor other agencies have determined how they will implement the executive order. It would be a tall order for the chronically underfunded Postal Service, with just months to go before Election Day.

World.title: Massachusetts woman wanted in police officer husband’s death believed to be dead
World.content:
Karen Solomon, a Massachusetts mental health advocate for law enforcement who was being sought in connection with the death of her police officer husband, appears to have been found dead Monday, ending a multiday search.

Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier told reporters Monday that a body officials believed to be Solomon’s was found in a wooded area near a gun. Authorities are awaiting confirmation of her identity.

Karen Solomon. Worcester Police Department

Investigators believe the deaths of Karen and Kurt Solomon, an officer with the department who was found dead on Aug. 18 at the couple’s home in Worcester, west of Boston, were the result of a murder-suicide, Saucier said.

In a statement read by Saucier, the Solomon family described the events of the last week as a “nightmare” that “has left our family heartbroken and rudderless. The compassion, dedication, and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness.”

“For those in Massachusetts and throughout the world who have offered up prayers and sympathies, they have helped us through each minute of the day,” the statement added. “Thank you for your basic human compassion.”

The search for Solomon began Tuesday after Kurt Solomon’s body was discovered. He was off duty at the time. Police had been called to the residence about 5:30 a.m. following a report of a person down.

Multiple agencies, including the U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations, assisted in the search. Saucier had said Karen Solomon should be considered armed and dangerous.

For years, she had advocated for the mental health of police officers and their families through First H.E.L.P., an organization she co-founded. She wrote two books. “Hearts Beneath the Badge” is about the experiences of law enforcement and their families, and “The Price They Pay” is about the emotional and physical effects of traumatic events on officers.

Karen Solomon. Worcester Police Department

She also wrote articles about law enforcement suicide, according to a biography on her organization’s website, and participated in a 2020 Justice Department hearing of the President’s Commission on Law Enforcement and the Administration of Justice, where she testified on a panel focused on support for officers and their families.

Kurt Solomon was a patrol officer with the Worcester Police Department for more than 30 years and was nearing retirement, Worcester police union leader Thomas Duffy III said.

Authorities have not said how Kurt Solomon died, but they described his death as “an act of domestic violence.” Saucier said at Monday’s news conference that there was no history of domestic abuse in the family.

World.title: South Carolina Senate race heads to runoff today
World.content:
South Carolina Republicans will decide Tuesday who will replace Sen. Lindsey Graham on the ballot in November's midterm election, after a rushed campaign in the wake of his sudden death in July.

Graham's sister, Sen. Darline Graham, faces Rep. Ralph Norman in Tuesday's runoff vote. The two candidates were the top two vote-getters in the special primary election on Aug. 11, with Darline Graham getting nearly 33% of the vote to Norman's almost 25%, after neither won 50% of the vote.

The runoff contest comes after Darline Graham was appointed to serve out the remainder of her late brother's term, which ends early next year. The four-term senator had been seeking reelection, and had already won the Republican primary in June.

The winner of Tuesday's runoff will take on Dr. Annie Andrews, who won the Democratic primary in June. Although the South Carolina Senate race is usually a fundraising boon to Democrats, the state remains solidly Republican and has just one Democratic representative in Congress.

President Trump, who had been close with Lindsey Graham, has thrown his support behind Darline Graham. He campaigned for her in South Carolina last week and held a tele-rally for her on Monday.

Darline Graham, who has no prior experience in elected office, has also garnered the support of South Carolina's other senator, GOP Sen. Tim Scott, who said after her first few weeks in the Senate and her first-place finish in the primary that he's "confident she's the real deal."

The newly minted senator has billed herself as "a problem solver, a critical thinker, and a leader," with decades of experience working for South Carolina. Darline Graham, 62, most recently served as commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind. She has focused on domestic issues during the brief campaign, and her lack of a foreign policy background has raised some questions about her preparedness.

In a debate last week, Graham conceded that she's inexperienced in some regards, most notably when she stumbled on a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea. She said she's "not that informed on national security," in a stark contrast to her brother, an outspoken foreign policy hawk.

"I'm not a polished politician," Graham said. "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

Graham had a close relationship with her brother, who never married or had children. She's cited their upbringing, where she and her brother observed their parents working long hours at their bar and liquor store in central South Carolina, for their shared work ethic. And as she's pledged to carry out her brother's legacy, she's also emphasized that she would chart her own path in the Senate, which could be more conservative than her brother's. During last week's debate, she quickly made her views on transgender athletes in sports, abortion and gun rights known.

Meanwhile, Norman, who has represented South Carolina in the House since 2017, has presented himself as an experienced legislator with a track record as a conservative fighter, while calling Graham an "unknown candidate."

The real estate developer and longtime member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus was one of a handful of Republicans to jump into the special primary race despite the president's endorsement of Darline Graham. And for Norman, who was one of only two House Republicans to back former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley in her bid to challenge Mr. Trump for the GOP nomination in 2024, it wasn't the first time he's been willing to break with the president.

Norman, 73, has the backing of Haley, who also served as ambassador to the U.N. during the first Trump administration, and called out Darline Graham's lack of experience after her debate performance.

"Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States' national security. Darline Graham admits she's not," Haley said on X. "This is not something you inherit. And it's critical in the U.S. Senate."

World.title: Trump and Kennedy's health industry deals are at risk of vanishing
World.content:
In the thick of his competitive reelection race in Michigan, Republican Rep. Tom Barrett joined Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at a sprawling 400-acre apple orchard, farm, and winery. They touted Trump administration efforts to improve the American diet, including the removal of some artificial dyes from processed foods.

"We had a great discussion about healthy options for all Americans and taking back control of our healthcare," Barrett said in a mid-June Instagram post, after sampling the farm's apple cider.

Like the focus on artificial dyes, however, many of the administration's highest-profile health initiatives rely on voluntary agreements. The goals, such as lower drug prices and nutrition classes for doctors, have widespread appeal, cutting across party lines and economic divisions.

But the administration-industry deals lack the enforcement teeth of more traditional federal regulation. Their details are vague, and minimal oversight makes it hard to monitor progress. In some cases, the administration has claimed victories that have yet to materialize.

Republicans consider the deal-making a winning strategy. It fits with the party's anti-regulatory stance, they say, and enables the administration to quickly forge agreements President Trump and his allies can tout as accomplishments. In the run-up to the midterm elections, some, like Barrett, hope to woo voters by trumpeting the Trump administration's efforts to shape health policy.

The practice also raises questions. Though the deals are announced with great fanfare — often during televised events on stages, with live audiences — there's little documentation or follow-through, creating doubts about whether the administration's health agenda will lead to lasting change or unravel once the political attention fades.

The distinction could prove important to voters as Republicans defend their health records in November's midterm elections.

"These deals are often not transparent, so there's no way for the public to judge how meaningful they are," said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.

Dealing with dyes

The push to remove certain artificial dyes from food and drugs, for example, was a headline grabber. In April 2025, Kennedy strode onto an HHS stage to announce deals with food makers. He was flanked by young children and mothers holding placards reading "Make America Healthy Again."

He and former Food and Drug Administration commissioner Marty Makary drew a standing ovation from an audience selected by Kennedy's staff as they said companies had pledged to phase out all petroleum-based synthetic dyes from the nation's food supply and medicines. They targeted nine synthetic dyes for removal.

Voters love the idea of stopping the use of such dyes. In a nationally representative March survey by Consumer Reports, 72% of adults said they were at least somewhat concerned about synthetic dyes, and two-thirds said companies should be required to phase them out.

A year after making the first announcement at HHS, Kennedy declared victory during a discussion at the Conservative Political Action Conference, an annual political event.

"We've gotten rid of the nine synthetic-based food dyes," he said.

Not quite. At the initial HHS event, federal officials said companies would voluntarily stop using six specific synthetic dyes by the end of this year. (The administration has also revoked or proposed revoking authorization for two other synthetic food dyes.)

Later, the FDA on its website quietly changed the deadline to the end of 2027. So, most are still in use.

In fact, the FDA posted a list of 27 companies it said had made voluntary pledges as of December 2025 to remove six synthetic dyes from products such as Doritos and Kellogg's Froot Loops. More than a year and a half later, seven food makers — fewer than 30% of those who bought in — had met their promised goals.

Many major food makers such as the Coca-Cola Co. and Unilever have made "no concrete commitments" to remove the synthetic dyes, according to Consumer Reports. In addition, no pharmaceutical companies have publicly said they have plans to remove dyes from drugs.

"It's just all talk," said Leslie Dach, who chairs Protect Our Care, a healthcare advocacy group that supports the Affordable Care Act. "They just govern for a day of publicity, and then it's over. None of it happens. Yet the people don't know because they have busy lives, so they think, 'Just look at all these initiatives.'"

In fact, the administration loosened labeling requirements, allowing companies to say their products contain no artificial colors — as long as they don't use petroleum-based dyes. Previously, food makers could not make that claim unless their products contained no added colors. Some food dyes made from natural ingredients can contain contaminants and may pose their own health risks, such as diabetes.

"The federal government hasn't taken any regulatory action on food dyes, for the most part, since the beginning of this administration," said Melanie Benesh, vice president for government affairs at the Environmental Working Group, an advocacy group.

HHS said the voluntary approach has yielded significant action, including commitments to remove synthetic dyes from products sold in schools by the 2026–27 school year.

"HHS and the FDA are moving forward with clear timelines and concrete industry commitments, with major changes expected in foods served in schools during the coming school year and across full product portfolios by the end of 2027," HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said in an email.

At the same CPAC convention event, Kennedy said "the MCAT testing companies are going to put nutrition on the MCAT for the first time, so the students will actually want to do it." MCAT refers to the Medical College Admission Test, which is an exam required for admission to medical schools.

Again, not quite.

The Association of American Medical Colleges administers the MCAT. Spokesperson Stuart Heiser said Kennedy misspoke and may have meant to refer to a test taken by students to be licensed as doctors.

An insurance deal falls short of promises

Kennedy again took to the HHS stage in June 2025, this time with Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, to make what was billed as a game-changing announcement. Major insurers, they said, had agreed to reduce the volume of healthcare services subject to prior authorization, a practice widely used by the insurance industry that often requires patients or their medical teams to seek preapproval before undergoing treatment.

The administration said 80% of insurers pledged changes to preauthorization requirements for 80% of diseases and injuries by January 2026. The administration also promised "public dashboards" to track progress.

"It will happen very quickly," Oz said at the event. "Necessary care will be delivered when it's needed, in the right way."

As of July, months past that January target date, health plans have reduced prior authorization for medical services by about 11%, according to AHIP, the insurer trade group. But no public dashboards have debuted to track the deal, and some insurers that signed the pledge last summer told KFF Health News this year that they will not implement all the promised reforms as outlined by AHIP.

Hilliard did not respond to questions about the pace of progress.

The American Medical Association, in a 2025 web-based survey, asked 1,000 practicing doctors whether they believed the voluntary pledges would make a meaningful difference. Only 1 in 3 believed they would.

Insurers made a similar promise in 2018, during the previous Trump administration. The next year, more than 80% of doctors said the number of prior authorization requests for drugs and medical services had been increasing, based on another AMA survey.

Meanwhile, the administration is testing an artificial intelligence-powered prior authorization system for Medicare, the federal health program for people 65 and older or with disabilities. In six states, Medicare beneficiaries must get preapproval for a few treatments the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services considers to have little clinical benefit and to be susceptible to fraud or waste, including skin substitutes and knee arthroscopy for arthritis. The program began in January, the same deadline insurers had set for curtailing preauthorization delays.

Deals and deregulation

The healthcare industry's voluntary agreements appeal to voters who feel government regulation drives up costs and places unnecessary burdens on businesses, some supporters say.

"Secretary Kennedy is the antithesis of a public health industry that uses coercion over communication — and has demonstrated this by taking the time and effort to push voluntary initiatives over the typical approach of governmental mandates," said David Mansdoerfer, a political consultant who was a political appointee at HHS in Mr. Trump's first term.

But voluntary agreements with the health industry can prove ineffective. Former President Jimmy Carter in 1977 proposed a legislative plan to curb rising hospital costs.
