Congress races the clock on reform

Honduras’s Congress said on 23 August 2026 that it was moving toward an agreement on the energy reform. Lawmakers aim to build consensus within about 15 days, per official statements.

The reform has been pending its third and final debate for weeks. Negotiations continue, but no vote has been scheduled yet.

On 20 August 2026, reports said the reform still had not advanced to the third debate. The lack of agreement has frustrated the government’s timeline.

Congress postponed discussion on 11 August 2026 at the Executive’s request. The delay aimed to prioritize consensus over speed, according to local reports.

What the reform would change

The Honduras energy reform would transform ENEE, the state electricity utility, into three independent units. These units would handle generation, transmission, and distribution separately.

The official Congress channel described the reform presentation as imminent on 24 August 2026. It called the overhaul a major step for the sector.

Splitting ENEE aims to improve efficiency and attract investment. The current single-entity structure has faced chronic financial and operational problems.

Lawmakers from the Liberal Party prepared their own reform proposal on 11 August 2026. This counterproposal added another layer to the negotiations.

Government’s fallback options

With consensus elusive, the government is considering emergency measures. Reports on 20 August 2026 listed emergency tenders and decrees as possible paths.

These fallback options would bypass the need for full legislative approval. They could address urgent issues while the reform remains stalled.

The government has not detailed which measures it would activate first. The government has not detailed which measure it would activate first; the reform bill remains in play.

ENEE warned in late July 2026 that time was running out to rescue the utility. The warning added pressure on Congress to act.

New trade gateway with Belize

Separately, Honduras is seeking a new commercial door with Belize. Infobae reported on 24 August 2026 that this would strengthen ties to the Caribbean.

The main idea is a trade-exchange agreement to expand product flows. It would create opportunities for firms and investors in both countries.

Belize participated in a regional dialogue on connectivity and trade on 15 August 2026. This included a cargo-pass initiative to improve cross-border movement.

These efforts align with broader logistics cooperation across Central America. A stronger link could diversify Honduras’s trade partners.

Timeline of the legislative battle

The reform’s journey through Congress has been rocky since mid-2026. On 11 August, the Liberal Party unveiled its own proposal for the National Congress.

Later that same day, Congress postponed the reform discussion. The Executive had requested the delay to prioritize consensus.

By 20 August, the reform had not advanced to the third debate. Stalemate persisted despite ongoing negotiations among parties.

On 23 August, Congress expressed hope for an agreement within 15 days. The official channel then called the presentation imminent the next day.

Why the reform matters

The Honduras energy reform could reshape a sector vital to the economy. ENEE’s instability has long affected businesses and households.

A successful overhaul might lower costs and improve service reliability. Investors are watching closely for signs of progress.

The split into three units is a common model in power markets. It aims to create clear accountability and competition.

Without reform, ENEE may need repeated bailouts from the state. That burden falls on taxpayers and consumers alike.

Belize deal complements energy push

A trade-exchange agreement with Belize could open Caribbean markets. This fits with Honduras’s broader connectivity goals.

The cargo-pass initiative, discussed on 15 August, aims to speed up border logistics. Faster movement of goods benefits regional trade.

No specific products or volumes have been disclosed yet. Officials say the deal would target firms and investors first.

What’s next for the reform

Congress faces a tight window to deliver on the Honduras energy reform. The next two weeks will test whether consensus is achievable.

If no deal emerges, the government may activate emergency decrees. That could change the sector without full legislative input.

The third debate remains the key hurdle before a final vote. Lawmakers have not set a new date for that session.

Movement could come by early September 2026 if the 15-day consensus goal holds, based on the 15-day goal. The outcome will shape ENEE’s future for years.

Latin America · FINANCE

Key Facts — What happened The IDB Group and Japan announced an expanded partnership on 24 August 2026 at a Tokyo business forum.

— How big Total financing potential reaches US$14 billion, combining US$6.5 billion in Japanese resources with US$7.5 billion in co-financing.

— The catch The US$14 billion is a potential ceiling based on historical averages, not a guaranteed single loan package.

— Who pays Japan’s JICA supplies the US$6.5 billion expansion; the US$7.5 billion in additional co-financing is an estimate based on recent historical averages.

— What comes next New priorities include critical minerals, agriculture, and the silver economy, with health cooperation expanding.

— New tools A US$30 million grant initiative and a NEXI loan-insurance arrangement were signed at the forum.

The expanded IDB Japan partnership covers critical minerals, agriculture, disaster resilience, and the silver economy, with new co-financing tools and a US$30 million grant initiative.

The IDB Group and Japan announced on 24 August 2026 an expanded cooperation package bringing total financing potential to US$14 billion for Latin America and the Caribbean. The announcement came at the Japan-LAC Business Forum in Tokyo, marking the 50th anniversary of Japan’s accession to the IDB.

The IDB and Japan expanded their co-financing partnership to US$14 billion for Latin America.

A Landmark Announcement in Tokyo

The IDB Group and Japan unveiled a significantly expanded financing partnership on 24 August 2026. The announcement took place at the Japan-LAC Business Forum in Tokyo, held to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Japan’s accession to the Inter-American Development Bank.

IDB President Ilan Goldfajn joined Japanese officials to present the package, which combines resources from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and other partners. The total financing potential for Latin America and the Caribbean now stands at US$14 billion.

This figure combines US$6.5 billion in Japanese and JICA resources with an estimated US$7.5 billion in additional co-financing. The co-financing estimate is based on recent historical averages for similar partnerships.

The IDB Japan partnership marks a deepening of ties that have supported development across the region for half a century. Japanese officials and IDB leaders both spoke of a shared commitment to resilient and sustainable growth.

Expanding the JICA CORE Facility

The JICA CORE facility, a key co-financing mechanism within the IDB Japan partnership, has been increased from US$4 billion to US$5 billion. This expansion allows for a greater volume of joint projects across the region.

New priorities for CORE financing include critical minerals and agriculture, adding to existing areas such as quality infrastructure. Disaster-risk reduction, resilience, and health remain core focuses of the facility.

The increase reflects growing demand for co-financing that combines Japanese technical expertise with IDB project management. It also signals Japan’s intent to play a larger role in the region’s key economic sectors.

This facility is designed to mobilize private and public capital for projects that might not otherwise attract sufficient funding. The expanded capacity will support a wider range of development initiatives.

Boosting the TADAC Fund

The JICA TADAC fund has also grown, increasing from US$1 billion to US$1.5 billion. This makes it JICA’s largest private-sector co-financing fund active in the region.

TADAC, the Trust Fund Achieving Development of Latin America and the Caribbean, is a trust fund established at IDB Invest that supports private-sector investment. The larger fund will enable bigger and more numerous investments in Latin American businesses.

This increase underscores the importance of private-sector growth to the IDB Japan partnership. It aims to catalyze investment in productive sectors and create sustainable economic opportunities.

The fund’s expansion is part of a broader effort to deepen financial cooperation and unlock new sources of capital. It targets projects where Japanese expertise can add significant value.

Introducing the Japan Resilience Initiative

A new US$30 million non-reimbursable initiative, the Japan Resilience Initiative or JRI, was launched under the partnership. This grant-based facility supports project preparation and implementation across several key sectors.

Primary areas for JRI funding include critical minerals, quality infrastructure, disaster resilience, agriculture, and the silver economy. It also covers disaster resilience and the silver economy, which focuses on aging populations.

The JRI is designed to de-risk projects early in their development cycle, making them more attractive to investors. This type of support is crucial for complex ventures requiring specialized feasibility studies.

As a non-reimbursable instrument, the fund provides direct grants rather than loans. This lowers the financial barrier for projects with high social or environmental value but limited immediate returns.

Adding a Risk-Transfer Tool with NEXI

A new loan-insurance arrangement was signed with Nippon Export and Investment Insurance, or NEXI. This instrument will insure an IDB-guaranteed loan, reducing risk for lenders and opening doors for future transactions.

The risk-transfer mechanism is a first for the IDB Japan partnership, adding a financial layer that can lower borrowing costs. It effectively shares risk between Japanese insurers and the IDB.

By providing insurance on IDB-guaranteed loans, NEXI helps to attract private capital that might otherwise stay on the sidelines. This tool is expected to be replicated in future deals across the region.

The agreement specifically covers a loan that will now proceed with enhanced security. It represents an innovative approach to mobilizing additional financing for development.

Strengthening Health Cooperation

A new trilateral arrangement on health and care involves the IDB, JICA, and Japan’s Ministry of Finance. This agreement aims to strengthen health and care systems throughout Latin America and the Caribbean.

The cooperation will focus on building resilient health infrastructure and improving care services. It also addresses the needs of aging populations through the silver economy approach.

This health pillar complements existing work in disaster resilience, recognizing that strong systems are vital for recovery. The partnership will likely include technical exchanges and joint investments.

Japanese expertise in geriatric care and health technology will be leveraged in the region. The trilateral structure ensures coordinated efforts among key actors.

Renewing the JBIC Framework

The IDB also renewed a cooperation framework with the Japan Bank for International Cooperation, known as JBIC. This agreement focuses on identifying new co-financing opportunities across the region.

JBIC’s involvement brings a focus on large-scale infrastructure and industrial projects. The renewed framework will facilitate joint financing for projects with significant economic impact.

This cooperation is expected to target energy, transportation, and digital infrastructure sectors. It aligns with the broader goal of expanding the IDB Japan partnership’s reach.

By working together, the institutions can combine JBIC’s resources with IDB’s regional knowledge. This synergy aims to accelerate project implementation and delivery.

Sector Focus and Future Outlook

The expanded partnership places a strong emphasis on critical minerals, which are essential for the global energy transition. Japan’s interest in this sector reflects its need for a stable supply of these materials.

Agriculture, infrastructure, and disaster resilience remain central to the cooperation agenda. Health and care systems also receive significant attention under the new agreements.

The silver economy is a notable addition, addressing the needs of the region’s growing elderly population. This focus will likely expand as demographics shift over the coming decades.

With the new tools and increased funding, the IDB Japan partnership is set to deliver broader and deeper benefits. The US$14 billion potential marks a new chapter in regional cooperation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the US$14 billion figure represent? The US$14 billion is the total financing potential of the expanded IDB Japan partnership. It combines US$6.5 billion in Japanese resources with an estimated US$7.5 billion in co-financing based on historical averages. When was the partnership announced? The expanded partnership was announced on 24 August 2026. The announcement came during the Japan-LAC Business Forum in Tokyo, marking 50 years of Japan’s membership in the IDB. Which sectors are prioritized under the new financing? Key sectors include critical minerals, quality infrastructure, agriculture, health, and disaster resilience. The Japan Resilience Initiative also adds the silver economy to the funding priorities. What is the Japan Resilience Initiative? The Japan Resilience Initiative is a US$30 million non-reimbursable fund. It supports project preparation and implementation in critical sectors like minerals, infrastructure, and health. How will the NEXI risk-transfer instrument work? NEXI, Japan’s export credit agency, will insure an IDB-guaranteed loan under a new arrangement. This reduces lender risk and is expected to enable similar transactions in the future.

World.title: Petropar Enters Paraguay’s Aviation Fuel Market With Five Plants
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Paraguay · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Petropar began selling Jet A-1 and AVGAS aviation fuels in Paraguay on 24 August 2026.

— How big The company announced plans for five plants across Asunción, Ciudad del Este, Mariscal Estigarribia, and Concepción.

— Who pays A private operator assumed all investment costs through a public-private partnership, not Petropar itself.

— The catch Petropar invested no money in this operation, so the private partner finances the infrastructure; ownership and profit terms were not disclosed.

— What comes next The first plant is already running, with the remaining four sites to roll out later.

— Timeline La Nación reported the launch on 24 August 2026 and confirmed the model the next day.

Paraguay’s state oil company launches Jet A-1 and AVGAS sales, with private money building five plants.

Petropar, Paraguay’s state oil company, entered the aviation fuel market on 24 August 2026 with sales of Jet A-1 and AVGAS. The company announced a five-plant network across four cities, funded entirely by a private partner.

Petropar plans to enter Paraguay’s aviation fuel market, breaking a private monopoly. (illustrative)

The Market Entry

Petropar, the state-owned petroleum company of Paraguay, officially entered the aviation fuel market on 24 August 2026. The launch included sales of Jet A-1 for jet engines and AVGAS for piston-engine aircraft.

This move has Petropar compete in a sector long served by private importers. The company sees the entry as a strategic step to widen fuel supply options in Paraguay.

The announcement came from company officials at an official launch event. La Nación, a leading Paraguayan newspaper, covered the launch on 24 August 2026.

Petropar aviation fuel will now compete directly with established brands in the country. This gives airports and airlines a new, state-backed option for their fueling needs.

The Five-Plant Plan

The centerpiece of the strategy is a plan for five fuel plants in key locations across Paraguay. The first plant is already in motion, according to company statements reported by La Nación.

The network will cover Asunción, Ciudad del Este, Mariscal Estigarribia, and Concepción. These cities represent the main air traffic hubs and remote strategic points in the country.

Asunción is the primary international gateway, while Ciudad del Este borders Brazil. Mariscal Estigarribia serves the arid Chaco region, and Concepción extends coverage to the north.

The rollout will be phased, starting with the operational first plant and then expanding.

Public-Private Partnership Model

The most notable aspect is that Petropar is not investing in this operation, the company confirmed. Instead, a private operator has assumed the required investment for the project.

This public-private partnership structure means the state firm lends its national brand. The private partner bears all construction and operational costs.

This model reduces financial risk for Petropar while expanding its market presence. The financial terms of the partnership were not disclosed.

La Nación’s follow-up on 25 August 2026 confirmed that the private operator finances the entire operation. No total dollar figure for the five-plant plan has been disclosed publicly.

Product Details and Users

Jet A-1 is the standard fuel for commercial jet aircraft, used globally by airlines. AVGAS, or aviation gasoline, powers smaller piston-engine planes used for training and agriculture.

The launch targets both commercial carriers and general aviation operators in Paraguay. This includes international flights from Asunción and domestic routes across the country.

By offering both fuels, Petropar aims to be a one-stop supplier for all aircraft types. This could simplify logistics for airports that previously relied on multiple distributors.

The quality standards match international specifications, the company stated in the launch. This ensures that foreign airlines can refuel safely without equipment modifications.

Strategic Importance for Paraguay

Paraguay is a landlocked country that relies heavily on air transport for trade and travel. Having a state fuel supplier could lower prices and ensure supply reliability.

The Chaco region, where Mariscal Estigarribia is located, has growing economic activity. That area needs reliable fuel for mining, ranching, and emergency flights.

Ciudad del Este’s location near the Iguazú Falls attracts significant tourism. A steady fuel supply supports this sector and regional air connections.

This move aligns with broader national energy supply goals. It gives the state a direct role in a critical aviation input.

Competition and Market Impact

The entry of Petropar aviation fuel introduces a new player in the market. This could spur competitive pricing and better service at airports.

Existing suppliers will face a state-backed rival with a planned national network. The five-plant plan challenges incumbents at the country’s main airfields.

However, private operators retain advantages in logistics and customer relationships. The partnership model actually uses one private partner, not direct competition.

The full impact will depend on how quickly the remaining four plants come online.

Financial Transparency Questions

The absence of a disclosed investment figure for the five-plant plan raises transparency questions. Petropar has not published the total cost or expected returns.

Under the public-private model, the private operator’s financial commitment remains confidential. This lack of disclosure may concern lawmakers and watchdogs.

However, the company insists that state funds are not at risk in this specific operation. That point was made explicitly in the La Nación reports.

Future audits or parliamentary inquiries could reveal more details. Until then, the financial scale of the project remains undisclosed to the public.

Next Steps and Rollout Timeline

The first of the five plants is operational as of the launch date, 24 August 2026. The remaining four plants across these cities will follow.

Petropar has not given a specific completion date for the entire network. The phased approach allows the company to adjust based on demand and logistics.

Airlines and airport operators can now contact Petropar for fuel contracts, the company said.

The rollout will be watched closely by the aviation industry in South America.

Frequently Asked Questions

What fuels is Petropar selling for aviation? Petropar is selling Jet A-1 for jet aircraft and AVGAS for piston-engine planes. Both fuel types are now available at the first operational plant. Where will the five Petropar aviation fuel plants be located? The plants will be in Asunción, Ciudad del Este, Mariscal Estigarribia, and Concepción. The first plant is already running, with the rest to open later. How is the Petropar aviation fuel project funded? A private operator is funding the entire operation through a public-private partnership. Petropar itself is not investing in this specific project. When did Petropar enter the aviation fuel market? Petropar entered the market on 24 August 2026, announcing the launch of Jet A-1 and AVGAS sales. The company also outlined the five-plant plan that day. What is the total cost of the five-plant plan? The total dollar figure has not been published or disclosed by Petropar. The company only stated that the private operator assumed the required investment.

— The demands Doctors want a salary adjustment of about G. 3,000,000 (about US$500) each, plus permanent hiring and better supplies.

— The catch Emergency, intensive care, dialysis, and critical services continue running despite the strike.

Five-day walkout hits more than 1,500 health centers as doctors demand pay restoration and permanent jobs.

Paraguay doctors strike began on Monday, 24 August 2026, shutting down consultations and scheduled surgeries across the public health network. The five-day walkout, led by the Sindicato Nacional de Médicos (Sinamed), affects more than 1,500 centers nationwide.

Paraguayan doctors are striking over pay and staffing at public hospitals. (illustrative)

Strike begins across Paraguay

Paraguay doctors strike started on Monday, 24 August 2026, and is scheduled to run through Friday, 28 August. The Sindicato Nacional de Médicos (Sinamed), the national doctors’ union, leads the action.

The Círculo Paraguayo de Médicos, another medical group, publicly supports the strike along with other health organizations. The union calls it a response to a collapsing public health system.

The strike affects the Ministry of Health’s public network, which covers more than 1,500 centers nationwide. Hospitals in major cities and rural areas report reduced services, according to local media.

On the first day, some hospitals offered only basic and emergency care, local media reported on 24 August 2026. Consultations and scheduled surgeries were suspended across the network.

Salary demands and frozen pay

A central demand of the Paraguay doctors strike is a salary adjustment of about G. 3,000,000 (about US$500) per doctor. Doctors say their pay has been frozen since 2012, eroding their purchasing power.

The union argues that inflation has cut real wages sharply over the past 14 years. Restoring that lost purchasing power is the top priority for many physicians.

Doctors also demand double pay for holidays worked, as required by labor rules. The union says the state has not complied with this obligation.

The salary issue affects thousands of doctors across the public system, not just those in big hospitals. Many rural physicians face the same frozen wages, according to union statements.

Hiring and permanent jobs

The Paraguay doctors strike also demands formal hiring of thousands of doctors now on temporary contracts. Long-term temporary appointments have left many physicians without job security.

The union wants permanent positions in the public health system to replace these unstable arrangements. This would provide stability for doctors and patients alike.

Close to the strike, the health ministry named more than 11,000 functionaries, but the union says this is not enough. Temporary contracts remain widespread and underpin much of the workforce.

Doctors argue that new hospitals cannot function without dignified, permanent remuneration. The union has warned about sustainability for future health facilities.

Supplies and equipment shortages

Shortages of insumos, or medical supplies, and medicines are another key demand of the strike. Doctors also call for better maintenance of hospital equipment across the network.

Without reliable supplies, even basic procedures become risky, doctors told local media. Patients face delays and sometimes unsafe conditions in public centers.

The union says equipment breakdowns are common in major hospitals, affecting routine and emergency care alike. Maintenance funding has been insufficient for years, doctors claim.

These shortages compound the effects of frozen pay and unstable hiring, they argue. The collapsing system needs urgent investment, not just promises, union leaders say.

Government response and talks

The government held four tripartite meetings with the Ministry of Labor and the Ministry of Health before the strike. No agreement was reached because no concrete proposal was presented, according to reports.

Health Minister María Teresa Barán said the state could not commit to something it could not fulfill. She cited a lack of resources as the main barrier to meeting demands.

The ministry said it would try to maintain healthcare coverage during the Paraguay doctors strike. Emergency services and critical care units will continue operating, officials stated.

Union leaders said the government’s position showed a failure to address systemic problems. The lack of a proposal disappointed many doctors, who then began the strike.

Impact on hospitals nationwide

Major public hospitals affected include Acosta Ñu, Ineram, Incan, and the Hospital Nacional de Itauguá. Regional, district, maternity, and family health units are also hit.

These facilities suspended consultations and scheduled surgeries, as reported by local news outlets. Patients with non-urgent needs have been asked to wait or seek alternatives.

Urgencies, intensive care, dialysis, and other critical services are being kept running during the strike. Staffing for these units remains a priority for unions and hospitals.

The first day saw marches and plantones, or sit-ins, in Asunción and other cities. Doctors aim to keep public attention on the health system’s collapse.

Patients caught in the middle

Patients face long waits and uncertainty as the strike suspends routine care. Many worry about delayed treatments for chronic conditions and needed surgeries.

Doctors say the strike is necessary to force change, despite the hardship it causes. They argue that inaction would lead to more deaths in the long run.

Other medical organizations back the protest, amplifying the message. The broader workforce backs the doctors’ demands for better conditions.

Health authorities guaranteed emergency and critical care and called for the public’s understanding during the strike. The strike’s impact on daily life will grow if it extends beyond Friday.

What comes next after Friday

The current five-day strike ends on Friday, 28 August 2026, but doctors do not rule out an indefinite strike. Union leaders say further action depends on government responses.

Marches in Asunción are planned for the strike’s duration, with rallies expected daily. Doctors want to maintain public pressure on the government.

If no agreement emerges, the union could call for a longer, open-ended walkout. This would deepen the crisis in public health services.

Observers warn that the Paraguay doctors strike shows deep flaws in health funding. Without pay reform and investment, similar strikes are likely in the future, analysts say.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did the Paraguay doctors strike begin? The strike began on Monday, 24 August 2026, and is scheduled to last five days through Friday, 28 August. It affects the public health network nationwide. What are the main demands of the doctors? Doctors demand a salary adjustment of about G. 3,000,000 (about US$500) per doctor to restore purchasing power. They also seek permanent hiring, more supplies, and double pay for holidays worked. How many health centers are affected by the strike? More than 1,500 public health centers across Paraguay are affected. This includes major hospitals like Acosta Ñu, Ineram, and Incan, plus regional and district units. Are emergency services still running during the strike? Yes, urgent care, intensive care, dialysis, and other critical services continue to operate. Routine consultations and scheduled surgeries are suspended during the strike. What is the government’s response to the strike? The government held four tripartite meetings but reached no agreement, citing a lack of resources. Health Minister María Teresa Barán said the state cannot commit to unfulfillable promises.

World.title: Jackson Hole With a Rate Rise Priced: What Warsh’s Debut Means for Latin America
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

United States · RATES

Key Facts —The event: Jackson Hole runs 27–29 August at Jackson Lake Lodge, about 120 central bankers from more than 70 countries. —The debut: Kevin Warsh gives his first keynote as Federal Reserve chair at 10 a.m. New York time on Friday 28 August. —The theme: “Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy.” —What is priced: A September rate rise, not a cut — about one in three in futures, just over half on prediction markets — with energy costs tied to the Iran conflict cited as the driver. —The backdrop: Inflation above the 2 percent target for more than five years, and 30-year Treasury yields past 5.3 percent, near a two-decade high. —Why it is unpredictable: Warsh has convened fifteen external experts to review the policy framework, with recommendations due by the end of 2026, and he has said he dislikes forward guidance.

Most people living in Latin America on dollar income are still waiting for the Federal Reserve to cut. Markets are pricing the opposite. On Friday a Fed chair who has never given this speech before will stand up at Jackson Hole and say something about it, and every currency in the region will move on what he says.

{CAP}

What is actually happening on Friday

The Kansas City Fed’s economic policy symposium runs from Thursday 27 to Saturday 29 August at Jackson Lake Lodge in Wyoming, drawing about 120 central bankers, economists and officials from more than 70 countries. This year’s theme is financial innovation and its implications for payments and policy.

The part that matters is the keynote. Kevin Warsh speaks at 10 a.m. New York time on Friday 28 August, his first Jackson Hole address as chair of the Federal Reserve. Bloomberg and MNI have both confirmed the slot and the time.

The assumption most expat budgets are built on is wrong

Ask most foreign residents here what the Fed does next and the answer is some version of “cut, eventually.” That assumption underpins a lot of decisions about when to convert and how much dollar cash to hold.

It is not what the market currently thinks. Pricing has moved towards a September increase, with though the odds vary by venue: futures are pricing roughly one chance in three, prediction markets just over half. J.P. Morgan’s wealth arm has pencilled in a quarter point. The driver most often cited is energy, with costs pushed up by the Iran conflict feeding back into headline inflation.

The context is worse than a single print. Inflation has now run above the Fed’s 2 percent target for more than five years, and thirty-year Treasury yields have pushed past 5.3 percent, close to a two-decade high. That is not a market waiting for relief.

Why Warsh specifically makes this harder to call

A new chair is always uncertain, but Warsh has added to it. He has convened fifteen external experts to review the Fed’s policy framework, with recommendations due by the end of 2026, and there is open speculation the review could rewrite the 2020 average inflation targeting approach.

He has also been consistently critical of forward guidance as a tool. A chair who declines to signal the path is a chair who produces more volatility around each meeting, not less. Reporting suggests he has not settled whether Friday’s speech will be a broad framework argument or something closer to a policy signal, which is itself informative.

What it means where you live

Latin American currencies are trading off Fed pricing more than off local fundamentals right now. The Colombian peso reached a seven-year high last week on a mix of domestic fiscal signalling and a soft dollar; the Chilean peso and the sol firmed on the same tide. If Friday pushes the dollar back up, that reverses, and it reverses everywhere at once.

For anyone paid in dollars, a hawkish Warsh is good news for your local purchasing power and bad news for the price of anything you buy on credit. For anyone holding local fixed income at high nominal rates — Colombian paper at a 12 percent policy rate, Brazilian at 14 — a stronger dollar compresses the return in dollar terms even if the coupon does not change.

The practical version

Do not convert a large sum on Thursday. If you have a discretionary transfer this week, either do it before the speech or wait until the following Monday, because the twenty-four hours around a first keynote from an unpredictable chair is the worst possible window for a single large trade.

If you hold a variable-rate dollar loan, know what your rate resets against and when. And if your plan assumed cheaper dollar borrowing by year end, write down what you would do if it does not arrive.

What to watch

Three things in the speech itself. Whether Warsh addresses the September decision at all or stays at the framework level. Whether he says anything about the 2020 averaging framework, which would signal the direction of the review. And whether he offers any path guidance, given that his stated preference is not to.

Then watch the dollar index on Friday afternoon. That, rather than any single Latin American data release, is what will set the tone for the region into September.

Frequently asked questions

When does Kevin Warsh speak at Jackson Hole?

At 10 a.m. New York time on Friday 28 August 2026. It is his first Jackson Hole keynote as chair of the Federal Reserve. The symposium itself runs from 27 to 29 August at Jackson Lake Lodge in Wyoming.

Is the Fed expected to cut or raise in September?

Markets are currently pricing an increase rather than a cut, with futures near one in three and prediction markets just over half, and energy costs tied to the Iran conflict cited as the driver. Inflation has run above the 2 percent target for more than five years.

Why does this matter for Latin American currencies?

Because they are trading off Fed pricing more than off local fundamentals. The Colombian peso hit a seven-year high last week partly on a soft dollar. If Friday pushes the dollar back up, that move reverses across the region at the same time.

World.title: Argentina’s Wholesale Peso Breaks 1,500 for the First Time
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Argentina · CURRENCY

Key Facts —The record: The wholesale peso closed Monday 24 August at 1,507 to the dollar, the first time it has traded through 1,500. —The move: Up 11 pesos on the day, the largest single-session rise since 3 June. —Retail: Banco Nación 1,475 buy and 1,525 sell. —The parallel rates: Blue 1,540 / 1,560; CCL about 1,599, roughly 6 percent above the wholesale rate. —The backdrop: Country risk last printed at 505 basis points on Friday 21 August, wider on the month. —What is ahead: The fiscal path, and whether the bond sell-off runs into September.

Argentina’s wholesale dollar broke 1,500 for the first time on Monday. If you are paid in dollars and live in Buenos Aires, your rent just got cheaper. If you hold peso assets going into October, that is not the way to read it.

{CAP}

What happened

The mayorista, the wholesale rate that banks and large importers actually transact at, closed Monday 24 August at 1,507 pesos to the dollar. It rose 10 pesos on the session, the biggest single-day move since 3 June, and it is a nominal record.

The rest of the board followed. Banco Nación’s retail counter went to 1,475 buy and 1,525 sell. The blue, the street rate, closed at 1,540 and 1,560. The contado con liquidación, the rate at which institutions legally move money offshore by buying securities locally and selling them abroad, closed at about 1,599, roughly 6 percent above the wholesale rate.

This is a bond story before it is a currency story

The peso did not move in isolation. Argentine sovereign bonds have been selling off through August, and country risk — the premium investors demand over US Treasuries — has widened over the month. The last published reading was 505 basis points on Friday 21 August.

That combination matters. A currency weakening while risk premia widen is a market pricing fiscal uncertainty, not one responding to a policy decision. And there is no ballot to blame it on: the midterms were held in October 2025 and the next presidential and legislative vote is not until October 2027. This is the market trading the government’s accounts.

If you earn in dollars

The arithmetic is straightforward and it is in your favour. A US$3,000 monthly transfer converted at Monday’s official buy rate of 1,475 bought 4,425,000 pesos. It is not a windfall, but the direction has been consistent since the start of the month and the wholesale rate is now at a nominal record.

The wider gap to watch is the CCL. At about 1,599 against a wholesale 1,507 there is a wedge of roughly 6 percent, and that wedge is the real cost of moving capital out of the country. If you are planning to repatriate savings rather than bring them in, that number is the one that decides your timing.

If you hold pesos or peso assets

The picture is the mirror image, and it is less comfortable. Peso-denominated holdings are losing value against the dollar at an accelerating rate, and the bond market is telling you that investors want more compensation to hold Argentine risk than they did three weeks ago.

That does not make it a crisis. The peso has moved less than 1 percent on the week in wholesale terms, and the blue-to-official gap remains narrow by Argentine standards. But the trend and the risk premium are pointing the same way.

What to do about it

If you have peso obligations coming — a rent renewal, school fees, an annual insurance premium — the case for converting early is stronger this week than it was last week. If you have discretionary dollars and no deadline, the case for waiting is that a move driven by risk premia usually overshoots before it settles.

And do not conflate the rates. The rate you get depends entirely on which channel you use, and the official retail buy counter at 1,475 and the CCL at about 1,599 are roughly 8 percent apart, a larger gap than most people’s entire annual salary increase.

What to watch

Country risk first. If the premium keeps widening through September, the currency will follow, and the government’s room to defend a level narrows with it. Then the fiscal accounts, which are what the bond market is actually trading on.

And, this week, watch Washington. Markets are pricing a Federal Reserve rate rise in September, and Kevin Warsh gives his first Jackson Hole keynote as chair on Friday. A stronger dollar pushes on every emerging-market currency at once, and Argentina is rarely the one that absorbs it best.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the dollar worth in Argentina today?

At Monday’s close the wholesale rate was 1,507, a record. Banco Nación retail was 1,475 buy and 1,525 sell, the blue 1,540 and 1,560, and the contado con liquidación about 1,599.

Why is the Argentine peso weakening?

It is tracking a bond sell-off rather than a policy change. Country risk, the premium investors demand over US Treasuries, has widened through August and last printed at 505 basis points on Friday 21 August. There is no national election due until October 2027.

Which exchange rate should I use?

It depends on the channel. The official retail counter and the contado con liquidación are currently about 8 percent apart. If you are bringing money in, the official and blue rates matter; if you are moving savings out, the CCL is the number that decides your cost.
