World.title: Are we getting more Oasis shows in 2027 – and will any be in mainland Europe?
World.content:
After their sold-out Oasis Live ‘25 reunion tour, fans of Oasis are hungry for more. And growing impatient.

 

The Britpop band reunited after 16 years apart, following a long running feud between brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher. Their comeback shows were a massive success, and the tour was estimated by Pollstar to have grossed around £398 million (approx. €465m).

Now, Liam Gallagher may have given an indication that there are more Oasis gigs to come...

In a post on X, he seemed to suggest he’s waiting on his brother Noel to share the official announcement: “Ffs RKID announce the tour we’re all losing our minds.”

This comes after rumours that a 12-night residency in their home city of Manchester at the Etihad Stadium could be on the cards, as well as a Knebworth residency. This year marks the 30th anniversary of the band’s legendary Knebworth shows in 1996, where they played to a combined audience of 250,000.

Further fanning the Knebworth flames was news earlier this month that SJM Concerts, the promoter behind the Oasis reunion tour, had secured a licence to host events at Knebworth indefinitely.

As of writing, no dates have been confirmed.

Beyond possible UK dates, European fans are also anxious to find out whether the band will be adding any EU dates to their calendar, as the Oasis Live ‘25 tour spanned the UK, Canada, US, Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Brazil, South Korea, Japan and Australia – but no concerts in mainland Europe.

There had been reports last year that negotiations were underway in Rome, but no further news... Same goes for the band writing new music, as many are speculating Oasis could return to the studio to record a follow up to their last album, 2008’s 'Dig Out Your Soul'.

Elsewhere, Liam shut down rumours that Oasis would be headlining Glastonbury next year, telling one fan in an expletive-filled response: “It’s not HAPPENING so all you croc wearing flag waving shit cunts can calm the fuck down”.

Charming.

Oasis headlined Glastonbury twice before - in 1995 and 2004 – but the band seem to have fallen out of love with the festival, with Noel criticising Glasto on a podcast earlier this year, slamming it for “virtue-signalling” and claiming that it was getting “kind of preachy”.

In the meantime, next month sees the release of a new documentary following the brothers on their Live ‘25 tour. It will premiere at this year’s Venice Film Festival, with the brothers set to attend.

Titled Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger, the film is “an unapologetically uplifting account of the biggest musical event of 2025, capturing the experience and emotions of the band and their fans across the world,” according to a statement by Disney+. “The unique perspective includes rehearsal, backstage, and onstage access as well as the first joint interviews with Noel and Liam in over 20 years.”

The documentary hits cinemas on 11 September and will stream exclusively on Disney+ later in the year.

World.title: Where you can go on holiday in Europe for less than €100 a day
World.content:
The past year has seen travel habits change massively, with long-haul flights out as jet fuel prices soar.

 

Still committed to travelling internationally this September? Then you might just want to take your pick from this list of 13 city breaks across the continent.

Thomas Cook crunched the numbers across more than 50 popular destinations to find the best-value breaks under €100 per night next month.

To calculate that, the travel agency looked at the average costs of things like a three-star hotel stay, a meal at an inexpensive restaurant, a coffee, a daily bus pass, and paid attraction tickets.

Top value city breaks

The result? If you want the most bang for your buck, Albania’s capital Tirana is where you need to be headed as it has a daily approximate cost of €59 per person.

Three-star accommodation comes out at an average of €32 per person, per night, while dinner at an affordable restaurant is €8.50 and a local beer will set you back just €1.50.

Second place went to Bucharest in Romania, where dinner out costs just over €12 on average, and a daily bus pass is around €1.50.

Two places in Türkiye made the top five: Antalya in joint third with Warsaw in Poland, and Istanbul in fifth.

Hotels in Istanbul were among the most affordable, priced at an average of €28 per person, while an inexpensive meal was between €8 and €9.

“Eastern European and Turkish city destinations consistently deliver affordability and with growing tourism numbers, they won’t remain a secret for long,” Nicholas Smith, dynamic packages director at Thomas Cook, said.

08/25/2026 August 25, 2026 Strait of Hormuz sees lowest daily vessel count since May

The strait has become a central flashpoint in the war between the United States and Iran Image: REUTERS

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply, with just two commodity tankers transiting the vital energy chokepoint on Monday, the lowest daily total since early May.

Shipping data from Kpler showed both vessels entered the Gulf, well below the recent daily average of 14 crossings. Some ships may not have been counted after switching off navigation transponders.

Before the conflict, the Strait of Hormuz carried about one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas flows.

Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers for violating passage rules and threatened action against vessels involved in ship-to-ship transfers with them.

Analysts said it remained unclear how Tehran would enforce those measures, but warned that any escalation or attack in the waterway could further disrupt traffic.

In a sign of how dangerous the crossing can be, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Monday an oil tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman.

The vessel was disabled but the crew was reported safe. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the attack.

World.title: Trees are vital for cooler cities, but they need help too
World.content:
Record-breaking heat and drought are putting urban trees at risk. Experts explain how to protect these essential assets and build city forests that can withstand the climate challenges ahead.

Walking beneath the trees this historically hot summer, sometimes felt like autumn had already arrived: dry, dead leaves crunching underfoot, and crowns tinged yellow or completely bare.

That's a problem because large leafy trees help make our cities more livable. They block sunlight, reduce pollution, store carbon, provide habitats for biodiversity to thrive, soak up otherwise harmful stormwater runoff and even boost the mental and physical health of residents.

"When trees go away, those things go away as well," Nina Bassuk, who runs the Urban Horticulture Institute at the US-based Cornell University, told DW.

That's why cities and scientists are racing to figure out how to save trees and choose smarter ones for the future.

Why cities need trees

As humans have burned fossil fuels to power industry and heat homes, the planet has become hotter, making the role of urban trees ever more vital.

Why? Because they essentially act like giant air conditioners, which makes a big difference in hot cities. Inside a tree's canopy, temperatures can be up to three degrees cooler than the surrounding area. This is down to evapotranspiration, the process of trees absorbing water and releasing water vapor through their leaves.

In addition, trees cast shade, which keeps their surroundings from heating up in the first place.

"When we stand under a tree, the temperature we perceive can be 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (18 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than right next to it," said Matthias Beyer, a hydrologist at the Institute of Geoecology at TU Braunschweig.

And it's not just cooling. There have been numerous

studies correlating all sorts of other positive effects of robust trees.

One showed that cities with more tree canopy had lower rates of cardiovascular disease . Another concluded that greener school surroundings were associated with better grades in high schools. And further research suggested that more greenspace exposure during pregnancy can lead to healthier outcomes for newborns."

How much water do trees need to survive drought?

Though a warmer climate makes trees more necessary, it also makes it harder for them to thrive.

Healthy trees need a minimum of 10 to 15 liters of water a day, but mature ones with full foliage require up to four times that.

Different ages of trees require different volumes of water to keep healthy Image: Claus Völker/dpa/picture alliance

While there may be a temptation for cities to focus on planting new, less water-hungry trees, experts agree that the priority should be protecting older, struggling ones.

Research shows it would take around 400 saplings to replace the benefits of an old tree with a crown circumference of 20 meters. Once trees reach maturation, their benefits can be exponential, but this takes time and lots of maintenance.

"A lot of trees can't deliver the full function until 40, 50 years from the day they were planted," said Henrik Sjoman, a researcher at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences.

The best way to water trees

It's better to give trees a large amount of water over a short period so it can soak down deep, rather than letting it stay in the upper soil layers, where much of it evaporates.

For newly planted trees, a ring of metal or sturdy plastic is often fixed into the ground around the trunk. Where that's not available, a shallow depression around the tree can be created, allowing the water to pool. What matters is not damaging any surface roots in the process.

When the soil is extremely hardened, so-called irrigation bags or cushions can help. Water drips slowly but steadily into the soil through small holes on their underside. It's important that the water doesn't sit on the surface for long periods, since that can cause rot, which damages the tree.

If they don't have the right growing conditions, trees can struggle to put down roots in cities Image: IMAGO/viennaslide

But sometimes the soil has been heavily compacted to support sidewalks above, meaning water can't get through at all. Thirty years ago, Bassuk helped pioneer a method that mixes specially-sized gravel in with the soil. It allows the stones help bear the load of the sidewalk, while leaving more space for roots to stretch across dense urban ground.

"As long as you get the soil and the stone proportions right, you can compact it and yet trees can access that and grow for long distances," Bassuk said.

How to choose the right trees for cities

When it comes to climate adaptation, there's also the question of which trees to plant in the first place.

Historically, Sjoman says urban tree selection was often driven by aesthetics and design, which led to the over-planting of single species that were vulnerable to threats like pests or disease. Horror stories of Dutch elm disease wiping out entire populations in the 20th century helped to transform urban forestry planning, placing the focus far more on diversity and climate adaptation.

It can take a long time for trees to reach their full potential in terms of how much they can cool their surroundings Image: Philipp Böhme/DW

The 10-20-30 rule of thumb was coined in 1990 by the late

Frank Santamour, who worked as a research geneticist at the US National Arboretum. It states that urban forest populations should include no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of a single genus or 30% of any family.

In Germany, there are several tools and databases that offer planting guidance, and a number of cities are taking part in an official street tree test. The idea is that 45 species are tested at more than 220 locations to gather knowledge of

how they thrive.

Another resource is the CITREE database, which categorizes almost 400 species of woody plants, sortable by more than 50 different features, including leaf density, fruit color, allergy potential, limb breakage and more.

The key feature cities need to select for is droughttolerance — considering the immense biological strain urban

trees are facing in an ever-warming world. But knowing the benefits trees offer a city, means that is not the only factor.

"The demands of trees today — it's so much bigger, so much deeper than it was just a couple of decades ago," Sjoman said.



This article was adapted from German, with additional reporting.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: Canada set to announce retaliatory tariffs on US goods after talks fail
World.content:
Tariffs of 50% on Canadian goods came into effect after trade talks collapsed. US President Trump has warned Ottawa to "fall in line," but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has refused to accept a "bad deal."

Canada is set to announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, as relations between the neighbors nosedived following failed trade talks last week.

Here's what you need to know:

Washington ‌and ​Ottawa were racing to reach an agreement beforeUS President Donald Trump's steep new US tariffs, announced in July, were due to take effect

Talks broke down days after the US President announced the neighbors were close to agreeing to a trade deal

The collapse in negotiations triggered Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods the next day

Canada moved to announce its own retaliatory tariffs effective September 8

Why is Canada imposing new tariffs?

While the US and Canada have shared one of the world’s largest trade relationships, the recent talks signal a breakdown in relations.

"An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" is "not something we’re going to accept," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

"We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum," Carney said, opting for an even blunter approach in French. "That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal."

US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are expected to unveil Canada's response on Tuesday.

What did the US say?

Trump, on Monday, threatened he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027, and took to social media to unleash a tirade against the historic partner.

Trump hits Canada with 50% tariffs in major trade escalation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"On trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst nations in the world to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president said.

Canada relies heavily on the US as its top trading partner, with American-bound exports making up 70% of the country's total. The relationship runs both ways, too: government data shows Canada was the second-largest US trading partner in goods this year, just behind Mexico.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.

World.title: Germany news: Third drone found in Leipzig airport probe
World.content:
08/25/2026 August 25, 2026 German construction sector posts strong June growth

Germany's construction sector has recorded a sharp increase in orders, sales and employment, official data has shown.

New orders in the main construction industry rose 11.3% year on year in June after adjusting for prices and calendar effects, while inflation-adjusted sales increased 6.6%, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

Large orders helped boost activity in both building construction, which includes housing, as well as civil engineering projects such as roads and bridges.

Orders also rose strongly over the broader April-to-June period.

Employment increased by 1.5% from a year earlier to around 545,000 people in June.

"The month of June was a good one for the construction industry," said Felix Pakleppa of the ZDB construction association.

However, he cautioned that after a volatile first half of the year it was too early to speak of a sustained turnaround.

The industry is benefiting from billions of euros in federal spending on roads, railways and other infrastructure.

Housing construction remains weaker, partly because higher interest rates have made building more expensive for households and investors.

World.title: Australia's music chart bars fully AI-generated music
World.content:
The ARIA chart is drawing a line between artists who use AI as a tool and songs created largely by machines.

Australia's official music charts will no longer allow wholly AI-generated tracks to qualify, under new rules announced by the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) .

The changes take effect with the ARIA chart dated August 31 and distinguish between music generated primarily by artificial intelligence and recordings where AI is used only as a supporting creative tool.

What AI music will still be allowed in Australia's charts?

Recordings made with generative AI can remain eligible if they are substantially human-made and do not raise concerns about manipulation of streams or chart positions.

ARIA will use an industry-wide distinction announced in July between:

AI-generated music, where AI creates all or the main creative elements of a recording

AI-assisted music, which remains substantially human-created but uses generative AI for some elements

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said artists were already using AI creatively and the charts should allow room for that.

Folk singer fights back against AI-generated fake album To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This gives everyone who releases music in Australia a clear rule to work to. We call on all parties who have a role in deciding the music played and promoted to Australian audiences, particularly radio, to support human artistry and implement similar changes across their own codes," said Herd.

What happens if an AI track enters the charts?

ARIA can refuse to accept an ineligible recording, remove it from the charts either retrospectively or in advance, change chart positions and withdraw accreditations.

It can also revoke an ARIA No. 1 Award, while an ineligible track will not qualify for an ARIA Award. Artists and their representatives will be able to challenge exclusions and provide evidence that a recording meets the rules.

The move is part of a broader initiative led by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), which represents the recording industry globally.

IFPI announced principles in July intended for use across official charts internationally. They require eligible AI-assisted recordings to remain substantially human-made, use lawful and authorized AI services and avoid artificial manipulation of streams.

World.title: US: Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 visas from asylum seekers
World.content:
The State Department is reportedly looking to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who sought asylum after entering on tourist or business visas, in what could be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.

United States President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of foreigners who applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the country, the State Department said in a statement on Monday.

It didn't say how many visas would be affected, but the Associated Press put the number at up to 200,000, citing State Department documents ‌and ​two US officials. If carried out, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.

What did the State Department say about revoking visas?

The State Department is expected to announce the revocations in the coming weeks, targeting so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to holders who have sought or are now seeking asylum. These visas are generally issued for business travel, tourism, family visits or medical care.

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said, referring to the Department of Homeland Security.

He declined to give a specific number, saying the count "remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Officials said the revocations would not necessarily lead to immediate deportation. Most people with pending asylum cases would instead be recategorized, losing their status as business or tourism travelers, according to officials who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity.

Trump's America: End to the American dream for immigrants? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump official slams visa use

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau criticized the use of tourist and business visas as a path to asylum claims.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," he wrote on social media platform X, adding, "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

He separately alleged that the US immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims" and cited the case of a Colombian national who entered the US on a tourist visa in 2015 before applying for asylum.

Applicants for B1 and B2 visas are currently required to affirm they will not seek asylum and to demonstrate intent to return to their home countries. It remains unclear how many current visa holders have actually filed for asylum.

Who has been impacted by Trump's immigration crackdown?

The move is the latest in a series of visa restrictions under Trump's second term, which has included expanded social media vetting, new bond requirements, and outright bans on visa issuance for citizens of certain countries.

The State Department said it has revoked roughly 175,000 visas over the past 18 months, citing reasons ranging from criminal convictions to public criticism of US policy, particularly regarding the Middle East. The administration has also targeted "birth tourism," and has repeatedly sought to end birthright citizenship. Courts, including the Supreme Court, have rejected those efforts.

H1-B and the AI revolution: Threats to your tech career? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rights groups have criticized the broader immigration crackdown, arguing it has infringed on free speech and due process rights while creating an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who could face racial profiling. The administration maintains the crackdown is intended to strengthen domestic security.

Despite campaigning largely on illegal immigration, the administration has also tightened legal immigration pathways, including through new, costly fees for certain work visa applicants. Several aspects of the crackdown are facing ongoing legal challenges.

World.title: Tornado in France damages homes, injures dozens
World.content:
A tornado tore through southwestern France, uprooting trees, damaging dozens of homes and causing transport chaos across the region.

A tornado damaged dozens of homes and injured around 40 people after tearing through a village in southwestern France on Monday, officials said.

The town of Pomas in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains, home to around 1,000 people, was hit the hardest.

The tornado damaged approximately 300 homes in the village, uprooting trees and ripping the roofs off some buildings.

The tornado left a trail of damage in its wake Image: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP

Fifteen of the injured, including a pregnant woman whose house collapsed while she was inside, were brought to hospital, AFP reported.

More than 120 firefighters and emergency personnel were sent to the scene to help with clean-up efforts, local officials said.

Emergency shelters have been set up for people whose homes were damaged.

What else do we know about the tornado in southern France?

Meteo-France, the national weather service, said the storm packed winds as high as 117 kilometers (73 miles) per hour in the nearby village of Arquettes-en-Val.

French authorities had issued orange storm alerts for much of the country's south and southwest. Several areas were affected by power cuts and severe transport disruption.

Around 2,800 households were still without power on Monday evening, officials said.

France sees several dozen tornados on average each year Image: Christian Dussaud/Bestimage/IMAGO

Roads were closed due to fallen trees, and trains were delayed, while airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice and Toulouse, as well as Paris, reported flight delays and cancellations, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said.

The third stage of the Vuelta a Espana, due to take place in the Aude department, was canceled after a hailstorm interrupted the cycling race.

World.title: Haiti: Gang members kill dozens near Port-au-Prince
World.content:
At least 40 people were killed, some of them execution-style, during the attack in Kenscoff. The local mayor described "a night of terror" in the town that has been plagued by gang violence for months.

At least 40 people were killed after gang members attacked displaced persons sheltering inside a church outside Haiti's capital city, Port-au-Prince, the local mayor and the United Nations said Monday.

"We have counted around 40 bodies. Searches are continuing. Some people are still missing," Kenscoff mayor Massillon Jean told the AFP news agency.

Several of those killed on Sunday night had already fled violence earlier this year, Jean said.

"The bandits raided a displaced persons camp located in a church. They executed several people. There are fatalities and dozens of wounded. Some people were abducted by the criminals," Jean said.

Many of the victims had already been displaced by gang violence Image: Patrice Noel/REUTERS

What do we know about the attack near Haiti's capital city?

The UN said the attack had left at least 47 people dead and more than 22 injured and warned that casualty estimates could still change.

Rights group RNDDH said between 30 and 40 people were killed and 15 to 20 were injured during the attack, which started at around 10:30 p.m. on Sunday.

In a statement, the office of Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé condemned the "heinous attack," adding that security forces were on the highest alert and reinforcements were being deployed.

Residents have called for the local police chief to resign amid allegations that police failed to protect people sheltering in the church, which is just minutes away from the police station.

Kenscoff lies in the hills outside the Haitian capital and has been plagued by gang violence for months.

Early last year, gang attacks resulted in more than 260 people being killed and 200 homes destroyed or set ablaze, displacing 3,000 people, according to the UN. At least 10 more attacks have taken place since.

Residents confronted police on Monday after the gang raid the previous night Image: Fildor Pq Egeder/REUTERS

Kenscoff is in a strategic location overlooking several routes into Port-au-Prince.

"Kenscoff will not be abandoned. Haiti will not be handed over to bandits. The Republic will prevail," the statement said .

What is the security situation in Haiti?

Haiti's capital and the surrounding regions have increasingly come under the control of an alliance of criminal groups in recent years.

Attempts by the international community to support Haiti's ill-equipped police force have failed to rein in the violent gangs.

Haiti is the poorest nation in the Americas. The Caribbean country suffers from deep-seated political instability, corruption, natural disasters and gang violence.

The UN estimates that nearly 1.5 million Haitians are currently displaced out of a total population of 11 million people. More than five million face severe food insecurity.

The violence worsened in 2024, after criminal groups sparked a wave of violence that culminated in the unelected prime minister resigning.

The last time Haiti held an election was in 2016. Its previous president, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated in 2021 and has not been replaced.

Haiti is scheduled to hold elections in December this year.

World.title: Última hora de la entrada de inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | Sánchez reúne hoy al Consejo de Seguridad Nacional para abordar la crisis de Ceuta
World.content:
El PP asegura que la atención a los menores en Ceuta puede provocar un “efecto llamada” para que “los padres se puedan desentender” de sus hijos

La portavoz del PP en el Congreso, Esther Muñoz, ha insistido en la idea de que el Ejecutivo debe “ampliar los turnos de los funcionarios” para agilizar la gestión de las devoluciones de los migrantes que entraron en Ceuta los pasados 30 y 31 de julio y gestionar también el retorno de los menores. En su opinión, esta situación puede producir un “efecto llamada que provocaría que el mundo viera que, en España, los servicios sociales atienden a cualquier menor y que los padres se pueden desentender” de sus hijos. “Lo que no puede ser es que sigan quedando miles de inmigrantes irregulares en Ceuta sin ningún tipo de control y que no se les esté devolviendo a Marruecos”, ha expresado la portavoz de los populares, antes de indicar que los casos de los solicitantes de asilo se tienen que estudiar “individualmente”, pero que “no procede el asilo” a quienes proceden de Marruecos.

Respecto a los menores, Muñoz ha hecho hincapié en que el Gobierno ha cambiado de opinión, pues “dijo que no se iba a quedar nadie que había entrado irregularmente en Ceuta y de repente ahora hablan de reparto”. “Lo que no puede hacer el Gobierno es intentar repartir los problemas para disolver responsabilidades”, ha indicado antes de hacer referencia al posible “efecto llamada” que puede provocar esta situación. “El Gobierno debería haber comenzado con estas devoluciones y con estos procesos administrativos hace mucho tiempo y haber incrementado los funcionarios para que lo pudieran estar haciendo. Lo que no pueden hacer es cronificar este problema en Ceuta y en España”, ha apuntado antes de avisar de que algunas comunidades dirigidas por el PP no irán a la Conferencia Sectorial de Infancia de este jueves porque “lo que está intentando hacer el Gobierno de España es solidarizar la responsabilidad que tiene el Gobierno de España”.

“Hace unos días dijo el Gobierno de España que ningún menor y ningún inmigrante irregular iba a ir a la península y ahora quieren repartirlos”, ha zanjado.

World.title: Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena
World.content:
Declarados patrimonio de la Unesco desde 2011, estos establecimientos de la capital austriaca ofrecen en verano sus terrazas para cenar bajo las estrellas, desayunar a ritmo de jazz o cumplir con el ritual del café con tarta viendo pasar la vida

En 2011, la Unesco declaró la cultura de los cafés vieneses patrimonio cultural inmaterial de la humanidad. La descripción oficial decía: “Son lugares donde se consumen el tiempo y el espacio, pero en la cuenta solo aparece el café”. Ciertamente, por muy elevado que sea el precio de la factura, nunca llega a pagar la experiencia completa: el derecho a sentarse durante horas leyendo los periódicos, siempre presentes en los expositores de prensa de madera; el asiento de primera fila a la vida, a la gente y al modo de ser de una cultura; el ritual diario de la tarta y el café de media tarde; el poder escuchar la música de un piano o la orquesta que toca en vivo, el sol que se filtra por la ventana anunciando la primavera, la conversación espontánea con el de la mesa de al lado o la posibilidad de encontrar un amigo, un amor, un confidente.

En una ocasión leí un libro sobre testimonios de supervivientes de los campos de exterminio nazis. Uno de ellos, francés, desvelaba su secreto para evadirse de aquel infierno. Varias horas al día, en su imaginación, dejaba el campo y se trasladaba a la terraza de un café parisino para tomarse un pastis.

Los rituales tienen una función y sirven para anclarnos a una cultura, a un modo de vida, a las costumbres de una época que ya se fue. Los cafés de Viena conocen esta fórmula y la cumplen a rajatabla. El café llega en una pequeña bandeja de plata, siempre acompañado de un vaso de agua del grifo (que en la capital austriaca es excelente, ya que, según dicen, procede de manantiales en los Alpes de Baja Austria y Estiria) y con una cuchara boca abajo. El camarero, a quien uno deberá dirigirse como herr ober (señor jefe de sala), puede parecer poco cordial, pero no se trata de un mal servicio: es el wiener schmäh (humor vienés), una mezcla de ingenio mordaz y hosquedad teatral que forma parte del espectáculo.

Una de las tartas que se sirven en el Café Central de Viena. Mark Green ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Quien piense que los cafés de Viena son simples cafeterías está muy equivocado. Fueron las oficinas de pensadores como Stefan Zweig, los cuarteles generales de artistas como Gustav Klimt; las cocinas de revoluciones, con chefs como León Trotski (que vivió en Viena de 1907 a 1914); también el consuelo de los solitarios, que formaban parte del mundo el tiempo que duraba un café, y el domicilio declarado de excéntricos, como el poeta Peter Altenberg, que recibía correspondencia en el Café Central de Viena.

La terraza del Café Central. E.Westmacott ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Hay que conocer ciertos códigos para evitar la mirada perpleja del camarero. Aquí no hay que pedir un café, a secas. Aquí hay que especificar. Un wiener melange, el café vienés por excelencia, es un expreso con leche caliente y espuma por encima. Básicamente, un capuchino. El einspänner es un café solo fuerte o un expreso doble, servido en un vaso de cristal con una generosa montaña de nata montada (originalmente diseñado para que los cocheros pudieran beberlo sin derramarlo). El großer brauner es un expreso doble servido con leche o nata aparte, para que cada uno añada la cantidad a su gusto. Y, por último, el franziskaner es una melange que utiliza nata montada en lugar de espuma de leche, llamado así por su similitud con el color del hábito de los franciscanos.

En verano, a algunos de los cafés más emblemáticos de Viena se añade el encanto de sus terrazas. Estos son los que cuentan con las zonas exteriores más hermosas, pintorescas o escondidas de la capital austriaca.

Café Landtmann (Universitätsring, 4)

Al lado del Burgtheater, el teatro nacional de Austria, y delante del Ayuntamiento, este café fundado en 1873 por Franz Landtmann presume de ser el más elegante de la capital austriaca.

Bienvenidos al universo de los desayunos largos y las comidas cortas de negocios, ya que cuenta con un menú del día a un precio bastante asequible (sopa y segundo por 16,90 euros o plato principal por 15). La cocina, aunque con buenos ingredientes, es algo aburrida, pero eso se subsana con los maravillosos postres, entre los que destaca el brazo de gitano (actualmente, con otros nombres) relleno de chocolate negro.

Con un deslumbrante mobiliario y una exquisita atención al cliente, todavía continúa siendo un lugar de encuentro para las altas esferas políticas y económicas del país. Por aquí han pasado Peter Altenberg, Sigmund Freud, Gustav Mahler, Max Reinhardt, Marlene Dietrich, Romy Schneider, Burt Lancaster, Hillary Clinton o Paul McCartney. Su terraza, rodeada de una jardinera con flores, es de las más agradables en los meses de verano.

Un mundo de exclusividad, pero también de vida urbana; ya que en Viena no solo los ricos van a estos cafés, sino también los jubiladas de clase media, los estudiantes y cualquiera que quiera aprovechar el sol del intenso, pero corto, verano.

Café Schwarzenberg (Ringstraße Galerien. Kämtner Ring, 17)

El interior del Café Schwarzenberg. Art Kowalsky ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Como la mayoría de los cafés de la Ringstraße, dispone de un schanigarten; es decir, una terraza. Término que no debe confundirse con el gastgärten, esa especie de jardín privado que tienen algunos bares, pero que no forma parte de la acera o la calle. Como todos los cafés vieneses, el Schwarzenberg es un viaje en el tiempo a una estética muy precisa, a un servicio impecable y una bandeja con vasos de agua y azucarillos, aunque la terraza se asome ya más al siglo XXI, de manera irremediable.

Además de eventos culturales (lecturas, exposiciones y veladas musicales), ofrece varios días a la semana música de piano y el jazz brunch, de 10.00 a 12.00. Durante la temporada de baile vienesa (entre noviembre y febrero), cuando la capital austriaca celebra más de 450 galas tradicionales —siendo su evento más emblemático el Baile de La Ópera—, este es uno de los pocos que ofrecen el llamado Katerfrühstück (literalmente, desayuno de resaca), en el que los asistentes al baile, al término de este (a eso de las cuatro de la madrugada), recuperan fuerzas con un pequeño goulash (un guiso de carne de ternera) y un seidl de cerveza.

Su selección de tartas es casi patrimonio cultural.

Café Museum (Operngasse, 7)

La terraza del Café Museum, en la capital austriaca. Emmanuele Contini ( NurPhoto / Getty Images)

Decorado por Adolf Loos, el establecimiento, que abrió sus puertas en 1899, pronto fue el cuartel general de artistas y escritores. Su decoración se distinguía de la de sus contemporáneos, más ornamentales, por su simplicidad y funcionalidad, que aún se observan en las sillas y mesas de la marca Thonet. A principios de los años treinta, el diseño fue cambiado considerablemente, pero la restauración de 2003 le devolvió su apariencia original. Se encuentra cerca del popular mercado callejero Naschmarkt, de la Karlsplatz y del Pabellón de la Secesión Vienesa, en la Ciudad Vieja de Viena.

A principios del siglo XX, cuando no existían las zonas VIP y los artistas se mezclaban con el pueblo llano, el café contaba entre sus habituales a Gustav Klimt, Elias Canetti, Peter Altenberg, Hermann Broch, Otto Wagner, Robert Musil o Joseph Roth. Y todavía guarda una estrecha y amistosa relación con la literatura, y hay lecturas mensuales seguidas de coloquios y firmas de libros con entrada gratuita.

La terraza del Museum recuerda a las parisinas, con dos filas de pequeñas mesas, donde en los meses de verano se puede degustar mil y una formas de desayunar, de tomar un menú del día o de honrar la vienesa tradición del café con tarta mientras se arregla el mundo.

Café Sacher (Philharmoniker Str., 4)

La terraza del icónico Café Sacher de Viena. Mark Green ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

La terraza de este café y hotel está revestida de un aura de exclusividad a pie de calle, donde es fácil acabar hablando con el vecino de mesa al mismo tiempo que se tiene la total certeza de estar en un lugar importante. Con su moqueta roja y su decoración de candelabros, cuadros de época y mesas de mármol, ha salido en películas como La dama de oro (2015) y Tarta Sacher (2022).

Esta especialidad dulce austriaca se puede degustar en cualquier café que se precie, pero quizás el nombre del lugar y el hecho de que aquí se sirve con crema batida sin azúcar, como manda la tradición, hace que mucha gente venga para pedir su café y su porción de tarta Sacher. Esta fue creada en 1832 por un joven de 16 años llamado Franz Sacher, que trabajaba en la cocina del príncipe Wenzel von Metternich como aprendiz. La historia cuenta que el príncipe había pedido a su jefe de cocina que preparara un postre para impresionar a unos invitados muy importantes, pero entonces el jefe cayó enfermo, dejando esta gran tarea al joven aprendiz, que creó un pastel de bizcocho con crema de albaricoque y chocolate.

Este café presume también por su impecable selección de los expresos más preciados del mercado cafetero y por su catálogo de tés, procedentes de todos los rincones del mundo. En temporada alta se recomienda reservar con suficiente antelación para vivir esta experiencia.

Café Rüdigerhof (Hamburgerstraße, 20)

Para desayunar, comer, cenar o para tomar el tradicional café con tarta, su terraza ajardinada, alejada de las zonas turísticas de Viena, es perfecta en los días de verano. Está además ubicada en un edificio estilo Secesión de 1902 y guarda una decoración interior estilo años cuarenta, con su tapicería, sus muebles y lámparas art déco, y sus visillos que tapan media ventana para ver sin ser vistos.

El edificio del Café Rüdigerhof. Zoonar GmbH / Alamy / CORDON PRESS

Bajo sus árboles, los locales y turistas despistados hacen una parada para retomar fuerzas. Y si la Sacher es el bocado dulce que hay que probar en Viena, el salado es el schnitzel, una especie de filete empanado de cerdo, ternera o pollo, que el Café Rüdigerhof borda a las mil maravillas y sirve con ensalada. Los desayunos, a la sombra de los árboles o al sol dependiendo de la climatología, cuando los clientes son todavía escasos, son muy agradables, mientras que las cenas congregan a una mayor y más ruidosa clientela.

Café Prückel (Stubenring, 24)

El exterior del Café Prückel. Jon Bilous ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Este café, abierto en 1903 por Maxime Lurion, excampeón europeo de ciclismo, ha experimentado varias transformaciones en sus más de cien años de historia. Inicialmente conocido como Café Lurión, cambió su nombre a Café Miramonte antes de convertirse en el de hoy gracias a Wenzel Prückel, quien en 1906 logró obtener el permiso para colocar mesas en el exterior.

Destaca por su decoración de los años cincuenta, con especial atención a los detalles, incluyendo muebles de caoba con incrustaciones y sillas tapizadas en moquette francés. La ubicación es también privilegiada, ya que se encuentra entre Stubenring y Dr. Karl-Luegen-Platz. Además de su música de piano en vivo, bajo el café se encuentra el Lucky Punch Comedy Club, un lugar donde disfrutar de monólogos cómicos.

En el apartado de la gastronomía hay que destacar el café, que aquí es excelente, y el wiener melange. Otro punto fuerte es la prückel creme, una especialidad de la casa. Y, por supuesto, hay que probar el dulce por excelencia: el kaiserschmarrn, una especie de crêpe troceado y dulce que aquí es también todo un clásico.

World.title: Italia quiere poner orden en el caos de sus 12.000 playas privadas: más transparencia y nuevas tasas
World.content:
Entre el 33% y el 42% de los arenales del país son de pago. El Gobierno de Meloni, presionado por Bruselas, abrirá a concurso su gestión

Italia presume de sus 8.000 kilómetros de costa, pero disfrutar de ellos no siempre es gratis. Mientras que en otras partes ir a la playa significa buscar un hueco en la arena, en Italia la experiencia suele ser muy distinta. Encontrar un espacio donde plantar la sombrilla sin pagar puede convertirse en toda una aventura. En amplios tramos del litoral, el acceso al mar está gestionado por empresas privadas, mediante concesiones públicas, que han transformado las playas en un negocio multimillonario. El resultado es una de las estampas más características del verano italiano: bosques interminables de sombrillas perfectamente alineadas, acompañadas de sus respectivas tumbonas, esperando a ser alquiladas por precios que pueden superar los 35 euros al día.

Este modelo, muy arraigado en el país y marcado por una gestión plagada de irregularidades, afronta una reforma que lleva años aplazándose a pesar de la presión de Bruselas para poner orden. Las playas gestionadas por concesionarios privados no han dejado de ganar terreno. Según la asociación ecologista italiana Legambiente, ocupan ya más del 42% de los arenales del país. El Ministerio de Infraestructuras rebaja esa cifra al 33%, una diferencia que se explica por el criterio utilizado para el cálculo: el Gobierno utiliza para sus cuentas toda la línea costera italiana y no únicamente las zonas aptas para el baño.

Desde hace décadas, las empresas, casi siempre familiares —las concesiones suelen heredarse—, pagan cánones relativamente bajos al Estado por explotar espacios públicos, mientras los precios para los usuarios han aumentado de forma exponencial. Las concesionarias gestionan los servicios como los baños, las duchas, los vestuarios, los aparcamientos, además del alquiler de sombrillas y tumbonas. También controlan los chiringuitos y cafeterías y se encargan de las labores de salvamento. Mientras que las zonas públicas suelen estar descuidadas, a menudo sucias, y desprovistas de servicios públicos.

Se trata de un asunto sensible que divide a la opinión pública italiana. Para unos, las playas de pago garantizan orden, limpieza y comodidad; para otros, representan la privatización de un bien público que debería ser accesible para todos. La principal crítica al sistema es la enorme diferencia entre lo que pagan las concesionarias por explotar las playas y los beneficios que obtienen. El Estado recauda entre 80 y 100 millones de euros al año por las concesiones, mientras que el sector, marcado por la opacidad, mueve más de 2.000 millones de euros anuales, según distintas estimaciones. El propio Tribunal de Cuentas italiano ha advertido de que los cánones abonados por los empresarios no suelen ser proporcionales a los ingresos que obtienen.

Uno de los aspectos más controvertidos del modelo italiano es que las concesiones se han renovado durante años casi por inercia. Sin concursos abiertos ni una competencia efectiva y sin controles ni transparencia, los mismos operadores han conservado la explotación de amplios tramos del litoral público durante generaciones, consolidando un sistema difícil de encontrar en otros países europeos.

Un paso adelante

Bruselas lleva años reclamando cambios. La Comisión considera que Italia incumple la directiva Bolkestein de 2009, que obliga a garantizar la libre competencia en la adjudicación de este tipo de concesiones, y ha presionado repetidamente a Roma. Tras décadas de aplazamientos y enfrentamientos, el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha abordado la cuestión. La reforma aprobada prevé que para el 30 de septiembre de 2027 salgan a concurso público todas las playas de pago, unas 12.000 repartidas por todo el país. Además, las concesiones tendrán una duración limitada, de entre cinco y 20 años, y habrá compensaciones económicas para los actuales titulares por las inversiones y obras que hayan realizado.

La perspectiva de abrir el mercado ha despertado, sin embargo, inquietud entre muchos empresarios del sector, que temen que los concursos favorezcan la entrada de grandes grupos turísticos o fondos de inversión capaces de desplazar a los negocios familiares que tradicionalmente han dominado las costas italianas.

World.title: Deadlock looms in budget talks as opposition drive hard bargain
World.content:
Talks to secure support from opposition parties for next year’s budget are entering their final days with no sign of a breakthrough.

Jesse Klaver, leader of the left-wing opposition group Pro (previously GroenLinks/PvdA) said the two sides had “not moved a step closer to each other” after emerging from negotiations on Monday.

Michiel Hoogeveen, of the right-wing JA21, accused the coalition parties of “kicking the can down the road”, while the hardline Protestant party SGP said a deal was “a long way off”.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen has a deadline of August 28 to submit a draft budget to the Council of State before the formal presentation of his plans at the state opening of parliament on September 15.

MPs will not vote on the measures until late in the autumn, but the cabinet wants to do a deal with the opposition to secure majority support in both houses before budget day.

Yo-yo politics

Prime minister Rob Jetten said earlier: “This cabinet has big ambitions to make major investments in the next few years in more affordable houses, more security and the economy of the future. It’s good to do that with others if we want to avoid yo-yo politics.”

The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of 10 opposition MPs in the lower house and 16 senators to pass its legislation.

Asylum minister and deputy prime minister Bart van den Brink, of the CDA, said the government was prepared to take “big steps” to accommodate the opposition groups. But Klaver said he had seen little sign of movement from the coalition.

Pro wants the cabinet to shelve plans to cut welfare spending by €6.5 billion in order to raise money for other departments, chiefly defence, where the Netherlands is striving to hit the new Nato target of 3.5% of GDP.

Wealth taxes

The party argues that the money should be raised by raising wealth taxes instead. “The cabinet seems to be mainly concerned with the position of millionaires in the Netherlands while we are worried about the people who are paying the bills,” Klaver said.

But Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, is opposed to wealth taxes and would prefer to make concessions to parties on the right such as JA21 and SGP, who want to see tax cuts instead. But SGP MP André Flach said on Tuesday that the coalition’s plans “are not enough at the moment”.

The SGP, which draws its vote from Bible-Belt communities, wants the cabinet to suspend plans to legalise surrogate motherhood and permit late-term abortions of up to 22 weeks in some hospitals.

The party has teamed up with JA21 to form a right-wing block of 12 seats, which would be enough to give the coalition a majority in the Lower House. However, they would still be short in the Senate, where any right-wing majority depends on the support of the farmers’ party BBB.

BBB key

The BBB has not been invited to the talks so far because of its staunch opposition to the cabinet’s plans to reduce nitrogen pollution, which would require some livestock farmers to give up or drastically reduce the size of their herds.

Party leader Henk Vermeer is meeting Heinen on Tuesday, but the BBB is not expected to compromise on its stance. “Anyone who can count can see they can’t do without us”.

The 20 seats held by Pro would give the cabinet a clear majority in the lower house, while only one small party such as Volt would be needed to pass the budget in the Senate.

But the right-wing VVD is reluctant to rely solely on Klaver’s party, which was kept out of the coalition in February on the insistence of VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz.

World.title: Dutch cocaine-broker case in Colombia grows to 55 suspects
World.content:
An investigation into two Dutch men accused of brokering cocaine shipments from Colombia has grown into a much wider case, with prosecutors now pursuing 55 suspects, 35 of them already arrested, for drug trafficking, money laundering, extortion, violence and planned kidnappings.

Pre-trial hearings began on Monday at Zwolle district court, broadcaster NOS reported. The two main suspects, Dutch men aged 42 and 47, were arrested in Colombia in February and are still awaiting extradition, which can take more than a year.

The case grew out of a national police investigation opened in January 2025. Prosecutors say the pair connected Colombian cartels with cocaine buyers in the Netherlands and arranged shipments of hundreds of kilos at a time.

Intercepted chat messages then led investigators to a web of associates, and twelve further investigations are now running.

One concerns four men who allegedly prepared to kidnap the girlfriend of a man suspected of stealing a cocaine shipment in 2024, a theft that left a debt of more than €700,000. The kidnapping did not go ahead, and prosecutors say they do not know why.

Another involves two men accused of extorting around 1,000 clients of the sex-work website Kinky, who allegedly faced threats of serious violence unless they paid. Police believe the pair took more than €100,000.

The Netherlands has invested heavily in police cooperation with Colombia, which prosecutors say is now producing results, with several Dutch nationals arrested there. The main suspects’ cases will not be heard in full until they are extradited

World.title: Health inspectors ban webshop from selling weight loss drugs
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Health inspectors have banned a website from selling unlicensed weight loss drugs that it advertised on social media.

De Peptidekoning sold two medicines prescribed to treat diabetes, semaglutide and tirzepatide, and a third, retatrutide, which is an experimental drug that has not been licensed in any country.

The Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) ordered the owners of the website to stop selling all three substances and warned patients not to risk their health with experimental treatments.

It said De Peptidekoning, which trades through several websites including puritybase.com, did not have a license to sell the medicines. “They have not adequately ensured that the medicines meet standards for quality, safety and effectiveness,” the IGJ said.

“The way in which the medicines were offered for sale does not give enough reassurances, which creates risks for public health.”

RTL Nieuws reported that unauthorised traders were profiting from a black market in slimming treatments for people who were not prescribed medicines such as Ozempic, which are only available in the Netherlands to treat diabetes.

Marloes Dankers, of the Utrecht-based Dutch Institute for the Rational Use of Medicine, an advisory body set up by doctors and pharmacists, said: “People are making guinea-pigs of themselves.

“These medicines are still being researched and we don’t know what exactly the risks are. That’s the reason for doing the research.”

Eli Lilly, the American manufacturer developing retratrutide, also urged people not to buy the drug online.

“What is being sold on the black market is not a medicine, it has not been approved or verified in any way and it is not worth the risk,” the company said.

World.title: Both Dutch teams reach hockey World Cup semi-finals
World.content:
The Dutch men’s hockey team moved into the semi-finals of the World Cup in Amstelveen on Monday evening with a 2-2 draw against England in what was a tense and physical game.

The Dutch needed at least a draw to be sure of progressing to the next round, while England were chasing a win by a two-goal margin.

Playing in bright sunlight in a packed Wagener Stadium, England opened the scoring after five minutes, with the Dutch equalising with just 40 seconds remaining before the end of the first half.

England went into the lead again 90 seconds into the second half but the Netherlands drew level once more. England took off their goalkeeper with seven minutes to go, but despite piling on the pressure, the Dutch kept them at bay, much to the delight of the largely orange-clad crowd.

The 2-2 draw was enough to put the Netherlands at the top of their group, with Argentina, who beat India 5-3, in second place. The Netherlands will now meet Spain in the semi-finals in Amstelveen on Friday, while Argentina will play Germany in Belgium, which is co-hosting the tournament.

In the women’s competition, the Netherlands are hot favourites and will meet Belgium in the first semi-final on Thursday at the Wagener Stadium. They beat China 4-1 on Sunday to reach the next stage. Argentina will play Spain in Belgium.

World.title: NS offers cheaper tickets to ease busy morning trains
World.content:
NS is making some rush-hour train tickets cheaper from Tuesday, in an effort to ease its busiest morning services and free up seats.

The national rail operator is extending its PrijsTijd Deals – advance-purchase tickets that give a discount for travelling on quieter trains – to the edges of the morning peak. Discounts there will average around 30%, against up to 60% in the quietest off-peak hours. The tickets must be bought at least a day ahead.

The move is separate from the €49 summer pass for unlimited off-peak travel, which runs until September 1. It is also exactly the same as an earlier NS plan to add a surcharge to peak fares, which MPs blocked in 2023.

NS says the crush is worst on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, when large numbers of passengers travel within a single hour. Nudging even a fraction of them onto a train 15 or 30 minutes earlier or later, it argues, spreads the load and means more people get a seat.

“The NS, like electricity grid operators for example, has to deal with peak load,” said NS timetabling director Tijmen Voet. “But if a small percentage of travellers choose a less busy alternative, passengers have to stand far less often.”

Limited reach

Rail passengers’ association Rover welcomed the extension but said more was needed to make a real difference. It has long argued the discounts should also be bookable on the day of travel, rather than only up to a day ahead.

The reach is likely to stay limited, a Rover spokesperson said, because many hyper-peak travellers hold season tickets paid for by their employer and feel no price incentive. Others cannot shift their journey because of fixed school or work hours.

An NS trial last year found a fifth of passengers would take a quieter train in return for a discount, with most willing to wait up to half an hour. That, Voet said, lets the operator run fewer long trains for peak crowds that otherwise travel largely empty for the rest of the day.

World.title: Smoke-free 2040 goal failing as young adults keep vaping
World.content:
A survey has suggested that four in ten young adults in the Netherlands smoke or vape, pointing to how far the country remains from its goal of a smoke-free generation by 2040.

Under the National Prevention Agreement, the government wants nobody in the younger generation to be smoking or vaping by then, and fewer than 5% of adults to do so.

The 40% figure comes from a poll of 2,000 people by comparison website Independer, which found the habit most common among 18-to-29-year-olds. The share drops to around 30% among people in their thirties, 17% among the over-45s and 10% among the over-60s.

Independer is a commercial comparison site rather than a statistical agency, and its figure is well above official data. National statistics agency CBS put the proportion of 18-to-25-year-olds who smoke or vape at roughly a quarter in 2024.

Doctors want a ban

Paediatric lung specialist Noor Rikkers, of the Artsen slaan alarm (doctors sound the alarm) campaign group, called the numbers shocking and said the rise of vaping was drawing in ever-younger children.

She wants the government to ban all products that contain nicotine, arguing that a blanket ban would be simpler to enforce than the current patchwork of rules.

Social media a factor

The survey also pointed to social media. About three-quarters of young adults said they saw videos of people smoking or vaping, and a third of those said the clips tempted them to try it.

More than a quarter of the young smokers who watched such videos said they bought cigarettes or vapes through social media, even though online and social-media sales of tobacco and vapes have been banned since 2023 – a rule dealers have been flouting on Snapchat.

Flavoured vapes have been banned since January 2024, but doctors and inspectors say a black market keeps supplying illegal products.

World.title: Dutch broadcaster AvroTros to boycott Eurovision again in 2027
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch broadcaster AvroTros will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year in 2027 in protest at Israel’s continuing participation.

The company called in a statement for “transparent rules” on countries involved in military conflicts to restore the “neutrality” of the event.

“It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character,” director-general Taco Zimmerman said. “The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division.”

The Netherlands was one of five countries that refused to enter last year’s competition in response to the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, although the contest in Austria was still shown on Dutch TV by public broadcaster NPO.

The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has since changed its rules to ban winning countries from hosting the following year’s event if they are involved in a “sensitive geopolitical situation” that affects the “security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region”.

But AvroTros said the revision did not go far enough to reassure it that the “independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored”.

Humanity

“Participation is therefore no longer consistent with the values of AvroTros: trustworthiness, independence and humanity,” it said.

The new rules are essentially a recognition of existing practice: Ukraine won the contest in 2022, but the following year’s event was held in the UK because of the Russian invasion.

NPO said it would consider whether it would broadcast next year’s song contest, which is being held in Bulgaria.

A spokesman said it was “a great shame” that AvroTros was boycotting the event. “We see that the geopolitical tensions are having a divisive effect. That makes it a difficult decision for our colleagues.”

World.title: Saints and Stars gym chain fined €300k for breaching work rules
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Amsterdam gym chain Saints and Stars has been hit with more than €300,000 in fines for breaching Dutch employment laws.

The biggest fine of €234,000 after labour inspectors found it hired 25 non-EU nationals without permits and had failed to check the identity of three staff.

The gym was at the centre of controversy last year when city newspaper Het Parool reported that it forced cleaners from Indonesia and the Philippines to work 17 hours a day and share beds with strangers while working in its four branches.

The exposée prompted several trainers and influencers to cancel their memberships at the €139-a-month gym. Last December a judge awarded five Filipino cleaners €15,000 each in compensation.

The latest fines also included €60,000 for failing to comply with the laws on minimum wage and holiday pay, after inspectors were unable to determine how many hours employees had worked and whether they had received the minimum wage.

The chain was also fined €22,500 for not observing mandatory break times.

The inspectors also issued two official warnings to Saints and Stars, meaning the gyms could be temporarily closed if they breach the rules a third time in the next five years.

The company said it would not appeal against the fines. “This should not have happened,” owner Tom Moos said in a press statement.

Polish state defence firm Mesko has signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.9 billion) agreement to supply its Piorun man-portable air-defence systems to the armed forces of Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia. The deal is being financed through the European Union’s SAFE mechanism. The agreement represents the largest-ever purchase of Pioruns, which have become an export hit for Mesko after proving their worth during Ukraine’s defence against Russian aggression. Previous buyers include Sweden, the United States, Belgium, Estonia and Norway itself. Nowy etap #PolskaSAFE. Rozpoczynamy wspólne zakupy i to znów w polskim przemyśle! To jak to było,… pic.twitter.com/YIDWBGBvpm — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) August 24, 2026 The deal will see the firm provide “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles for its shoulder-fired Piorun systems, which target low-flying aircraft such as planes, helicopters and drones. Over 80% will be supplied to Poland’s armed forces, with the remainder going to its three NATO allies. The purchase is being funded through SAFE, which provides loans at preferential terms for defence spending. While SAFE can be used individually by countries to make purchases for their own armed forces, some funds are designated for joint procurement by groups of countries (including non-EU member Norway). “Our partners from Lithuania, Latvia and Norway have decided to purchase from Poland,” declared deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who oversees Poland’s participation in SAFE. “We are a leader in the SAFE mechanism and are the first to create such agreements. For the first time, the [Polish defence ministry’s] Armaments Agency is making purchases not only for the Polish armed forces, but also for those of our allies.” “This is a measure of the success of the Polish arms industry,” declared defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, as the deal was announced on Monday. “This is the moment when Poland can proudly say: we are a European leader.” He noted that Mesko’s production capacity is now 2.5 times larger than it was when the current government took power in December 2023. Since SAFE launched in May, the firm’s staffing, which stood at 3,200 by the end of last year, has increased by around 200, added the minister. Poland is by far the largest recipient of SAFE funds, with around €44 billion. The government says that SAFE will not only bolster Poland’s defence capabilities but also provide a boost to the domestic defence industry, where around 90% of the funds will be spent. However, the programme has been opposed by the right-wing opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argue that it will give Brussels too much influence over Polish defence spending and burden Poland with decades of debt on uncertain terms. World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. We explain what @KosiniakKamysz actually said and how it came to be misinterpreted https://t.co/S3bozRIJTA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
