The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Fitch highlights gold’s impact on Azerbaijan’s SOFAZ assets
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Gold is the largest component of the investment portfolio of the State Oil Fund of Azerbaijan (SOFAZ), accounting for 36% of its assets.

This was stated in a new report by the international rating agency Fitch Ratings.

According to the report, SOFAZ’s assets as of the end of the first quarter of 2026 totaled $73.5 billion, which corresponds to 93.2% of Azerbaijan’s projected GDP for 2026.

Fitch notes that gold assets directly contributed to a $19.4 billion increase in SOFAZ’s assets between 2023 and the first quarter of 2026. Of this growth, 26% was attributable to the volume effect.

"Azerbaijan’s ‘BBB-’ rating, according to Fitch, is also being upgraded by one notch due to the significant volume of SOFAZ’s assets. These assets provide the country with a high level of foreign currency liquidity and the status of a net external creditor.

Rising gold prices have a positive impact on the value of SOFAZ’s assets; however, this effect may be offset to varying degrees by changes in the volume of gold reserves. Specifically, in the period from January through April 2026, SOFAZ carried out accumulated sales of a portion of its gold reserves as part of a rebalancing of its investment portfolio.

“The rise in gold prices supports Azerbaijan’s rating, but in the near term, it is unlikely to be a factor in its further upgrade,” the agency reports.

Overall, Fitch notes a significant increase in the gold reserves of central banks and sovereign wealth funds in the Caucasus and Central Asia amid rising gold prices.

World.title: Kazakhstan's international reserves rise nearly 90% since early 2024 - Fitch
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Kazakhstan's international reserves increased by nearly 90% from the beginning of 2024 to reach $67.6 billion, or 18% of projected 2026 GDP, in May 2026, according to Fitch Ratings.

The growth was largely supported by an increase in the value of the country's gold reserves.

"While Kazakhstan is one of the largest producers of gold in the world (with production of 87 tonnes in 2024), gold accounted for only 0.5% of its exports that year. Nonetheless, Kazakhstan’s international reserves have risen by nearly 90% from the start of 2024 to USD67.6 billion (18% of 2026F GDP) in May 2026, aided by a 169% increase in the value of gold reserves. Gold reserves now make up 78% of international reserves (end-2023: 54.3%)," Fitch said.

The agency noted that Kazakhstan's large external asset position is underpinned by its sovereign wealth fund, the National Fund of the Republic of Kazakhstan (NFRK).

"The NFRK’s assets totalled USD66.4 billion (17.7% of GDP) as of May 2026, around 11% larger than the start of 2024, with gold making up about 6.5%. The government aims to increase the NFRK’s assets to USD100 billion by 2030 as part of its public finance management framework," Fitch said.

Fitch also noted that global gold mining output grew by an average of 2% annually in 2011-2025, while the largest increase was recorded in the Central and Central Asian (CCA) region, including Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

"The average annual growth of gold mining output globally was 2% in 2011-2025. The largest increase was achieved in the CCA region (Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan (BBB/Stable), Kyrgyzstan (B/Stable)), where growth averaged 4.7% annually. In Uzbekistan, production rose by 8% in 2024 to reach a peak of 129 tonnes (2.9x 2010 levels), before moderating by 3% in 2025. Production in Kazakhstan peaked at 88 tonnes in 2023 (3x 2010 levels), and has since declined," Fitch noted.

World.title: Kazakhstan steps up energy infrastructure preparations for heating season
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Kazakhstan has allocated 384 billion tenge (about $809.0 million) for repair programs at power plants ahead of the 2026-2027 heating season.

This was announced by the press service of the Kazakh Government, citing Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov's remarks at the Government meeting.

According to the information, the meeting reviewed preparations for the country's energy and utilities infrastructure for the upcoming autumn-winter period, including repair works, fuel reserves and digital monitoring tools.

Under the system operator's schedule, nine power units, 55 boilers and 51 turbines are due to undergo repairs this year. Work is already underway at various stages on three power units, 33 boilers and 24 turbines.

The total funding for power plant repair programs has increased by 9% compared with last year.

Regional electricity grid companies have planned repairs on 17,100 km of transmission lines and 444 substations. Readiness currently stands at 91% and 84%, respectively.

The number of technological incidents at power plants decreased by 5.6% year-on-year to 891 in the first seven months of the year. At the same time, increased accident rates at several facilities were investigated by the Committee for Atomic and Energy Supervision and Control, with relevant measures taken.

The minister said that to take urgent measures to prepare energy infrastructure, 27.9 billion tenge (about $58.8 million) has been allocated from the Government reserve. Of this amount, 12.7 billion tenge ($26.8 million) was allocated for the repair and construction of heat sources, 8.4 billion tenge ($17.7 million) for heating networks, and 6.8 billion tenge ($14.3 million) for the reconstruction of power grids.

A total of 196.8 billion tenge ($414.7 million) has been allocated for the reconstruction and overhaul of 377 km of heating networks. This includes 82.5 billion tenge ($173.8 million) in budget funds, 98.1 billion tenge ($206.7 million) under the National MEXS Project, and 16.2 billion tenge ($34.1 million) under tariff estimates.

Funding for heating network preparations has increased by 34%, while the volume of work has grown by 14%. So far, 246 km, or 65% of the planned volume, has been upgraded.

Energy facilities have also accumulated the required fuel reserves, including 4.2 million tons of coal and 137,000 tons of fuel oil, 2% more than last year's level.

A schedule has been approved for the delivery of 255,000 tons of socially important fuel oil starting in September. At the same time, Akkenzhenov called for the prompt repayment of energy companies' outstanding debts for supplied gas. Their debt to QazaqGaz Aimaq currently amounts to 71.9 billion tenge ($151.5 million).

Households and the utilities sector are expected to require 7.3 million tons of coal during the upcoming heating season, including 1.6 million tons for the utilities sector and 5.7 million tons for households.

Demand has declined from 8.3 million tons last year due to the implementation of Kazakhstan's General Gasification Scheme through 2035.

To prevent shortages of solid fuel, the Energy Ministry has launched a unified digital platform incorporating artificial intelligence and predictive analytics. The system integrates data from 36 coal mining companies, 29,000 railway gondola cars, 586 coal terminal operators, and more than 1.2 million consumers, enabling real-time monitoring of supply chains and automatic identification of logistics risks.

World.title: Gold boom bolsters financial resilience across Caucasus and Central Asia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Rising gold prices and increased gold reserves have strengthened the external financial positions of countries in the Caucasus and Central Asia, enhancing their resilience to external volatility.

According to a new report by the international rating agency Fitch Ratings, the region’s international reserves have grown significantly since 2023, with gold purchases and rising gold prices playing a major role. At the same time, Fitch notes that an increase in the share of gold in reserves and exports could become a source of vulnerability in the event of a sharp decline in gold prices.

“Gold has gained greater importance in the structure of the region’s external sovereign buffers. Uzbekistan has the world’s highest share of gold in its international reserves, while gold also accounts for the bulk of Kyrgyzstan’s reserves. Azerbaijan’s sovereign wealth fund, which forms the basis of the country’s substantial foreign reserves, holds significant assets in gold.

Rising gold prices have also supported the balance of payments of gold-exporting countries. In Uzbekistan, the current account deficit narrowed significantly between 2023 and 2025, driven by growth in gold exports. Kyrgyzstan also benefited from gold price and export trends, although its export performance remained volatile,” Fitch notes.

The coverage of current external payments by international reserves has improved in the countries of the region, and reserve adequacy remains an important factor in assessing the credit ratings of all sovereign borrowers in the Caucasus and Central Asia.

Fitch notes concentration risk as a factor limiting the credit benefits of rising gold prices. Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan are the most vulnerable to a sharp decline in gold prices.

“In the event of such a decline, the nominal GDP, fiscal indicators, and balance of payments indicators of gold-producing countries will deteriorate, and the value of reserves will decline in countries with a high proportion of gold in their reserves.

The decline in gold prices is expected, in and of itself, to lead to negative rating actions against these sovereign borrowers,” Fitch said in a report.

World.title: Education union 'blindsided' by ACT public school budget shake-up
World.content:
Public schools in the ACT have received their budgets for next year, with a change in the way their funding is calculated, seeing a number of schools facing a reduction.

The budget shake-up is being made in response to a review of public school resourcing, which found there needed to be more of a focus on equity and student need.

ACT Education Director-General Jo Wood said the independent Public School System Resourcing Review found a significant portion of financial pressures were in primary schools, but the way funding was calculated gave more weight to older students.

Jo Wood says the directorate is commissioning a holistic review of the public school funding formula. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

"That independent review found one of the pressures on the system and one of the equity issues was the higher weighting that's given to the per-student funding depending on the stage of schooling," Ms Wood said.

"So for example, primary schools get a lower per-student amount than, say, a college.

"The review said we needed to look at that whole funding formula, and we are commissioning a holistic review of that funding formula, but as a first step for 2027 we've made a small adjustment to the weighting for colleges … so that we can get a better distribution of funding across the system."

Eighteen schools will see their funding drop by more than 5 per cent, 31 will see an increase of more than 5 per cent, and 43 schools will receive about the same amount as they did in 2026.

'A significant financial adjustment and a very short turnaround'

Among those worse off are the ACT's nine colleges — which are facing a combined $4 million budget reduction, according to the Australian Education Union (AEU).

AEU ACT branch president Angela Burroughs said some schools had been "blindsided" by the changes.

Angela Burroughs says the scale of the changes to funding for colleges may force them to cut whole programs. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

"The scale of it, and the way that it's being implemented, is very unexpected," Ms Burroughs said.

"It could be whole programs that have to go. It could be a performing arts program that's no longer viable, or a language education program that's no longer viable.

"It's a significant financial adjustment that college principals need to make, and a very short turnaround time to get ready for 2027."

Executive officer of ACT Parents, Veronica Elliott, said the organisation was "surprised" to learn the 2027 funding changes included a reduction in the funding weighting for colleges.

"The ACT college system is highly valued by families because of the breadth and diversity of courses and pathways available to students," Ms Elliott said.

"We support the objective of greater equity across public education, but changes to college resourcing could affect staffing and the courses colleges are able to offer next year.

"That's particularly important because students have already enrolled and submitted their preferences for 2027."

Veronica Elliott says changes to college resourcing could affect the courses that are able to be offered. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

AEU ACT branch vice-president Simon Vaughan, who is also the principal of an ACT public college, said he did not know what classroom choices his school would be able to offer new year 11 students next year.

"There is a quantum of savings I will have to find," Dr Vaughan said.

"Extracurricular things would probably be areas we need to target.

" And if we have to, for example, cut staff, that may cut programs. "

Ms Wood said the ACT Education Directorate would be offering extra support for schools whose funding was being reduced.

The ACT Education Directorate says it will offer extra support to schools whose funding is being reduced. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"We do have some funding in a central pool that, as we do the work with schools about how they can make those reductions, where there are circumstances that they can't reduce by as much as that, we have the capacity to provide some supplementation," she said.

"And the main thing we want is that people, our principals and school leaders, feel that it's OK to ask for support.

" We're not asking any principal to do this work alone. We are available and have a range of different expertise to provide support. "

Schools will need to finalise their arrangements for 2027 in the coming weeks.

World.title: Luke Gosling charged with breach of bail just weeks after alleged assaults
World.content:
Federal politician Luke Gosling has been charged with breaching his bail conditions, less than a month after he was arrested over allegations he assaulted the Northern Territory Administrator.

In July, the Labor MP was charged with two counts of assault over an alleged incident involving NT Administrator David Connolly at a community event held in Darwin earlier that month.

Mr Gosling is the Commonwealth's special envoy for defence and veterans' affairs, and has held the seat of Solomon — which includes Darwin and its satellite city of Palmerston — since 2016.

The administrator is the Crown's representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.

David Connolly took on the job of Northern Territory Administrator earlier this year. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

Mr Gosling's bail conditions were varied in Darwin Local Court on July 31, with the federal MP banned from coming within 50 metres of the NT's Government House — where Mr Connolly resides.

Judge Stephen Geary also ordered Mr Gosling to give Mr Connolly's office 48 hours' notice before attending any event where both men would be in attendance.

If the two do attend the same event, Mr Gosling is required to stay 15 metres away from the administrator at all times.

In a statement released to media this afternoon, NT Police said Mr Gosling allegedly breached his bail conditions on August 14.

"Today he was served with a summons to appear in Darwin Local Court on 30 September 2026," NT Police said.

Gosling to fight assault charges

In a statement released this evening, a spokesperson for Mr Gosling said no details had been shared by police regarding the alleged breach.

Last month, Luke Gosling faced Darwin Local Court where he was granted bail. (ABC News: Matilda Colling)

"Neither Mr Gosling nor his office have been made aware of the nature of the alleged breach and have been provided no information from police other than a summons," the spokesperson said.

"On Friday, August 14 Mr Gosling did not attend any events at the same time as the administrator.

"Mr Gosling is discussing the matter with his legal team, and will be defending the charge."

The statement said Mr Gosling's office would not comment further "as the matter is before the court", listed to be heard on September 30.

During Mr Gosling's first court appearance, the court heard the assault charges related to two separate incidents which allegedly occurred 30 minutes apart.

Luke Gosling to be prosecuted by Commonwealth DPP The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions is set to take over the case against Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling, to avoid a perceived conflict of interest within the Northern Territory Director of Public Prosecutions.

In discussing the reported details, Mr Gosling's lawyer Marty Aust SC told the court the first alleged incident had occurred "in a manner in which the administrator was unable to see the approach".

The court heard the second charge pertained to an alleged hip-and-shoulder collision between the two men, during which Mr Gosling allegedly drew back his left elbow and struck Mr Connolly in his upper rib.

Mr Gosling has strenuously denied the assault allegations, with his lawyer previously telling media the charges would be contested in court.

The federal MP has faced pressure to step down from his political role since news broke of the alleged assault, including from Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson and NT Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price.

Federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor urged Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to stand down the Solomon MP.

In a statement released after news broke of the fresh charge, Angus Taylor urged the prime minister to stand down the Solomon MP. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"When these serious charges were first laid, we said this was a test of the prime minister's leadership and Luke Gosling should be stood down from his special envoy role while the matter is dealt with," Mr Taylor said in a statement released this afternoon.

"Now Mr Gosling has also been charged with allegedly breaching his bail, the case for the prime minister to act is even stronger.

"These allegations are matters for the courts, but Anthony Albanese has a decision to make about who serves in his government. He should stand Mr Gosling down today."

But Mr Albanese has doubled down on his earlier stance, claiming again this evening that it would be inappropriate to comment while legal proceedings play out.

"There is a legal process underway. No further comment at this time," a spokesperson for the prime minister said.

World.title: Distress beacon borrowing program proposed after teen hiker's death
World.content:
A New South Wales mayor has described Lily Hooper as an amazing woman full of spirit and adventure who was taken too soon, while promising to establish a bushwalking safety program in her honour.

The 18-year-old's body was found in bushland of the Nattai National Park, near Mittagong, last Thursday after an eight-day search.

Almost 1,000 people from multiple agencies took part in the search when she did not return from her solo hike on the Bonnen Pic Walking Trail.

The cause of her death is not yet known, but NSW Police have said her body was located a significant distance from the path.

Wollondilly Shire Council held a minute's silence at its council meeting on Tuesday afternoon.

Mayor Matt Gould said the council would collaborate with NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service to make bushwalking safety equipment more readily available.

Lily Hooper, 18, went missing while hiking in Nattai National Park. (Supplied: NSW Police)

"I've spoken with Lily's family about how our community might permanently remember her," Cr Gould said during council's ordinary meeting on Wednesday.

"Rather than creating a single physical memorial … we will establish a program in Lily's memory where council purchases personal locator beacons and makes them available for residents and bushwalkers to borrow free of charge, alongside practical bushwalking safety information.

"A personal locator beacon is something you hope nobody ever needs to activate, but if someone does find themselves in trouble in remote country, having one can make an enormous difference.

"My hope is that this becomes a living and practical legacy in Lily's name, something that helps people enjoy the bush safely."

Matt Gould says the community's response to Lily Hooper's death has been overwhelming. (ABC News)

Cr Gould also thanked emergency crews involved in the search for Ms Hooper and said there had been an enormous outpouring of community grief.

"While most of us never knew Lily personally, I think over the past two weeks, our community has come to understand just how special she was through the people who did," he said.

Purple lights, flags lowered

Tributes left in memory of Ms Hooper at Oakdale's Willis Park, south west of Sydney, have been carefully collected after the town was hit by wet weather.

With the support of her family, council staff gathered some of the cards and signs on Monday to protect them from rain.

The items have been passed on to the Hoopers, with the memorial space to remain open to the community until Friday.

An outpouring of grief has followed the death of bushwalker Lily Hooper. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Just hours after Ms Hooper's body was found, Wollondilly Performing Arts Centre was lit up purple and the council chamber's flags flown at half mast.

Ms Hooper's former school, Campelltown Performing Arts High School, posted an online tribute, describing their 2025 graduate as a kind, humorous and respectful young woman.

"[She] lit up every room with her infectious smile, positive energy and determination to live life to the full," the post read.

"This loss has had a significant impact on our students, staff and wider school community."

Meanwhile, a fundraiser organised by the Rotary Club of Wollondilly North in support of the Hooper family has raised a growing $30,000.

Dozens of community members, friends and family have flocked to Oakdale's Willis Park to pay their respects to Lily Hooper. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

State government honour

NSW Premier Chris Minns on Monday promised to work with Ms Hooper's family on a special tribute to honour her.

Her father, Jim Hooper, told 7NEWS he would like the flag on the Sydney Harbour Bridge lowered as she worked as a Bridge Climb tour guide.

"I want to talk with them and work on it together, but we'll do something special for Lily and frankly it's the least we can do," Mr Minns said.

" It's a terrible life lost and it's a lovely family. "

NSW Deputy Premier Prue Car said on Sunday the government was open to reviewing safety signage in national parks to prevent deaths like Ms Hooper's.

"We are open to ideas on that. We are constantly saying to people, 'Try and get your kids off their phones and into nature,' but we have to make sure we are making that are safe as possible," she said.

Lily Hooper went missing is in rugged terrain south of Sydney. (Supplied: NSW National Parks)

The comments come just days after Mr Minns vowed to apologise in person to Ms Hooper's family after he told parliament their daughter was found alive.

"I'm also absolutely devastated and profoundly sorry that anything I said may have added to the grief that that family has gone through," Mr Minns said on Friday.

Emergency services are examining whether a miscommunication about a police code may have led to Ms Hooper being incorrectly identified as alive.

A coronial investigation is also underway.

World.title: SA wildlife park to vaccinate 100 birds against deadly H5 bird flu
World.content:
About 100 captive native birds at Cleland Wildlife Park will be vaccinated against H5N1 bird flu.

They include critically endangered orange-bellied parrots and, regent honeyeaters, endangered red-tailed black cockatoos and vulnerable regent parrots, in addition to 26 other bird species at the park.

Primary Industries and Regional Development Clare Scriven said Cleland would be the first South Australian wildlife park to gain approval to administer the H5N1 vaccine to its captive birds.

It recently received federal funding to upgrade several aviaries in anticipation of the arrival of bird flu in Australia.

Cleland Wildlife Park general manager Kelly Bramhill said biosecurity measures have restricted public access to three other aviaries not subject to the upgrades.

"Vaccination for us really is that last line of defence," she said.

Vaccine not a 'silver bullet'

Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said Australia currently had around 1,500 vaccine vials available.

The vaccines are not fully protective against the disease, and would require two shots to maximise immunity.

Native Australian species are receiving the vaccine for the first time, and will be monitored before undergoing the final dose.

Ms Scriven said the vaccine was "not a silver bullet".

"We are not 100 per cent sure of the effectiveness of the vaccines on particular species," she said.

Cleland Wildlife Park general manager Kelly Bramhill said vaccines are the last stage of efforts to protect the sanctuary's native birds. (ABC News)

Ms Scriven said logistical difficulties capturing, vaccinating and monitoring wild birds meant captive and endangered species were the government's current priority.

SA's chief veterinary officer Dr Skye Fruean said Zoos SA, which operates the Adelaide Zoo and Monarto Safari Park, was the only other organisation working through a vaccine approval process with the Department for Primary Industries and Regions.

"We’re working with them to make sure that it can meet all the regulatory requirements and can be done safely … we’ve been discussions with them for a little while and will meet them again this week," Dr Fruean said.

A vaccination program for Phillip Island's little penguin colony is also underway.

World.title: Brumby cull on hold after advocate launches last minute court action
World.content:
The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) has temporarily suspended aerial culls and trapping operations in a northern NSW national park following an urgent injunction from an advocate, claiming the killing of brumbies there is unlawful.

The five-day aerial culling operation of feral horses, pigs, foxes and deer was scheduled to take place from Monday in Yuraygir National Park, north of Coffs Harbour, but has been postponed for at least two weeks to allow for court proceedings.

Anti-brumby culling advocate Carmen Jackson filed an urgent injunction to the Land and Environment Court about 1am on Monday, with the matter adjourned to later that morning.

Carmen Jackson (right) says she filed the injunction at 1am on Monday, concerned National Parks and Wildlife did not have the authority to conduct brumby culls in Yuraygir National Park. (Supplied: Carmen Jackson)

Justice Rachel Pepper today adjourned the matter, telling the court final hearings would be heard on September 9 to allow both parties to gather their evidence.

She told the court there was "urgency involved".

"The undertaking has been given in good faith by the department, again at short notice and I do think the matter needs to be dealt with quickly for your sake, the animals in question and the department," Justice Pepper said.

Speaking on behalf of the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, the department's principal legal officer Nicholas Sandstrom told the court they would "suspend trappings and all operations until that date".

In a statement, a spokesperson for the NSW NPWS said they acknowledge the proceedings and will comply with any directions from the court, confirming all aerial, ground shooting and trapping operations in the National Park and State Conservation Area would be suspended.

Aerial culls of wild horses, foxes, deer and pigs in the national park were due to commence on Monday. (ABC South East NSW: Adriane Reardon)

"Animal welfare is a high priority, and all operations are conducted under strict procedures," the statement read.

"As the matter is before the court, it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Brumby debate re-ignited

Ms Jackson said she was concerned NPWS did not have the statutory authority to perform the culls.

She said she does not support brumby control measures, with the court proceedings sparking renewed debate over their handling.

"Our brumbies are our Australian heritage; they're also sentient beings on Country," she said.

"I believe all animals have the right to be on Country. How do we signify that a brumby is less significant than a native animal on Country, considering they've been here 200 years."

State member for Clarence and Nationals MP Richie Williamson welcomed news this week's operation had been put on hold.

Richie Williamson has voiced opposition to the operation in Yuraygir National Park. (Supplied: Richie Williamson)

Community members also gathered at Halfway Creek on Saturday ahead of the planned culls, calling for the operation's end and arguing the north coast brumby population was small.

Professor David Watson, from Charles Sturt University, said brumbies were incredibly destructive for the habitat of other native animals, which were forced to compete for food and resources.

"Four or five animals aren't going to have a huge impact on a huge national park, but they breed … the right number is no horses," he said.

David Watson says feral horses are incredibly destructive and do not belong in national parks. (Supplied: David Watson)

" Our ecosystems have had no evolutionary history of dealing with a large hoofed animal like this, so they really do wreck the place. "

He said while he understands concerns, brumbies were as destructive to the Australian environment and wildlife as other feral pests.

"I get it … I love horses, they are special animals and humans have had a connection with horses for a long time."

"[But] from an ecological point of view that goes out the window."

World.title: Two Victoria Police officers cleared of manslaughter over man's death
World.content:
Manslaughter charges against two Victoria Police officers have been thrown out by a magistrate who contrasted the case with the death of George Floyd.

Luke Briggs, 35, died eight days after he was arrested in a convenience store car park at Hoppers Crossing, in Melbourne's south west, in July 2024.

Constable Alexander Papanastassis, 30, and Sergeant James Fitzgerald, 46, were each charged with negligent manslaughter over his death, but they fought the charges at a committal hearing.

Luke Briggs, 35, died eight days after he was arrested by two officers. (Supplied: Robinson Gill Laywers)

Melbourne magistrate Patrick Southey on Tuesday determined there was insufficient evidence for the case to go to trial and dismissed the charges.

"The evidence is so weak that the prospect of a conviction is minimal," Mr Southey said.

"It may be the manner in which Mr Briggs was restrained was the substantial and operative cause of death, but we'll never know."

Mr Briggs allegedly became unresponsive during the arrest, and the officers performed CPR before calling for medical assistance.

The 35-year-old died in a Melbourne hospital intensive care unit on July 23, surrounded by family.

Photos at the time showed bruising on his arms as he lay in a hospital bed.

Mr Briggs's family suing the state

In delivering his ruling, Mr Southey referred to the high-profile case of African American man George Floyd in the United States.

Mr Floyd was murdered by a white police officer who was arresting him in May 2020.

His dying words of "I can't breathe" were also said by Mr Briggs, the magistrate noted.

"It seems to me the parallels end there," Mr Southey said.

"There is no comparison to this case where … the police were doing the best they could.

"It was not a perfect job but the best they could do in all the circumstances."

The magistrate noted Mr Briggs was a large, powerful man whose behaviour had been irrational due to methamphetamine use.

"It was an unfortunate, tragic chain of events but in my view, it does not amount to criminal negligence," Mr Southey said.

He awarded costs to Constable Papanastassis and Sergeant Fitzgerald, who have both been suspended from duties since the incident.

Members of Mr Briggs's family were visibly upset as the decision was handed down on Tuesday afternoon.

The family is separately suing the state, accusing the officers of breaching their duty of care and Victoria Police of failing to "properly supervise, control or train their employees, officers and/or agents".

Mr Southey indicated his ruling had no basis on any civil proceedings and the prosecution could still choose to directly indict the two officers on fresh criminal charges.

The Police Association Victoria said it stood by its members throughout the whole process and would continue to support them.

"That night they did what any of their colleagues would have done," secretary Wayne Gatt said.

"They pulled over a suspicious vehicle and attempted to speak to the driver.

"When the situation escalated into a physical confrontation, they tried to manage it peacefully, but they were not afforded that opportunity."

Mr Gatt said the officers' actions "did not amount to criminal negligence, nor did their conduct warrant the intervention of the criminal law" and acknowledged the sometimes dangerous work officers did in the field.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Chinese factory workers accidentally caught on camera glasses
World.content:
Factory workers who helped make a Chinese-brand of camera glasses appear to have been unknowingly filmed by the devices in accidental videos.

7.30 bought a pair of budget glasses made by Shenzhen-based company Oho Sunshine online and found footage already on the device, which appears to be from inside the factory.

The collection of four short videos, dated last year, shows a number of workers sitting at their desks inspecting the glasses, while listening to jaunty electronic music.

Video appears to have been filmed inside a factory while the glasses were being made. (ABC News)

One video clearly identifies a worker lifting a pair and shaking them vigorously.

Another three videos, up to 10 minutes long and dated this year, show only black with atmospheric audio, suggesting the glasses were activated while inside a case or box.

The shoot button on the side of the frames is sensitive and easily switched on.

The workers appear to be filmed unknowingly by the glasses. (ABC News)

7.30 approached Oho Sunshine, with questions about the apparent privacy breach but received no response.

Oho Sunshine was founded in 2009 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in Guandong province, north of Hong Kong, as a smart wearable technologies manufacturer, according to the company's website.

The accidental leak perhaps proves not even the workers who make camera glasses are safe from being filmed and provides a rare insight into the globalised production chain.

Do you know more about this story? Contact Jason Om at Om.Jason@abc.net.au.

Rise of camera glasses

7.30 reporter Jason Om wearing the Oho Sunshine camera glasses that already had footage on them. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Camera glasses are enjoying a surge in popularity as cheap brands flood the market. Oho is just one of numerous companies manufacturing similar devices.

They look like ordinary glasses and allow you to record video and audio, largely without people knowing.

While some models have a built-in light to indicate filming, there are now services that remove the indicator cheaply.

A pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

The glasses can play music and make calls, with more high-tech versions allowing users to live-stream or swipe through messages on a display in the lenses.

Meta's fashionable Ray-Ban smart glasses can cost up to $700 a pair, but basic versions can be bought online for as little as $40.

Kmart Australia's $89 Anko brand of camera glasses recently sold out, prompting an online petition to stop their sale amid concerns about privacy and their use by male content creators recording women without their knowledge and uploading the videos to potentially millions of followers.

While filming in public places is generally legal, the devices have raised new concerns around privacy.

Filmed without consent on 'rizz cam'

Beth Knight was filmed with camera glasses at a train station and later found the video of herself online. (ABC News: Daniel Ioh)

Beth Knight, 18, found herself the subject of lurid commentary from online users after a man filmed her with camera glasses and uploaded it to social media without her knowledge.

At the time of the incident late last year, she was 17 and by herself at London's busy Waterloo station.

"I'd missed my train, so I had 40 minutes to wait in the station," Ms Knight told 7.30.

"Then pretty much immediately a man approached me and opened with, 'I've seen you, I found you attractive,' and I immediately shut him down and I said I had a boyfriend."

She discovered that their conversation had been turned into content after she heard about other cases.

"I started looking up buzzwords. I was looking up "picking up girls", "Meta glasses", "Waterloo", all of those into the TikTok search bar and that's when I found his page."

She saw a video of her interaction titled, "POV: You approach her instead of walking by".

Beth Knight says she asked the content creator to remove the video of her and he blocked her. (Instagram)

"It was framed as a successful pick-up, like a win, when I know in the moment I was incredibly uncomfortable … because it was a strange man refusing to accept my soft hint of a no," she said.

"He had very much framed it as, 'Look, I've picked her up, I got her Instagram, I've won here,' and over the top of the video he was instructing men watching that when girls say they have a boyfriend they're lying."

Ms Knight was not lying and thought the man would get the message and leave.

The man is a content creator who touts himself as a pick-up artist and advertises male coaching on his social media account.

Digital extremism researcher Milica Stilinovic, from Sydney University, said such content was known as "rizz cam" — rizz being slang for charisma — when women are sometimes filmed without their consent.

"I would find it horrendous to be treated that way and then subjected to a global audience," she told 7.30.

Ms Stilinovic led a study that reviewed more than 350 Instagram videos filmed with camera glasses.

Milica Stilinovic is concerned about the use of camera glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"Pick-up artists are adjacent to the manosphere, or part of the manosphere, and they have a dual purpose to exist," she said.

"One is to build the self-confidence of men, supposedly through the subjugation of women, and the second part is to sell male coaching, which is basically like a multi-level marketing scheme.

"Some of the worst examples included underage girls. Some of [the filmers] approached women who were inebriated. Some of them approached women who were semi-nude at beaches."

Ms Knight said her experience left her feeling angry.

"It's weird to watch it back," she said.

"But the anger definitely came from the fact that it was spun so heavily to look good on his part.

" I went home and sobbed to my parents. "

She said she asked the content creator to take the video down, but he blocked her.

7.30 has contacted the creator for comment, but he did not respond.

Is it legal?

According to Australia's Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind, the use of camera glasses in public is largely legal, with laws varying across states.

"Wearing smart glasses in public to capture images of things that happen in public is generally not illegal under Australian law," Ms Kind told 7.30.

"[But] when you are in a private premises or a private space, and that might include a private home, a vehicle, or potentially a semi-private space like a gym or a workplace, for example, then you're likely going to run up against laws that do prohibit the use of surveillance devices."

Carly Kind is worried about the use of camera glasses in workplaces and around "vulnerable groups". (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

In Victoria, where filming inside a private business is generally allowed, one content creator known as "The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses to review coffee around Melbourne.

He is not a pick-up artist, but his videos feature staff and customers.

"The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses as he reviews coffee around Melbourne. (Instagram)

One 19-year-old cafe worker said she did not consent to being filmed while serving him.

Her aunt, Tara Venn, told 7.30 her niece was upset after seeing herself in a video online.

She was new in the job.

"It was a bit affronting [for her]," Ms Venn said.

She said content creators should consider the ethics of filming someone.

This cafe worker says she did not give consent to be filmed by The Latte Bloke. (Instagram)

"Common sense says you are polite and you ask if you are going to invade a person's privacy by filming them without them knowing," Ms Venn said.

"I just want people to think and to actually use good manners and decency."

The content creator declined to be interviewed but told 7.30:

"Latte Bloke is all about filming the latte experience and having a bit of fun reviewing the coffee. The focus has never been on the staff or customers, and I'd never intentionally want to make anyone feel uncomfortable."

Potential real-world consequences

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked Australia's Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses in Australia.

Ms Kind says she was already worried about them.

The Albanese government has asked the Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"If you think about their use in workplaces, there's a high likelihood that corporate espionage could be permitted through these kinds of glasses without proper control," Ms Kind said.

"I think the theft of personal information through the use of the glasses is also a potential offence that we could see spiralling out here, and [there are] obviously real risks around vulnerable groups, women and children."

In New South Wales it is illegal to create or share sexually explicit videos or audio of someone without their consent.

Last year, new federal privacy laws made serious invasions of privacy an offence; however, the commissioner told 7.30 there was a high bar to prove it was intentional and caused harm.

In the UK, some pubs and restaurants have reportedly banned the devices, while in Germany, rights advocacy group HateAid has lodged a complaint to German prosecutors against Meta and other companies, claiming such devices breach the country's covert recording laws.

Ms Stilinovic wants camera glasses temporarily banned in Australia.

"I would suggest that we stop the rollout of smart glasses until regulation and policymakers have caught up to keep societies safe," she said.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays at 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: PM, corporate titans flock to Sofitel for Business Council dinner
World.content:
NationalCBD Opinion PM, corporate titans flock to Sofitel for Business Council dinner John Buckley CBD columnist Updated August 25, 2026 — 8:23pm , first published 7:35pm

Updated August 25, 2026 — 8:23pm ,first published 7:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Few events in business and politics get the high-calibre turnout that the Business Council of Australia’s annual dinner has come to deliver. And that’s before factoring in the will-he-won’t-he speculation over whether Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn would be among the major corporates to show face for the get-together at the Sofitel Hotel in Sydney’s CBD on Tuesday evening. (To our surprise, Comyn was there.) Keynote address: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the BCA dinner. Janie Barrett The guest list had no shortage of talent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was billed as the headline guest, with a gaggle of senior Labor figures in tow. Also from the government, Trade Minister Don Farrell, showed up to mingle with execs ahead of dinner, as did Assistant Science, Technology and Digital Economy Minister Andrew Charlton, and Assistant Productivity Minister Andrew Leigh, who, if our eyes didn’t deceive us, arrived to the ballroom with his backpack slung over his shoulder.



Man of the moment: CBA head honcho Matt Comyn. Janie Barrett Money man: Daniel Mookhey, Treasurer of NSW. Janie Barrett NAB chief economist Dr Sally Auld. Oscar Colman But if reporting from our colleagues on Monday was any indicator, Albanese was no doubt bracing for a tough crowd. The star-studded audience was led by BCA chief executive Bran Black, who was preparing to send the government a warning shot on productivity, according to speech notes reported by this masthead. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese tells Queensland to get with the program on AI revolution



Our guess is Black will have no shortage of backers for his message. The top executives of Australia’s biggest companies were expected to turn out in force for the annual get-together, including Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady, Coles chief Leah Weckert and representatives from the big four banks. Apart from Comyn, the bankers included NAB chairman Philip Chronican, who was on the list but who we didn’t get eyes on, as well as Westpac chief Anthony Miller and ANZ’s still-relatively-new CEO Nuno Matos. Also expected were Citi chief executive Mark Woodruff and Macquarie boss ⁠Stuart Green. The Minns government was also represented, with NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey firmly ensconced. Public servants were also well represented. ASIC chair Sarah Court and ACCC chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb were each set to turn out for the function, as was Steven Kennedy, secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, and Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson. Jan Adams, secretary of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, was also expected to go along, as was Department of Climate Change and Energy secretary Mike Kaiser. Bondi Partners founding partner and president Joe Hockey (left) and Business Council of Australia president Geoff Culbert (right). Oscar Colman



As with all of these types of functions, there is always a reliable turnout from the hangers-on. So it was little surprise to see former federal treasurer turned Trump whisperer Joe Hockey back on the list this year, along with former defence minister Christopher Pyne. The pair were among the eager and enthusiastic who turned up unfashionably early. (Those relationships aren’t going to cultivate themselves.) Christopher Pyne is in the house. Oscar Colman Robin Khuda Air Trunk, Adam Watson, APA Group, Damien Nicks, AGL Energy. Janie Barrett Jodie Haydon and husband Anthony Albanese are greeted by Bran Black. Oscar Colman AGL Energy chief executive officer Damien Nicks (left) and Mirvac group chief executive officer and managing director Campbell Hanan (right) . Oscar Colman



Chris Bowen flirts with Murdoch’s son-in-law Earlier this month, Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen slipped into a flannelette overshirt and stared down what we’d assume was an iPhone camera to talk up how the government is making it easier for farmers to go solar. Related Article Farming How Rupert Murdoch’s son-in-law solved crisis at family farm As part of the roadshow, Bowen met with board members of Growing Australia’s Nature Economy, otherwise known as “GANE”. So far, so unremarkable. But it was the name of another high-profile Australian who appeared on the minister’s register of interests, days later, that piqued our interest: Alasdair MacLeod. The man would need no introduction to our good friends over at Holt Street. That’s because this is the same Alasdair MacLeod, Bowen’s office confirmed, who is married to Prudence MacLeod, the eldest daughter of none other than Rupert Murdoch.



MacLeod, according to Bowen’s disclosure, hosted the minister as a guest at his home for a night following a tour of carbon farming initiatives. Bowen, we’re told, dropped in on MacLeod’s farm in Yass for a two-day seminar that brought together experts in wildlife, conservation, agricultural science and climate to talk about how farmers can get more income out of soil carbon capture. (How fun!) Prue and Alasdair MacLeod are big nature, agriculture and climate action enthusiasts. In 2019, the pair founded the Macdoch Foundation, which, at least according to its website, has invested extended philanthropic grants worth $44.5 million to 65 organisations. But something tells us the couple’s love of nature isn’t the only reason Bowen might be feeling pleased with himself. A chain of popular Brisbane sushi shops is in financial trouble, with external liquidators appointed to several companies controlled by its owner.

Mitsuki Sushi opened its first shop on George Street in May 2021. It then went on to open a further three shops around the CBD and a Fortitude Valley restaurant in the next four years.

But liquidators were this month appointed to four companies linked to the shops, while the same administrators – from Sydney firm Balance Insolvency – were last week appointed to restructure the company running the Valley restaurant.
