World.title: Essendon claim heritage was not a factor, but McVeigh’s return feels like a homecoming
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Essendon claim heritage was not a factor, but McVeigh’s return feels like a homecoming Andrew Wu August 25, 2026 — 8:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite Essendon president Andrew Welsh’s insistence that Mark McVeigh’s Bombers heritage had little bearing on his appointment as coach, his unveiling could not have felt more like a homecoming. Just days after the club secured just their second wooden spoon in 93 years, there was a buoyant mood at “the Hangar” for McVeigh’s coronation in front of the Bombers’ entire men’s and women’s lists. They gave him a rousing ovation as he entered the stage. Mark McVeigh is Essendon’s new coach. The Age “It’s a great day for the Essendon Football Club,” Welsh opened. “Mark, congratulations! We’re rapt to have you back in the red and black.” Coaching announcements are significant moments for a football club, marking the start of what they hope is a new and more prosperous era, but the reaction to McVeigh’s selection, or rather James Hird’s non-selection, has been mixed among the Essendon constituents.



For elements of the supporter base, all yearning for a return to the days of glory and fame, Hird is still revered as the club’s most recent premiership captain and the face of their last golden era despite his role in the drugs saga that crippled the club in the 2010s. Related Article AFL briefing

AFL 2026 United Dons vow no ‘jumping at shadows’ now that McVeigh has top job McVeigh is no Hird but, given his 232-game career as a heart-and-soul Bomber, has the record to cut through among the more nostalgic of the red-and-black faithful. What McVeigh lacked on his playing resume compared to Hird, he more than made up for with his coaching CV. Like Josh Fraser, appointed at Carlton with contrastingly minimal fanfare a week earlier, McVeigh has completed an extensive apprenticeship.



As Hird ventured into the business world and dipped his toes in the coaching waters at AFL expansion club GWS and Port Melbourne in the VFL, McVeigh immersed himself in just about every aspect of coaching at the Giants and Sydney. Leaving home daily at 4am for the 90-minute commute to Sydney, McVeigh has served as an interim, been a long-time assistant and also coached juniors, the latter significant as he takes the helm of one of the youngest lists in the league. Loading “Our members, our fans, and our club wanted us to set out with a very rigorous process to undertake to find what is the best coach for our football club,” Welsh said. “That went all the way back to looking at what a success profile looked like for the best candidate as a coach. “Understanding the Essendon Football Club, or being an Essendon person, was something that wasn’t held in as high regard internally with the panel that it was externally with some of the commentary going around.”



There is no time for McVeigh to get his feet under the table. The Bombers are an issues-rich club. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview He will meet with Zach Merrett, who watched the announcement with his teammates, “at an appropriate time” to discuss the former captain’s future. Welsh was adamant 12 months ago Merrett would remain a Bomber in 2026. McVeigh adopted a more conciliatory tone about 2027. He was non-committal when asked if he would attempt to persuade Merrett to stay should his heart still be set on leaving. “You must respect your champions, I’m big on that,” McVeigh said.



“I think it’s really important we understand the players’ feelings. It’s not just about the club’s feelings. It’s about his feelings and where he’s at. I respect him. I want him to be here, but I’ll listen to him as well.” Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Put my heart and soul into it’: Hird disappointed as Dons prepare to endorse McVeigh as coach He was unequivocal about his great mate Dean Solomon, laughing off reports of tension between the pair. Solomon was among the throng watching on. “I absolutely want Dean Solomon as part of the group,” McVeigh said. But the spectre of Hird still hovers. Welsh and McVeigh know how deeply Hird is loved, not just by the rank and file but the high net worth supporters. Both Welsh and McVeigh called for unity.



“I want to call out the Essendon armada, the thousands of supporters, members, and coteries,” McVeigh said. “I don’t ask for your patience. I ask for your realignment to our club. This is a significant day for our football club, and I can’t wait to start.” Loading Pointedly, Hird was yet to return Welsh’s calls before the announcement but, according to McVeigh, was warm in his congratulations of the new coach. Despite Hird’s affection for McVeigh, only wins will silence those who want the former golden boy to get his crack at redemption. “I don’t fear those people. I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it,” McVeigh said. “To be fair, he’s been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. And we spoke this morning, and the way he spoke to me of how proud [he is] of this moment for me – it hasn’t broken us.



“We’re still together, but I understand, and I embrace the feelings of people that love James Hird because I do, too.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Fewer construction projects leads to collapse in developer payments to council
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Fewer construction projects leads to collapse in developer payments to council William Davis August 25, 2026 — 8:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane property developers paid significantly less than expected into council coffers over the past year, likely due to a fall in construction projects. Initially forecast to contribute about $163.7 million, developers paid just over half that at $84.2 million. The figures were revealed in a financial report published ahead of Tuesday’s Brisbane City Council meeting. Brisbane City Council took in $84.2 million in developer contributions. William Davis A representative for the lord mayor’s office said multiple factors accounted for the shortfall, but the main one was the completion of fewer projects than expected.



Developer contributions are levied on projects when they are completed to help fund essential services. The $163.7 million projection from the 2025-26 budget was later revised to $112.3 million. Related Article City council Smart glasses spark ban on all photography and filming at Brisbane pools Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the report showed the budget was strong, pointing to a reduction in net debt and lower rates than those in surrounding local government areas. “We’ll hear the opposition moan and groan, but I did want to flag this: at the last election, the Labor Party and the Greens put together $3.5 billion worth of commitments,” he told the council chamber.



“That would have had a material impact on the financial statements if they were in administration today.” Greens councillor Seal Chong Wah highlighted the shortfall in developer contributions. She also pointed to millions of dollars in discounted charges offered to developers to incentivise construction, saying it showed big business was not paying its fair share towards the services Brisbane relied on. “This is unsustainable. We need this basic infrastructure for a growing city, and we need it now,” Chong Wah said in a statement. “The LNP are giving developers handouts for ‘affordability’, but Brisbane’s house prices overtook Melbourne and Canberra under this policy. Developers just pocket this for bigger profits. “The LNP are giving developers handouts in a housing crisis, but we should be taxing their super-profits.”



Council’s capital expenditure was also almost $100 million short of what had been expected, but the lord mayor’s office said this had nothing to do with reduced income streams and was instead attributed to accounting factors, including the transfer of Victoria Park. Related Article City council Brisbane Council questioned over ‘sneaky’ rate hikes It said 72 projects had been completed marginally under budget, while shipment delays and supply chain failures also contributed to council’s reduced spending. A lord mayor’s spokesperson also pointed to record high capital investment in previous years, including the Metro network, completion of new bridges, and other projects. But the Labor opposition said recent rate rises, which were higher for apartment owners, meant residents were getting a bad deal.



“Council have taken even more than they anticipated in general rates from general mum and dad and pensioner ratepayers in Brisbane, more than they ever imagined … but they underspent significantly on important projects,” leader Jared Cassidy said. “There’s less coming from developers, but there’s more coming from ratepayers.” Greens councillor Trina Massey said residents were not getting value for money, and the council was prioritising the interests of developers. “The question isn’t whether you’re paying more. You are. The question is, what are you getting for it?” she asked in a statement. “Brisbane residents should be getting safer streets, better pedestrian crossings, bus stops, footpaths, drainage, and a city ready for climate change and storm season.



“Instead, the LNP council is taking more from residents while investing less in the infrastructure we all rely on.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Albanese tells Queensland to get with the program on AI revolution
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese tells Queensland to get with the program on AI revolution Paul Sakkal August 25, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has challenged Queensland to sign up to a national plan on data centres before Wednesday’s national cabinet meeting as he reminds premiers about their promise to fund a trimmed-down NDIS. After urging pessimistic business chiefs to talk up Australia’s economy at Tuesday’s Business Council of Australia dinner, Albanese will head a meeting of state leaders seeking buy-in on regulation of artificial intelligence, a faltering gun buyback and fresh moves to reduce domestic violence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Perth on Monday. AAP Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has been a holdout on a federal plan to force data centre operators to create renewable energy to make sure electricity prices do not spike. The LNP and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor both want the data centre boom to be powered by any type of energy, including fossil fuels, threatening to jolt a bipartisan pact on the AI boom. Before Wednesday’s meeting of state and territory leaders, Albanese said: “I’m confident we can get consensus.”



“We want social licence… Which is why you need to have that additional investment to make sure [data centres are not] displacing energy and therefore increasing costs,” he said. Related Article Federal budget Tax attack: Business to serve it up to PM over dinner after Labor’s budget changes Albanese is likely to be confronted by angry east coast premiers after he committed to a GST top-up deal with Western Australia that the Productivity Commission said was a poor deal for the nation. Since he renewed his pledge to protect the WA deal on Monday, Albanese has been telling premiers that the Commonwealth, not states, funds the multibillion-dollar GST top-ups linked to the WA deal. He said it was incumbent on state leaders to hold up their end of the bargain on school, hospital and NDIS funding deals as federal debt grows past $1 trillion and NSW and Queensland’s credit ratings threaten to sink to Victorian levels of AA.



Premiers made a deal with Albanese in 2023 to accept an extra $25 billion in hospital funding and about $10 billion in extra GST in exchange for states stepping up to fund alternative services for children with autism and other developmental problems. The 2028 start date for the Thriving Kids program is under threat, however, as states baulk at some of the changes following Labor’s passage of its NDIS reform bill. Asked if he would raise the NDIS with state counterparts on Wednesday, Albanese said: “We remind them all the time.” Related Article Opinion

CBD PM, corporate titans flock to Sofitel for Business Council dinner John Buckley CBD columnist Federal cabinet discussed the proposed national standards on AI in Perth on Tuesday. Albanese will present the plan to premiers on Wednesday, and there is widespread agreement outside of Queensland. Business leaders have also expressed support for Labor’s plan to mandate offsets for data centre energy and water usage to avoid a US-style backlash against the computer factories.



This masthead reported on Tuesday that business groups were plotting a union-style campaign on living standards and economic growth before the next election, following a corporate-led campaign against Labor’s budget measures. Business Council of Australia chairman Geoff Culbert will tell the organisation’s annual dinner in Sydney that firms want to change the national debate on productivity and require Labor’s buy-in. Related Article Exclusive

Data centres Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash “Prime minister – I appreciate that your job is extremely difficult. You are trying to navigate the need for material structural reform in an environment where the time needed to effectively prosecute those ideas doesn’t align with political cycles. That is a problem faced by all modern democracies,” Culbert will say, according to speech notes. “We are asking you to partner with us to take Australia forward.”



The prime minister said the business political establishment should be more upbeat about the country and its financial performance as cost of living pressures translate to support for One Nation. Albanese argued Australia’s unemployment rate was relatively healthy and Australia was growing at a better rate than most G7 economies, countering a widespread view among economists that Australia’s economy is in trouble. “We’ve got to be optimistic,” Albanese said on Wednesday. “We’ve got to shape the future or the future will shape us. So how do we put all that together?” “What are the opportunities that we have? The comparative advantages that we have? AI is a good example: we have enormous space, which is the envy of the world. An island to ourselves. We have clean energy. We have everything under the earth with critical minerals and rare earths.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weeky Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Tracking devices, drones and poisoned dogs: CFMEU probe told of intimidation
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCFMEU Tracking devices, drones and poisoned dogs: CFMEU probe told of intimidation Cameron Atfield Updated August 25, 2026 — 7:56pm ,first published 2:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A security professional hired to protect a CFMEU-targeted worksite found a tracking device attached to his car and believes his dog was poisoned by baited meat dropped from a drone in a campaign of intimidation by the union, a commission of inquiry heard on Tuesday. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen was providing security services to construction firm BMD at the Centenary Bridge worksite when, he told the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry, he became the target of a sustained campaign of harassment. After attending the site on May 17, 2024, Killen said he sensed he was being followed during his drive back to his company headquarters near the Port of Brisbane. The tracking device found on Grant Killen’s vehicle. Commission of Inquiry Upon arrival, Killen said he immediately placed his car on a hoist, lifted it, and found a tracking device attached beneath the chassis.



“Once I found the device, I immediately put the vehicle on the ground as quick as I could. Then I left the facility,” he said. “Then I gave the admin staff at the office a call and directed them to pack up and close up for the day and go home.” Killen said he sped away from the site to put distance between the device and his staff. “I left the device on the vehicle mainly because I knew the device had a particular anti-removal device on there, an anti-tilt switch,” he said. “As soon as it gets removed, the people who put it on there, who have the software for that, would immediately be notified.”



Suspecting he was being followed by someone in a Toyota RAV4, Killen said he engaged in some “aggressive driving”, including deliberately running a red light to check if he was being followed. “I was followed through that red light,” he said. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry “Further down the road, we did an aggressive U-turn [to] see if it would keep up, and it did follow.” Killen eventually lost his tail, he said, and removed the device by the side of a road.



But he said the intimidation did not stop there, instead spreading to his family home. There were drive-bys in his cul-de-sac, and Killen said he managed a brief look at one of the drivers, who he identified as former police detective Mick Featherstone, whom the inquiry heard the CFMEU had engaged to collect intelligence on BMD personnel. Separately, Killen said he noticed several drones overhead. Then, the family dog got sick. “One of the questions the vet asked me, after a point where the vet had to operate on the dog and remove its stomach contents, was ‘Do you feed your dog cubed meat?’,” Killen said.



“We don’t, and I thought that was a strange question. But as I reflected shortly after and recalled, I formed the opinion that there was a possibility that the dog had been baited at some stage.” Related Article Building Bad Inquiry and CFMEU bosses seek answers and action over alleged bikie plot When counsel assisting the inquiry, Eddy Gisonda, KC, put it to Killen that he suspected one of the drones may have dropped baited meat on his property, he responded “yeah, correct”. Killen said the campaign was enough to make him walk away from the BMD contract. “With the tracking device on our vehicle, with everything that was occurring, I needed to step back and just concentrate on the safety of me and my family and our business,” he said.



Commissioner Stuart Wood asked Killen, a military veteran with service in Iraq, whether he had experienced anything of that level while deployed. “An assailant or an offender always has the upper hand about how they plan to do an overt act or assault someone or conduct an attack,” he said. “They choose the time, they choose the place, they choose the method. “All we can do is simply react the best that we can and try and mitigate it by having that planning in place. “So to put that in context, that’s what we tried our best to do in this particular situation.”



After lunch, BMD chief executive Scott Power recounted a similar experience at his father’s house. His father, Mick Power, still served as BMD chairman. BMD chief executive Scott Power giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry Similar to Killen’s situation, Power said, drones had been spotted above his father’s home before his dog fell ill. “They were concerned, obviously, for the well-being of their pet, but the timing of it seemed to coincide with the campaign in the local area surrounding their home, so they formed the view that it was connected [with the CFMEU,” he said. Gisonda: “And was it unusual for them to observe drones flying above their property?”



Power: “Yeah, it was particularly unusual. It’s not something they have ever previously discussed having observed.” Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies Earlier, Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said relations between the state trades and labour council and the CFMEU had greatly improved since the latter went into administration. “We have developed, I think, a fairly good working relationship, completely unlike what it was, and on the basis that we work with the Queensland branch to try to assist them on their path to getting out of administration,” she said. But King said there was still some way to go before the CFMEU could be reaffiliated with the Queensland Council of Unions.



“It is going to take time because, while the people who are in the union now are not the same people who were doing the activities and the conduct that was occurring pre-the High Court decision, relationships still take time to mend, and trust takes time to rebuild,” she said. The hearing continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCourts Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative Rob Harris Updated August 25, 2026 — 7:45pm ,first published 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing renewed calls to stand down Labor MP Luke Gosling from his role as special envoy after he was charged with breaching bail on Tuesday in relation to the ongoing allegations he assaulted Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly. NT Police said in a statement they allege Gosling breached his bail conditions on Friday, August 14, and served him with a summons to appear in Darwin Local Court on September 30. Police did not specify what is alleged to have occurred. Federal MP Luke Gosling, centre, at the TIO Stadium in Darwin on August 14. Facebook/Luke Gosling MP Gosling, 54, posted a picture to Facebook at the Test match in Darwin between Australia and Bangladesh on the date of the alleged breach. It was reported by the NT News that Connolly was at the venue, but it was unclear if that is where the alleged offence occurred. A spokeswoman for Gosling said neither he nor his office hade been made aware of the nature of the alleged breach and have been provided no information from police other than a summons.



“On Friday, August 14, Mr Gosling did not attend any events at the same time as the administrator,” she said. “Mr Gosling is discussing the matter with his legal team, and will be defending the charge.” The MP, who is the Albanese government’s special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia, was arrested at his home last month and charged with two counts of assaulting Connolly, with the offences carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment. He appeared in Darwin Local Court on July 31, successfully applying to vary his bail conditions so he could attend the same public events as Connolly, provided he stayed at least 15 metres away and gave Connolly’s office 48 hours’ notice. Judge Stephen Geary also banned him from coming within 50 metres of the NT’s Government House, where Connolly resides. The administrator is the Crown’s representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.



Prosecutors had opposed the variation, telling the court Connolly had cancelled public engagements because of concerns about encountering Gosling and arguing the restrictions were needed for the administrator’s “safety and wellbeing”. Related Article Crime Courts hears details of Labor MP’s alleged assault of NT administrator The alleged assaults occurred about 30 minutes between each other at the Darwin Thai Grand Festival on July 18. It was alleged in court that Gosling approached Connolly from behind in the first incident and, in the second, collided with him before drawing back his left elbow and striking him in the upper right rib area. Albanese has refused to stand down Gosling from his role as an envoy for veterans over the assault charges, despite calls from the Coalition. The PM’s office has declined to comment, citing an ongoing legal process.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said that the charges were already a test of the prime minister’s leadership. “Now Mr Gosling has also been charged with allegedly breaching his bail, the case for the prime minister to act is even stronger,” Taylor said in a statement released on Tuesday night. “These allegations are matters for the courts, but Anthony Albanese has a decision to make about who serves in his government. He should stand Mr Gosling down today.” Gosling denies the allegations, describing them at the time as “ludicrous”. His lawyer, Marty Aust, has described the prosecution case as “incredibly weak” and accused police of politicising the matter. Gosling has also disputed the police account of events leading to his arrest, saying he was first contacted while working in Queensland and that his office had been trying to arrange a meeting with detectives.



NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole said detectives had made multiple attempts to contact him before the arrest. The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions is preparing to take over the assault case from the NT DPP, which cited a perceived conflict of interest. It was reported by ABC Darwin the conflict relates to concerns about how the acting NT DPP’s handling of the case could be perceived given the prospect of a permanent appointment to the role. Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP convicted and sentenced for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment can be disqualified from parliament, meaning any conviction could trigger a byelection. He has held the seat of Solomon – which includes Darwin and its satellite city of Palmerston – since 2016. He held off a threat from the Country Liberals by just 1500 votes in May last year. A chain of popular Brisbane sushi shops is in financial trouble, with external liquidators appointed to several companies controlled by its owner.

Mitsuki Sushi opened its first shop on George Street in May 2021. It then went on to open a further three shops around the CBD and a Fortitude Valley restaurant in the next four years.

But liquidators were this month appointed to four companies linked to the shops, while the same administrators – from Sydney firm Balance Insolvency – were last week appointed to restructure the company running the Valley restaurant.

World.title: Essendon claim heritage was not a factor, but McVeigh’s return feels like a homecoming
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Essendon claim heritage was not a factor, but McVeigh’s return feels like a homecoming Andrew Wu August 25, 2026 — 8:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Despite Essendon president Andrew Welsh’s insistence that Mark McVeigh’s Bombers heritage had little bearing on his appointment as coach, his unveiling could not have felt more like a homecoming. Just days after the club secured just their second wooden spoon in 93 years, there was a buoyant mood at “the Hangar” for McVeigh’s coronation in front of the Bombers’ entire men’s and women’s lists. They gave him a rousing ovation as he entered the stage. Mark McVeigh is Essendon’s new coach. The Age “It’s a great day for the Essendon Football Club,” Welsh opened. “Mark, congratulations! We’re rapt to have you back in the red and black.” Coaching announcements are significant moments for a football club, marking the start of what they hope is a new and more prosperous era, but the reaction to McVeigh’s selection, or rather James Hird’s non-selection, has been mixed among the Essendon constituents.



For elements of the supporter base, all yearning for a return to the days of glory and fame, Hird is still revered as the club’s most recent premiership captain and the face of their last golden era despite his role in the drugs saga that crippled the club in the 2010s. Related Article AFL briefing

AFL 2026 United Dons vow no ‘jumping at shadows’ now that McVeigh has top job McVeigh is no Hird but, given his 232-game career as a heart-and-soul Bomber, has the record to cut through among the more nostalgic of the red-and-black faithful. What McVeigh lacked on his playing resume compared to Hird, he more than made up for with his coaching CV. Like Josh Fraser, appointed at Carlton with contrastingly minimal fanfare a week earlier, McVeigh has completed an extensive apprenticeship.



As Hird ventured into the business world and dipped his toes in the coaching waters at AFL expansion club GWS and Port Melbourne in the VFL, McVeigh immersed himself in just about every aspect of coaching at the Giants and Sydney. Leaving home daily at 4am for the 90-minute commute to Sydney, McVeigh has served as an interim, been a long-time assistant and also coached juniors, the latter significant as he takes the helm of one of the youngest lists in the league. Loading “Our members, our fans, and our club wanted us to set out with a very rigorous process to undertake to find what is the best coach for our football club,” Welsh said. “That went all the way back to looking at what a success profile looked like for the best candidate as a coach. “Understanding the Essendon Football Club, or being an Essendon person, was something that wasn’t held in as high regard internally with the panel that it was externally with some of the commentary going around.”



There is no time for McVeigh to get his feet under the table. The Bombers are an issues-rich club. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview He will meet with Zach Merrett, who watched the announcement with his teammates, “at an appropriate time” to discuss the former captain’s future. Welsh was adamant 12 months ago Merrett would remain a Bomber in 2026. McVeigh adopted a more conciliatory tone about 2027. He was non-committal when asked if he would attempt to persuade Merrett to stay should his heart still be set on leaving. “You must respect your champions, I’m big on that,” McVeigh said.



“I think it’s really important we understand the players’ feelings. It’s not just about the club’s feelings. It’s about his feelings and where he’s at. I respect him. I want him to be here, but I’ll listen to him as well.” Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Put my heart and soul into it’: Hird disappointed as Dons prepare to endorse McVeigh as coach He was unequivocal about his great mate Dean Solomon, laughing off reports of tension between the pair. Solomon was among the throng watching on. “I absolutely want Dean Solomon as part of the group,” McVeigh said. But the spectre of Hird still hovers. Welsh and McVeigh know how deeply Hird is loved, not just by the rank and file but the high net worth supporters. Both Welsh and McVeigh called for unity.



“I want to call out the Essendon armada, the thousands of supporters, members, and coteries,” McVeigh said. “I don’t ask for your patience. I ask for your realignment to our club. This is a significant day for our football club, and I can’t wait to start.” Loading Pointedly, Hird was yet to return Welsh’s calls before the announcement but, according to McVeigh, was warm in his congratulations of the new coach. Despite Hird’s affection for McVeigh, only wins will silence those who want the former golden boy to get his crack at redemption. “I don’t fear those people. I actually embrace how they feel, and I understand it,” McVeigh said. “To be fair, he’s been a constant in my life since I was 17 years of age. And we spoke this morning, and the way he spoke to me of how proud [he is] of this moment for me – it hasn’t broken us.



“We’re still together, but I understand, and I embrace the feelings of people that love James Hird because I do, too.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Fewer construction projects leads to collapse in developer payments to council
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Fewer construction projects leads to collapse in developer payments to council William Davis August 25, 2026 — 8:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane property developers paid significantly less than expected into council coffers over the past year, likely due to a fall in construction projects. Initially forecast to contribute about $163.7 million, developers paid just over half that at $84.2 million. The figures were revealed in a financial report published ahead of Tuesday’s Brisbane City Council meeting. Brisbane City Council took in $84.2 million in developer contributions. William Davis A representative for the lord mayor’s office said multiple factors accounted for the shortfall, but the main one was the completion of fewer projects than expected.



Developer contributions are levied on projects when they are completed to help fund essential services. The $163.7 million projection from the 2025-26 budget was later revised to $112.3 million. Related Article City council Smart glasses spark ban on all photography and filming at Brisbane pools Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said the report showed the budget was strong, pointing to a reduction in net debt and lower rates than those in surrounding local government areas. “We’ll hear the opposition moan and groan, but I did want to flag this: at the last election, the Labor Party and the Greens put together $3.5 billion worth of commitments,” he told the council chamber.



“That would have had a material impact on the financial statements if they were in administration today.” Greens councillor Seal Chong Wah highlighted the shortfall in developer contributions. She also pointed to millions of dollars in discounted charges offered to developers to incentivise construction, saying it showed big business was not paying its fair share towards the services Brisbane relied on. “This is unsustainable. We need this basic infrastructure for a growing city, and we need it now,” Chong Wah said in a statement. “The LNP are giving developers handouts for ‘affordability’, but Brisbane’s house prices overtook Melbourne and Canberra under this policy. Developers just pocket this for bigger profits. “The LNP are giving developers handouts in a housing crisis, but we should be taxing their super-profits.”



Council’s capital expenditure was also almost $100 million short of what had been expected, but the lord mayor’s office said this had nothing to do with reduced income streams and was instead attributed to accounting factors, including the transfer of Victoria Park. Related Article City council Brisbane Council questioned over ‘sneaky’ rate hikes It said 72 projects had been completed marginally under budget, while shipment delays and supply chain failures also contributed to council’s reduced spending. A lord mayor’s spokesperson also pointed to record high capital investment in previous years, including the Metro network, completion of new bridges, and other projects. But the Labor opposition said recent rate rises, which were higher for apartment owners, meant residents were getting a bad deal.



“Council have taken even more than they anticipated in general rates from general mum and dad and pensioner ratepayers in Brisbane, more than they ever imagined … but they underspent significantly on important projects,” leader Jared Cassidy said. “There’s less coming from developers, but there’s more coming from ratepayers.” Greens councillor Trina Massey said residents were not getting value for money, and the council was prioritising the interests of developers. “The question isn’t whether you’re paying more. You are. The question is, what are you getting for it?” she asked in a statement. “Brisbane residents should be getting safer streets, better pedestrian crossings, bus stops, footpaths, drainage, and a city ready for climate change and storm season.



“Instead, the LNP council is taking more from residents while investing less in the infrastructure we all rely on.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: SRL changes could leave us worse off
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters SRL changes could leave us worse off August 25, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. TRANSPORT I have concerns for some of the proposed changes to the Suburban Rail Loop as outlined by Premier Ben Carroll (″⁣Suburban Rail Loop to find $2 billion in savings through station changes″⁣, 25/8).

Connectivity matters. Scrapping underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley, a second station entrance at Clayton and pedestrian bridges in Burwood and Cheltenham, makes it more difficult for people, particularly those with accessibility issues, to use SRL and threatens patronage numbers.

This in turn may impact the cost-benefit ratio which determines whether the benefits to the community outweigh the costs.

Yvonne Bowyer, Surrey Hills Past point of no return

Despite an apparently imminent “crunch time” (“These suburbs may never be the same as Melbourne’s population soars to 10 million”, 25/8), Melbourne reached a point of no return some time ago.

Starting from Craigieburn station, I’ve trudged through kilometres of tract housing to teach at one or other of my institute’s far-flung outposts.

Its residents are forever committed to car transport that many of them, including refugees, can ill afford.

There is no way to turn back the clock in such areas, the locals long ago having been sold the Australian dream of an unused front garden and underutilised backyard.

The latest vogue of electric cars is no solution either; we remain locked into legacy private transport clogging our roads, necessitating an endless and fraught game of Big Build whack-a-mole to rectify issues that should have been prevented through better planning in the first place.

Marish Mackowiak, Ormond



Let’s hear it for the 508 bus

The 508 bus goes right past our place. It has an east-west route, Moonee Ponds to Alphington, and connects with no less than seven tram lines and three trains.

It’s regular, reliable, and drivers are unfailingly cheerful and polite. They wait for you to sit down before they take off. Some electric buses have been introduced. Lucky? You bet!

And then there’s the 59 tram direct to town and the scenic 58 that meanders through Royal Park. The 1 and 6 trams are handy for Lygon St and the amazing 96 takes you and lots of tourists all the way to St Kilda.

Trams, trains, buses taking people to work, school and a thousand other journeys.

There are occasional disruptions, and yes, and it’s true that many suburbs are not so well served by public transport.

But, can I just record my gratitude for our public transport system and the people who work in it?

Bruce Henry, Moonee Ponds Imagine a life of free Uber rides

Here’s a thought, Ben.

Let’s assume the Cheltenham to Box Hill SRL will cost the 2021 estimate of $34 billion (certainly an underestimate) and that 20,000 passengers would use that line on a daily basis (probably an overestimate), then that’s a cost of $3.4 million per projected passenger.

That’s enough to give each one of them a lifetime of free Uber rides as compensation for no SRL.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne Just finish the job

Premier Ben Carroll has decided to cut $2 billion off SRL stations. This will give future generations substandard station access. Build it once, build it properly.

George Djoneff, Mitcham THE FORUM City too crowded

The prospect of Melbourne becoming a megacity (“The suburbs that will suffer most in city of 10 million”, 25/8) is disturbing.

There is much talk about whether the city expands upwards or outwards – both unwelcomed by many current Melburnians and those who care for nature – but why isn’t there debate about the major driver, a growing population?

The answer is because the discussion is being driven by business, notably the property industry. How about we hear from residents who see their quality of life being degraded by more congestion and crowding?

I would like the forthcoming Age “Melbourne Assembly” talkfest to consider the scenario of Melbourne not growing.

Ian Penrose, Kew



Plan our future

All the political parties are throwing around immigration numbers in an attempt to woo the voters. But the sad truth is that none has a population policy detailing what is an optimal, sustainable population for Australia and how we achieve that. The result? Read “The suburbs that will suffer most in city of10 million” (25/8).

The reality is that a finite planet or country with fixed resources cannot sustain an ever-

increasing population without a declining quality of life and eventual collapse.

And affluent countries, such as Australia, have the highest environmental impact.

The climate emergency, reliance on desalination plants, impact on the natural environment, etc are signs that we have already exceeded the carrying capacity of the land.

We need leaders with a long-term plan. Increase labour participation rates by providing affordable daycare, and incentives for pensioners to keep working. Solve the labour shortage at the bottom by paying market – not award – rates.

Make use of AI and robotics to accept and manage the inevitable rise of an ageing population.

A stable population will solve the housing crisis. We can maintain the green wedges and rewild our diminished land.

Barry Lizmore, Ocean Grove All over the place

Reading that David Farley joined the Nationals, toyed with the idea of running for Labor or as an independent, and then chose One Nation should be a major red flag to anyone thinking of voting for him. No sign of deeply held beliefs here.

It does make you wonder, given how few actual policies One Nation has, whether political issues have anything to do with Farley’s decision to join the party, or indeed, vote for them.

Claire Cooper, Maldon Big business, as usual

Interesting, but not surprising, that big business is going to mount a campaign against the federal Labor government regarding recent policy changes.

Voters would be wise to wrack their brains to remember when was the last time big business supported any change to government policy that helped ordinary Australian workers.

Big business is interested only in profit margins and share prices and always need to be dragged into making any improvements for their workers.

Bill Walker, St Andrews Beach Whistleblower reform

There aren’t too many things about contemporary USA that I see worthy of emulation. However, it does have many schemes whereby whistleblowers are financially compensated pro rata, and this is certainly worth introducing here.

As it is, whistleblowers will never again work in their chosen industry, many suffer long-term post-traumatic stress disorder as a consequence, and are financially impoverished due to their actions.

They shine a light on dirty deeds that cost our economy and society dearly. Surely, this is worth financial acknowledgment?

Carmel Boyle, Alfredton Local input missing

First, it was gambling reform with the views of a significant number of caucus members being ignored.

Now, comes GST distribution, with a prime ministerial pronouncement made without there being time to have

consulted caucus.

There seems to be little point in voting for a Labor candidate if the elected local member has no say on critical decisions.

Jan Lacey, North Melbourne



Remember Tampa

August 26 marks the 25th anniversary of the notorious Tampa incident when the Howard government refused to allow the Norwegian ship, the MV Tampa, to offload a boatload of rescued asylum seekers onto Australia’s mainland.

The attitude of John Howard’s government was to demonise refugees and asylum seekers, and that has negatively affected the conversation to the present day.

In reality, genuine refugees are innocent, at-risk victims of war trying to find refuge to build a better life for their families.

It’s upsetting that we chose to act without compassion and kindness to those in need. Had we accepted the asylum seekers and processed them in a timely manner, we would now have former refugees who would be forever grateful for being accepted into our community, and contributing so much to make Australia a better place.

Robert Preston, McKinnon A suspect ally

It is not surprising that, as reported by The Age, the United States’ global image is declining as China’s improves. Unhappily, with or without Donald Trump in the White House, the US remains an increasingly dysfunctional society, and a suspect ally.

A reassessment of the values we supposedly share with the US, and fears and criticism of China’s global ambitions, is overdue.

China has well-publicised human rights issues, but it is hard to argue that some recent outcomes for US citizens have been better than the 800 million Chinese lifted out of poverty.

It is also hard to demonstrate that US involvement in international affairs has provided better outcomes than Chinese initiatives such as its Belt and Road project.

It was disgraceful that fear of being ″⁣wedged″⁣ on national security induced the Albanese government to endorse the AUKUS project without any searching analysis.

Norman Huon, Port Melbourne Global hunger

Early 2025: the Trump administration shuts down the respected USAID organisation and cuts almost all of the US international humanitarian assistance. It exhorts NATO allies to boost defence spending, and several European powers to reduce their overseas aid to make room for increased military expenditure.

UN agencies and respected charities operating in developing nations warn of the disastrous effects of the reduced aid on nutritional and health outcomes.

Mid-2026: central African nations struggle heroically, but with inadequate resources to contain an Ebola outbreak. Many Sudanese, fleeing warfare, go hungry and there is not enough international aid to assist them.

A famine is looming in Somalia and Ethiopia after years of unremitting drought. Millions of children are malnourished in these countries, and also in Afghanistan and Gaza.

Meanwhile, many billions of dollars are spent on senseless wars which only exacerbate the world’s woes and, in the case of the Ukraine nightmare, threaten food exports from an important grain-producing region.

Australia could start to reverse these shocking outcomes by leading a coalition of middle powers who increase their international humanitarian aid.

Andrew Trembath, Blackburn Time slows in Hawthorn

Thank you to writer Peter Craven for his excellent appraisal of Hawthorn (″⁣Hidden charm beyond the riches″⁣, 25/8) but he forgot to mention the Hawthorn Pool and Recreation Centre.

This excellent facility with wonderful staff has been welcoming Kew residents since June 2020 when the still-perfect 1989 Kew pool was closed by our council. The projected opening date for the new Kew centre is July, 2027.

It will take more than seven years for the ratepayers to pay for the mistakes of council in closing the centre; followed by the roof collapse of the new build in 2022 and the legal ramifications.

Seven years!

Maree Williams, Kew Head-in-sand syndrome

With record-smashing heatwaves and wildfires across the northern hemisphere this year, the decades-long warnings of climate scientists have come to fruition.

Humanity’s response so far? Extract and burn ever more coal, gas and oil.

What, apart from the obvious ″⁣Climate Catastrophe″⁣ or perhaps ″⁣Profit at all Costs″⁣, might we name the bastard love-child of cognitive dissonance and willful ignorance?

Helen Moss, Croydon



Paging Alan Fels

If you are lucky enough to be an MCC member, you can purchase a reserved seat to one of the Wildcard finals for $12. You are then slugged a “service and handling fee” of $9.25 for pushing a button on your computer keyboard.

When you get to the game, you might feel like a beer. A can will cost you $12.50 even though a six-pack of the same beer will cost you circa $20 at the bottle shop down the road.

How is such price gouging allowed, and where is Alan Fels when you need him?

Mark Hulls, Sandringham Unextraordinary

Three weeks ago, I decided to search for something – anything – that wasn’t iconic.

I’m still searching, so it’s not looking good.

Alan Eason, Miami, Qld AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Spell check

I think it’s great that the City of Melbourne has a “rapid response” van for the removal of graffiti (25/8), but it’s a pity that the word, “graffiti”, is spelt wrongly on the back of it.

Mary Lyon, Camperdown



Population

If Victoria is the basket case portrayed by Jess Wilson’s Liberal opposition, then how do we explain the state’s burgeoning population growth?

Peter Bennett, Clifton Hill As Melbourne’s population trends towards 10 million, I imagine it would be difficult to

find 10 people who relish the prospect. Incidentally, the average entire population of

each of the 10 happiest nations on Earth? 7.8 million.

Peter Rushen, Carnegie Among all the noise of calling out for curbs on immigration, it was heartening to recently attend an Australian citizenship ceremony where the mayor, himself a migrant, extolled the virtues of multiculturalism. Lovely warm vibes only, with my friend moved by her inclusion as an Australian citizen.

Ailsa Hamilton, Northcote Furthermore

I hope that US President Donald Trump’s ″⁣lovesick″⁣ assistant prints out Peter Hartcher’s opinion piece in The Age (25/8) and draws his attention to this matter.

John Bye, Elwood Richmond finished 17th on the ladder. They finish lower in the ″⁣reading the room″⁣ stakes.

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon



Re Letters ″⁣and another thing″⁣ (25/8) on making cars more difficult to steal: Can’t Elon Musk create a car that returns itself to its owner after it’s been stolen? He could call it the Homer.

Robin Jensen, Castlemaine Call it a miracle, but an ambulance arrived to help me with my 99-year-old dad’s medical emergency in under five minutes. They just happened to be going back to the depot. The joy of living in the inner suburbs shows itself again. Thank you, Ambulance Victoria.

Susan Scalise, Ascot Vale The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Albanese tells Queensland to get with the program on AI revolution
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese tells Queensland to get with the program on AI revolution Paul Sakkal August 25, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has challenged Queensland to sign up to a national plan on data centres before Wednesday’s national cabinet meeting as he reminds premiers about their promise to fund a trimmed-down NDIS. After urging pessimistic business chiefs to talk up Australia’s economy at Tuesday’s Business Council of Australia dinner, Albanese will head a meeting of state leaders seeking buy-in on regulation of artificial intelligence, a faltering gun buyback and fresh moves to reduce domestic violence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Perth on Monday. AAP Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has been a holdout on a federal plan to force data centre operators to create renewable energy to make sure electricity prices do not spike. The LNP and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor both want the data centre boom to be powered by any type of energy, including fossil fuels, threatening to jolt a bipartisan pact on the AI boom. Before Wednesday’s meeting of state and territory leaders, Albanese said: “I’m confident we can get consensus.”



“We want social licence… Which is why you need to have that additional investment to make sure [data centres are not] displacing energy and therefore increasing costs,” he said. Related Article Federal budget Tax attack: Business to serve it up to PM over dinner after Labor’s budget changes Albanese is likely to be confronted by angry east coast premiers after he committed to a GST top-up deal with Western Australia that the Productivity Commission said was a poor deal for the nation. Since he renewed his pledge to protect the WA deal on Monday, Albanese has been telling premiers that the Commonwealth, not states, funds the multibillion-dollar GST top-ups linked to the WA deal. He said it was incumbent on state leaders to hold up their end of the bargain on school, hospital and NDIS funding deals as federal debt grows past $1 trillion and NSW and Queensland’s credit ratings threaten to sink to Victorian levels of AA.



Premiers made a deal with Albanese in 2023 to accept an extra $25 billion in hospital funding and about $10 billion in extra GST in exchange for states stepping up to fund alternative services for children with autism and other developmental problems. The 2028 start date for the Thriving Kids program is under threat, however, as states baulk at some of the changes following Labor’s passage of its NDIS reform bill. Asked if he would raise the NDIS with state counterparts on Wednesday, Albanese said: “We remind them all the time.” Related Article Opinion

CBD PM, corporate titans flock to Sofitel for Business Council dinner John Buckley CBD columnist Federal cabinet discussed the proposed national standards on AI in Perth on Tuesday. Albanese will present the plan to premiers on Wednesday, and there is widespread agreement outside of Queensland. Business leaders have also expressed support for Labor’s plan to mandate offsets for data centre energy and water usage to avoid a US-style backlash against the computer factories.



This masthead reported on Tuesday that business groups were plotting a union-style campaign on living standards and economic growth before the next election, following a corporate-led campaign against Labor’s budget measures. Business Council of Australia chairman Geoff Culbert will tell the organisation’s annual dinner in Sydney that firms want to change the national debate on productivity and require Labor’s buy-in. Related Article Exclusive

Data centres Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash “Prime minister – I appreciate that your job is extremely difficult. You are trying to navigate the need for material structural reform in an environment where the time needed to effectively prosecute those ideas doesn’t align with political cycles. That is a problem faced by all modern democracies,” Culbert will say, according to speech notes. “We are asking you to partner with us to take Australia forward.”



The prime minister said the business political establishment should be more upbeat about the country and its financial performance as cost of living pressures translate to support for One Nation. Albanese argued Australia’s unemployment rate was relatively healthy and Australia was growing at a better rate than most G7 economies, countering a widespread view among economists that Australia’s economy is in trouble. “We’ve got to be optimistic,” Albanese said on Wednesday. “We’ve got to shape the future or the future will shape us. So how do we put all that together?” “What are the opportunities that we have? The comparative advantages that we have? AI is a good example: we have enormous space, which is the envy of the world. An island to ourselves. We have clean energy. We have everything under the earth with critical minerals and rare earths.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Tracking devices, drones and poisoned dogs: CFMEU probe told of intimidation
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandCFMEU Tracking devices, drones and poisoned dogs: CFMEU probe told of intimidation Cameron Atfield Updated August 25, 2026 — 7:56pm ,first published 2:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A security professional hired to protect a CFMEU-targeted worksite found a tracking device attached to his car and believes his dog was poisoned by baited meat dropped from a drone in a campaign of intimidation by the union, a commission of inquiry heard on Tuesday. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen was providing security services to construction firm BMD at the Centenary Bridge worksite when, he told the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU and Misconduct in the Construction Industry, he became the target of a sustained campaign of harassment. After attending the site on May 17, 2024, Killen said he sensed he was being followed during his drive back to his company headquarters near the Port of Brisbane. The tracking device found on Grant Killen’s vehicle. Commission of Inquiry Upon arrival, Killen said he immediately placed his car on a hoist, lifted it, and found a tracking device attached beneath the chassis.



“Once I found the device, I immediately put the vehicle on the ground as quick as I could. Then I left the facility,” he said. “Then I gave the admin staff at the office a call and directed them to pack up and close up for the day and go home.” Killen said he sped away from the site to put distance between the device and his staff. “I left the device on the vehicle mainly because I knew the device had a particular anti-removal device on there, an anti-tilt switch,” he said. “As soon as it gets removed, the people who put it on there, who have the software for that, would immediately be notified.”



Suspecting he was being followed by someone in a Toyota RAV4, Killen said he engaged in some “aggressive driving”, including deliberately running a red light to check if he was being followed. “I was followed through that red light,” he said. Concentric Concepts managing director Grant Killen giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry “Further down the road, we did an aggressive U-turn [to] see if it would keep up, and it did follow.” Killen eventually lost his tail, he said, and removed the device by the side of a road.



But he said the intimidation did not stop there, instead spreading to his family home. There were drive-bys in his cul-de-sac, and Killen said he managed a brief look at one of the drivers, who he identified as former police detective Mick Featherstone, whom the inquiry heard the CFMEU had engaged to collect intelligence on BMD personnel. Separately, Killen said he noticed several drones overhead. Then, the family dog got sick. “One of the questions the vet asked me, after a point where the vet had to operate on the dog and remove its stomach contents, was ‘Do you feed your dog cubed meat?’,” Killen said.



“We don’t, and I thought that was a strange question. But as I reflected shortly after and recalled, I formed the opinion that there was a possibility that the dog had been baited at some stage.” Related Article Building Bad Inquiry and CFMEU bosses seek answers and action over alleged bikie plot When counsel assisting the inquiry, Eddy Gisonda, KC, put it to Killen that he suspected one of the drones may have dropped baited meat on his property, he responded “yeah, correct”. Killen said the campaign was enough to make him walk away from the BMD contract. “With the tracking device on our vehicle, with everything that was occurring, I needed to step back and just concentrate on the safety of me and my family and our business,” he said.



Commissioner Stuart Wood asked Killen, a military veteran with service in Iraq, whether he had experienced anything of that level while deployed. “An assailant or an offender always has the upper hand about how they plan to do an overt act or assault someone or conduct an attack,” he said. “They choose the time, they choose the place, they choose the method. “All we can do is simply react the best that we can and try and mitigate it by having that planning in place. “So to put that in context, that’s what we tried our best to do in this particular situation.”



After lunch, BMD chief executive Scott Power recounted a similar experience at his father’s house. His father, Mick Power, still served as BMD chairman. BMD chief executive Scott Power giving evidence on Tuesday. Commission of Inquiry Similar to Killen’s situation, Power said, drones had been spotted above his father’s home before his dog fell ill. “They were concerned, obviously, for the well-being of their pet, but the timing of it seemed to coincide with the campaign in the local area surrounding their home, so they formed the view that it was connected [with the CFMEU,” he said. Gisonda: “And was it unusual for them to observe drones flying above their property?”



Power: “Yeah, it was particularly unusual. It’s not something they have ever previously discussed having observed.” Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies Earlier, Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said relations between the state trades and labour council and the CFMEU had greatly improved since the latter went into administration. “We have developed, I think, a fairly good working relationship, completely unlike what it was, and on the basis that we work with the Queensland branch to try to assist them on their path to getting out of administration,” she said. But King said there was still some way to go before the CFMEU could be reaffiliated with the Queensland Council of Unions.



“It is going to take time because, while the people who are in the union now are not the same people who were doing the activities and the conduct that was occurring pre-the High Court decision, relationships still take time to mend, and trust takes time to rebuild,” she said. The hearing continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCourts Federal Darwin MP charged with breaching bail after alleged assault on King’s representative Rob Harris Updated August 25, 2026 — 7:45pm ,first published 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing renewed calls to stand down Labor MP Luke Gosling from his role as special envoy after he was charged with breaching bail on Tuesday in relation to the ongoing allegations he assaulted Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly. NT Police said in a statement they allege Gosling breached his bail conditions on Friday, August 14, and served him with a summons to appear in Darwin Local Court on September 30. Police did not specify what is alleged to have occurred. Federal MP Luke Gosling, centre, at the TIO Stadium in Darwin on August 14. Facebook/Luke Gosling MP Gosling, 54, posted a picture to Facebook at the Test match in Darwin between Australia and Bangladesh on the date of the alleged breach. It was reported by the NT News that Connolly was at the venue, but it was unclear if that is where the alleged offence occurred. A spokeswoman for Gosling said neither he nor his office hade been made aware of the nature of the alleged breach and have been provided no information from police other than a summons.



“On Friday, August 14, Mr Gosling did not attend any events at the same time as the administrator,” she said. “Mr Gosling is discussing the matter with his legal team, and will be defending the charge.” The MP, who is the Albanese government’s special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia, was arrested at his home last month and charged with two counts of assaulting Connolly, with the offences carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment. He appeared in Darwin Local Court on July 31, successfully applying to vary his bail conditions so he could attend the same public events as Connolly, provided he stayed at least 15 metres away and gave Connolly’s office 48 hours’ notice. Judge Stephen Geary also banned him from coming within 50 metres of the NT’s Government House, where Connolly resides. The administrator is the Crown’s representative in the NT, a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.



Prosecutors had opposed the variation, telling the court Connolly had cancelled public engagements because of concerns about encountering Gosling and arguing the restrictions were needed for the administrator’s “safety and wellbeing”. Related Article Crime Courts hears details of Labor MP’s alleged assault of NT administrator The alleged assaults occurred about 30 minutes between each other at the Darwin Thai Grand Festival on July 18. It was alleged in court that Gosling approached Connolly from behind in the first incident and, in the second, collided with him before drawing back his left elbow and striking him in the upper right rib area. Albanese has refused to stand down Gosling from his role as an envoy for veterans over the assault charges, despite calls from the Coalition. The PM’s office has declined to comment, citing an ongoing legal process.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said that the charges were already a test of the prime minister’s leadership. “Now Mr Gosling has also been charged with allegedly breaching his bail, the case for the prime minister to act is even stronger,” Taylor said in a statement released on Tuesday night. “These allegations are matters for the courts, but Anthony Albanese has a decision to make about who serves in his government. He should stand Mr Gosling down today.” Gosling denies the allegations, describing them at the time as “ludicrous”. His lawyer, Marty Aust, has described the prosecution case as “incredibly weak” and accused police of politicising the matter. Gosling has also disputed the police account of events leading to his arrest, saying he was first contacted while working in Queensland and that his office had been trying to arrange a meeting with detectives.



NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole said detectives had made multiple attempts to contact him before the arrest. The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions is preparing to take over the assault case from the NT DPP, which cited a perceived conflict of interest. It was reported by ABC Darwin the conflict relates to concerns about how the acting NT DPP’s handling of the case could be perceived given the prospect of a permanent appointment to the role. Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP convicted and sentenced for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment can be disqualified from parliament, meaning any conviction could trigger a byelection. He has held the seat of Solomon – which includes Darwin and its satellite city of Palmerston – since 2016. He held off a threat from the Country Liberals by just 1500 votes in May last year.
