Tech.title: Americans Want to Know When Their Healthcare Providers Use AI
Tech.content:
AI chatbots are being used in healthcare, both in and out of the doctor’s office, more than ever before. Patient and medical providers alike are turning to AI for treatments and diagnoses, but transparency remains a key concern, a new survey by Pew Research Center shows.

A poll of 3,488 US adults conducted between June 22 and June 28 found that a quarter of respondents use chatbots to diagnose symptoms. Those turning to chatbots for health mainly cite convenience and affordability as their motive. Patients also use AI chatbots to find information quickly and at no cost, better understand a doctor’s diagnosis, interpret lab results and decide whether to seek in-person care.

Of these survey participants, almost half (47%) say the health information generated by the chatbot was “extremely” helpful, and 48% said the information was “somewhat” helpful. Only 5% said the results were not too helpful or not at all helpful.

AI chatbots work by simulating a conversation between two parties and responding to your prompts or inputs using the massive amounts of information the models were trained on. Many people appreciate the convenience they offer, as chatbots are available 24/7 and can often be accessed for free and sometimes without an account. Chatbots, however, are known to “hallucinate,” or generate false information in their responses, which can be particularly dangerous or alarming when your personal health is in question. Among other issues, they’re trained to produce a probable answer, not necessarily one grounded in truth, and they’re likely to sound particularly confident about that answer.

But generative artificial intelligence is also showing up at the doctor’s office — and Pew found that Americans have greater concerns about its use there.

Read also: ChatGPT Health Will See You Now, and It’s a Big Step Forward for Medical Queries

When doctors turn to chatbots

While recent numbers show that about one in three US adults have used chatbots for health-related questions, medical providers are also increasingly turning to AI in the office for note-taking, interpreting exams and more.

While views on AI use in doctors’ offices vary, one factor remains of critical concern to patients: transparency.

Of those surveyed, 72% say it is “extremely or very important” for their medical provider to disclose any use of AI. The survey also found that a vast majority of people (eight in 10) want to be told if AI is being used directly for care or medical decisions, such as diagnoses and the analysis of scans, X-rays and lab results. AI is frequently used for triage purposes — and has even been shown to outperform human ER doctors — as well as to complete clinical tasks more quickly. For instance, AI has been used effectively to reduce the window of X-ray interpretations from 11.2 to 2.7 days.

Although Americans want advance notice when AI is used in their healthcare, nearly half (47%) are unsure whether it has ever played a role in their treatment, underscoring limited awareness of when, where and how the technology is used.

Americans are not fully comfortable with AI

The survey shows that Americans may find AI chatbots convenient, but not entirely trustworthy.

Views are mixed on sharing personal health histories and diagnoses with AI. Among those surveyed, 29% say they are extremely or very comfortable sharing health information with chatbots, while 26% say they are uncomfortable doing so.

The findings suggest that although AI is increasingly used for health information and care, public confidence and understanding have not kept pace with its adoption.

Tech.title: Behind the Scenes of ESPN’s Animated Sports Alt-Casts
Tech.content:
When ESPN floated the idea of creating an animated alternative broadcast for games, it was all about creating “magical moments in sports.” Instead of watching sports stars shooting hoops or scoring touchdowns, there was suddenly an option to see Mickey Mouse, Buzz Lightyear, Lisa Simpson or Mike Wazowski do the honors.

For Michael “Spike” Szykowny, ESPN vice president of edit, animation, graphics innovation and creative production, this project is his baby. The animated alt-casts bring a different audience to sports, Szykowny said during a panel at Disney’s D23 convention last weekend.

“We took a bunch of technologies like live player tracking — we can track what the players are doing in the game and make our animated characters do the same things,” Szykowny said. ESPN brought Disney IP into the project and combined it with face-tracking and motion-capture technology.

ESPN studio host Drew Carter has been a live animated commentator for every alt-cast. He said that for the first one, he had to wear a full motion-capture suit. But now, he only has to wear a virtual reality headset.

“It’s a technological feat to track these players in real time,” Jay Ward, creative director of franchise at Pixar, said during the panel in Anaheim, California.

The players on the field wear devices that generate tracking data for NFL Next Gen Stats and into Sony’s Beyond Sports engine and Sony’s Hawk-Eye Innovations optical tracking. These technologies are then used to create live animations, “rebuilding each throw, route, block, kick and tackle in real time,” Disney says.

The commentators’ booth calls are synced with their animated avatars via their VR headsets.

Ward said Pixar wanted to be involved because the animation studio “is all about technology, creativity and storytelling.”

During the Toy Story version of Funday Football, which aired in 2023, the main toys were all seen playing an NFL game in Andy’s room, with the real players as toy-scale versions of themselves.

Blocks were used for goalposts; the claw machine manned by the three-eyed aliens brought the ball down for kickoff; Slinky Dog was the 1st and 10 marker; and there was a Duke Caboom halftime show. Carter appeared as a Pixar-ified version of himself doing the commentary on-screen.

The second iteration of Funday Football featured the characters of Monsters, Inc., and the scene had to be animated from scratch because the movie is 25 years old.

Random players were picked to become Mike and Sulley playing on the field, while the other players were just animated versions of themselves, and Roz was a sideline reporter. All the original voice actors from the Pixar movie returned to help with the alt-cast, as did Carter.

Dunk the Halls, a Christmas NBA game played between Mickey and his closest friends in December last year, was next. It was animated to look as if it were being played on a perfect replica of Main Street, USA, at Walt Disney World, with the team even bringing in animators from Walt Disney Studios to get it right.

Disney Legend and iconic animator Eric Goldberg drew hundreds of sketches of what “bits” the characters could do during the game.

But there was a problem.

“The tracking was off at one point,” said Renée Johnson, creative director of Disney Character Voices. The referee was accidentally turned into a player who scored a 3-pointer, so they quickly turned the character into Stitch.

ESPN tried its hand at an NHL game next, choosing the Pixar film Inside Out, given that the main character plays hockey. The game was designed to look like it’s being played inside Riley’s mind while she’s sleeping, with the ESPN Beyond Sports animation team building out Hockey Island in three dimensions for the alt-cast setting. That game aired in March this year and used NHL positional data for the players and puck, along with Sony Hawk-Eye Innovations’ optical tracking.

And for a Simpsons-themed Funday Football session in December 2024, ESPN brought in the whole Simpsons writing team.

“There was a little bit of fear because these are three giant iconic brands: NFL, The Simpsons and Disney — how will they work together?” said Joel Cohen, a writer and co-executive producer of The Simpsons. “We’re very particular about how we want our characters to be portrayed and what jokes we want them to tell.”

The team came up with 8 minutes of original Simpsons animation with a storyline that carried throughout the game. Animating for a live event is something that the animation team never gets to do, so it was “a super fun vibe that we never get to experience,” Cohen said, adding that even creator Matt Groening came along.

The writers of The Simpsons were texting Disney and ESPN during the event — though the NFL said no to some of the jokes the writers came up with.

“There’s a 1-minute delay, so we can see what play happens to insert characters and push forward the storyline,” Szykowny said. “(Like) quickly put Bart as QB, Lisa as receiver as they score.”

ESPN has yet to announce its next animated alt-cast, but the animation x sports project isn’t showing any signs of slowing down. You can rewatch the alt-casts on YouTube, Disney Plus and ESPN Plus, but they’re much more impressive to witness live, simultaneously with a game.

Tech.title: A New Interactive Tool Weighs Vaccine Risks for You
Tech.content:
We live in a time when mixed messages about vaccines are the norm. Often, the Trump administration says one thing, while public health officials say another, leaving at least half of Americans in what the independent health policy organization KFF called the “malleable middle.” They remain uncertain when presented with vaccine myths.

To address the confusion, the free “What’s the Risk?” tool launched in early August. It allows users to visualize the vaccine risks often described as “rare” or “uncommon” right alongside the risks associated with the diseases they were created to prevent.

The interactive tool was designed by the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy and Unbiased Science, a public health communication platform and podcast founded by Jessica Steier, a public health scientist.

More comparisons will be added over time, but right now, you can see the measles and the MMR vaccine and RSV alongside its vaccines and antibody products. Plus, you can compare them to life events, such as deaths caused by drowning, car crashes, falls, bee or wasp stings and lightning strikes.

How to use the vaccine risk tool

First, choose one of the suggested comparisons or build your own by selecting two from the dropdowns.

Life events like drowning and car crashes help put certain risks in perspective. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

But before you scroll down to see the comparison, Steier told CNET in an email that you should read the “Before you compare: a few things to know” list at the top. It explains, for example, that what happens if you get infected versus what happens if you get vaccinated aren’t equally likely. For the former, it depends on many factors, such as where you live and travel and how many people around you are vaccinated.

“They tell you what each side of the comparison is holding constant, and that shapes how you should read everything below it,” Steier said.

Scroll down to view the two side-by-side light gray boxes. Each represents 100,000 people in the population indicated above the boxes in color-coded bands. Comparisons are most reliable when comparing the same population, so when two different age groups are shown, you should treat the results as a rough sense of scale rather than a precise number.

Sources are shown below the squares, along with each risk and the number of those affected per 100,000 of the stated population. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

Plus, these are population averages. Your personal risk will depend on your age, health status and lifestyle circumstances.

All numbers are shown as an annual rate, unless labeled otherwise. Since everyday risks are usually published as lifetime figures, those had to be converted.

Within the light gray boxes, you’ll find colored squares representing each risk. They’re sized to indicate the number of people affected by the stated complication. “A very rare outcome shows up as a tiny speck and a common one as a large block,” said Steier.

Each square has a color meant to illustrate the severity of the outcome. Red indicates serious outcomes, while dark gray indicates those considered mild or temporary.

If you hover over a square or tap on it, you can read the details and see links to the sources for the number shown by the square.

Above the squares, you can switch to a grid view for a different perspective. You can also zoom in to see the risks represented in a population of 50,000.

What the grid view looks like. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

Ultimately, this tool takes numbers that can be difficult to contextualize and helps you visualize them to better understand the relative frequency and severity of vaccines versus their connected diseases.

How sources were chosen

To narrow down the sources for this tool, two rules were applied. “Every figure has to come from a public, citable source, and every figure has to be measured the same way as the one sitting next to it,” said Steier.

For the first rule, the tool’s creators went straight to the source: national surveillance systems and published studies, rather than news articles, fact sheets or advocacy pages that merely cited the original data. The tool links out to these sources, in case you’d like to check their work.

When you hover over a risk, you can see the sources used. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

The makers also matched both the vaccine and disease sides based on age group and population as closely as available data allowed. Where that match isn’t exact, the tool says so.

The goal

A single number or statistic won’t typically tell you everything you need to know when it comes to vaccine or disease risk. According to Steier, to understand a risk, you need three things: how likely the outcome is, how serious it would be if it happened, and what it compares to, including what happens if you do nothing.

“Part of what we’re up against is numbness,” said Steier. “Everyone throws scary numbers around constantly, so we’ve stopped registering them. ‘One in 10,000’ and ‘one in a million’ both just land as ‘rare,’ even though one is a hundred times the other.”

The hope with this tool is that users will better understand what those numbers actually mean and develop a habit of asking “compared to what?”

While not directly comparable due to age differences, it’s still eye-opening to compare vaccine complications with life events. Unbiased Science/CNET Screenshot

The tool’s future

In addition to working on the design and functionality, the team behind “What’s the Risk?” plans to add more vaccines and diseases. Plus, everyday life events, since those help people put an unfamiliar risk on a scale they already understand.

“The addition we’re most excited about is a way to reflect vaccine coverage, because coverage is what drives how likely you are to encounter these diseases in the first place,” Steier said. This could involve pulling in vaccine uptake by ZIP code so people can view their community, or a slider that lets users adjust vaccine coverage to see how disease risk changes.

This expansion would show that many of us live with a low risk of disease because of the number of people around us who are vaccinated.

Steier emphasized that the current version of the tool is merely version 1.0, so if you see anything that can be improved, you can email the team at vaccines@unbiasedscience.com.

Tech.title: Percy Jackson Cast Teases ‘Some People Get What They Deserve’ in Season 3
Tech.content:
The third season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians is fast approaching, and at Disney’s D23 convention in Anaheim, California, last weekend, we got a glimpse of what’s to come as the cast answered fan questions during a panel discussion.

Earlier during Disney’s D23 Entertainment Showcase, the show got a fresh, new trailer for November’s third season. Walker Scobell, who plays the title character of Percy Jackson, was joined on stage by Ming-Na Wen (Hera) and Andra Day (Athena) to present the new trailer, which showed Percy fighting underwater and in arenas as a titan emerges.

After the ill-fated, critically panned movies released in the 2010s made it only to the second book in Rick Riordan’s series, the Disney Plus original will be the first time The Titan’s Curse has gotten an adaptation. It follows Percy and his Camp Half-Blood crew on their mission to rescue the goddess Artemis (played by Dafne Keen).

“Season 3 is the season where some people get what they deserve,” Scobell said during Saturday’s panel. There will also be a lot of improv in season 3, Scobell said, with the cast now close enough to play off each other like siblings bantering (which they did, all panel long, arguing over who is the most powerful).

Tamara Smart, who plays Thalia, said scenes exploring the past and Olympus were her favorites to shoot. “Season 3 is the season where women run it,” she said.

“It’s great to play a powerful, confident woman,” Smart added. “She’s 100% angry, 100% sad, 100% yelling at Percy.” (She added that after every single take where she was forced to yell at Scobell, she apologized to him.)

Keen wasn’t allowed to tease much from the upcoming season, but said the newcomers to the show had a huntress camp where they all got to train together, learn as a pack and master archery.

“Love and loss inform all decisions,” she said of Season 3.

Saara Chaudry said bringing Zoë Nightshade to life in the new season “has been the absolute privilege of my life.”

“Season 3 is the season where the stars align,” Chaudry added.

Dan Shotz, a showrunner, writer and executive producer, had some more detailed hints about the upcoming season.

“We have this great source material, and we get to dive a lot deeper… You’re going to see all these great things you love from this book, but so much more,” he said. “We cannot have a season of this show without Annabeth.”

Shotz said we will meet all the gods this season, as well as get to see the junkyard of the gods.

But not everyone makes it out alive, executive producer Jonathan Steinberg said.

“I’m excited for everyone to go on that ride shown in the trailer,” Steinberg said. “The trailer doesn’t lie.”

The eight-episode season streams on Nov. 20 on Disney Plus.

Tech.title: Privacy-Focused GrapheneOS Is Coming to Motorola Phones in 2027
Tech.content:
GrapheneOS, a privacy-first, open-source mobile operating system, is expanding beyond Google Pixels to support Motorola smartphones next year.

The GrapheneOS Foundation, which develops the OS, wrote on Mastodon that initial support will begin with traditional flagship devices before reaching foldable models, like the Motorola Razr Fold.

GrapheneOS has rigorous security standards, which it said many 2026 Motorola models are close to meeting. The company revealed that the next generation of Snapdragon chips will meet these standards, which is why it expects GrapheneOS to land on Motorola devices in 2027. Current 2026 Motorola models won’t be supported retroactively because they lack a few crucial hardware security features.

Unlike Google’s Android operating system, GrapheneOS prioritizes hardware-level anonymity and zero-trust isolation by default by removing built-in tracking and stripping Play Services down to an isolated app sandbox. It pairs this “de-Googled” baseline with some active, OS-level privacy protections to give users more control over their data without relying on third-party fixes.

CNET senior editor Michael Sorrentino said the move could also bring more software support to Motorola devices, helping them to compete with Samsung and Google devices.

“If supporting GrapheneOS also means more of Motorola’s phones will more consistently get flagship-level software support, that could put Motorola at a better footing against competing phones,” Sorrentino said. Motorola devices running GrapheneOS are slated to receive seven years of full operating system updates. For comparison, Sorrentino noted the 2026 Razr Ultra gets three years of software updates and five years of security updates.

GrapheneOS in the wild

Until now, GrapheneOS has been limited to certain Pixel phones, which the GrapheneOS Foundation says “meet the stringent privacy and security standards and have substantial upstream and downstream hardening specific to the devices.”

CNET senior video producer Jesse Orrall, who recently switched to GrapheneOS, said this has frustrated some people, especially those trying to cut ties with Google but still have to use a Pixel device.

“Having GrapheneOS available on Motorola offers, for the first time, a non-Google alternative as well as foldable form factors,” Orrall said. “I am interested to see how GrapheneOS’s ecosystem of open source app developers will incorporate a foldable screen into their designs.”

GrapheneOS made headlines in July after the US government indicted an activist who gave border agents a duress passcode that deleted the data on their phone. Samuel Tunick is accused of giving the duress passcode after agents repeatedly asked for his device’s passcode. According to the indictment, once the code was entered, “the screen went blank, flashed several times, and the phone appeared to restart.”

Tunick’s legal team confirmed he had GrapheneOS installed on his Google Pixel phone.

Tech.title: Apple Reportedly Will Raise iPhone Prices, but Just How Much?
Tech.content:
New iPhones are likely coming next month, and so are higher prices. Shoppers should expect hikes of at least $100 on the iPhone 18 Pro and other products launching at Apple’s annual September event, says Mark Gurman of Bloomberg.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max and Apple’s first foldable phone (possibly named the Ultra) — also expected to be unveiled in September — could cost more due to an AI-driven RAM shortage that has sparked a supply crunch for phones, laptops, gaming consoles and other electronic devices.

If Gurman is right, the iPhone 18 Pro would start at around $1,200, up from the $1,100 for the iPhone 17 Pro. which launched last September.



Two months ago, Apple raised prices on select MacBooks, iPads and HomePods, with some devices going up 33%. The iMac went from $1,300 to $1,500, the MacBook Neo went from $600 to $700, and MacBook Pro models each rose by $300. Last week, the tech giant laid off about 200 workers from its Vision Pro and Siri teams, and shut down the Vision Pro gaming group.

A representative for Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Will price hikes affect consumer buying?

If Apple goes $100 higher for its new iPhones, that would match Samsung’s cost hikes for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, and Google’s hikes with the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro.

Gurman said in his report that “Apple has room to go higher.” If so, the company’s new Upgrade program — which allows customers to lease an iPhone, iPad, Mac or Apple Watch at prices starting at $18 a month for an iPhone — could mitigate sticker shock.

But higher iPhone prices aren’t likely to turn off many Apple fans, according to longtime tech analyst Paolo Pescatore.

“Its huge installed base, ecosystem and growing use of trade-ins, financing and monthly payments give it far greater pricing power than most rivals,” Pescatore told CNET. “The bigger risk is not consumers switching away from Apple but rather deciding to keep their existing iPhone for longer.”

But loyalty can only go so far, Pescatore added. Steeper prices need to correlate with bigger advancements.

“Samsung and Google raising prices gives Apple useful cover, but higher prices bring greater expectations,” he said. “Apple needs to show consumers meaningful advances in AI, cameras, battery life and new form factors. Brand loyalty is incredibly strong, but Apple still needs to keep giving users a compelling reason to move up the range.”

RAMageddon’s fault … or not?

Companies and analysts blame higher prices for most tech goods on component shortages and steep price increases for RAM and storage devices like hard drives and SSDs — mainly caused by the buildout boom in AI infrastructure by some of the world’s major tech companies.

Even though Apple has largely stayed on the sidelines as Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet (Google) and Meta have spent billions on AI investments, the iPhone maker has felt the ripple effects of the worldwide memory chip shortage, which it claims forced it to raise prices this year.

But with a profit margin reportedly at an astounding 27%, Apple would seem more than capable of keeping prices as affordable as possible for its millions of loyal customers.

Tech.title: If You Don’t Want Smart Glasses to Spy, Try a Bluetooth Detector App
Tech.content:
You can no longer assume a pair of black-rimmed glasses is just prescription eyewear.

As Meta AI smart glasses grow in popularity and other wearables join the race, they’re facing mounting public backlash over their hidden surveillance capabilities. Smart glasses can record, stream and process video without alerting anyone around them — unless you consider a tiny recording indicator light sufficient.

Broad concerns over privacy have led to a technical battle. On one side, hardware modifiers are tweaking wearable cameras to make them even harder to spot, often by disabling LED indicators. On the other, developers and privacy-focused coders are launching counter tech to give you a heads-up when a hidden camera walks into the room.

One of those developers has already gained traction with a free Apple iOS app called Zuckoff, a digital detection tool to spot nearby Ray-Ban Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles or similar hardware.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Sniffing out smart glasses

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

What drove Szydlowski to actively develop a software detector was seeing social media videos of people wearing smart glasses who recorded pranks or harassed women with pickup lines. None of the targets seemed aware that their content would appear online, which made Szydlowski angry. “There was not even a blur involved to try to censor them, to give them some sort of feeling of privacy,” he said. “These days, everybody feels entitled to post everything.”

App developer Pawel Szydlowski said he developed his app, Zuckoff, to help address people’s privacy concerns about smart glasses. Pawel Szydlowski

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Smart glasses detected… now what?

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an assistant professor of Information Systems at Carnegie Mellon University who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

Unlike with smartphones, where it’s easier to tell when someone is recording or taking photos, “smart glasses shift the burden of privacy entirely onto the person being photographed,” Ananthakrishnan said.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

Privacy-conscious smart glasses?

That surveillance anxiety may prompt some hardware-makers to release alternative versions of smart glasses that entirely avoid potential privacy violations.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker. Scott Stein/CNET

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

The future of smart glasses detectors

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Zuckoff’s Szydlowski said it’s possible a company could shrink the kind of 5G technology to fit in smart glasses, making them less dependent on phones and Bluetooth, but that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. If Meta or Snap deliberately updated their hardware to hide from detection apps and disable smart glasses’ digital footprint, it would further undercut any claim of privacy accountability.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

Tech.title: It’s Been 20 Years Since Astronomers Decided Pluto Isn’t a Planet
Tech.content:
Named for the ancient Greek god who presides over the afterlife, Pluto is now mostly known as the planet that lost its planethood 20 years ago. In August 2006, the International Astronomical Union, an organization that names and classifies celestial bodies, voted to reclassify what was once known as the ninth planet in our solar system.

Ever since that fateful vote, Pluto has been a dwarf planet. And two decades on, it’s still a controversial decision. Earlier this year, billionaire Jared Isaacman, who now serves as NASA Administrator, voiced his support for Pluto being recognized as a planet once again. Star Trek’s William Shatner isn’t happy about it either.

Astrophysicist David Gerdes, the dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at Case Western Reserve University, told CNET via email that our understanding of solar system objects changes as we learn more about them. “For example, large asteroids like Ceres, Pallas and Vesta that orbit between Mars and Jupiter were originally considered planets when they were discovered in the early 1800s,” Gerdes says.

“As more and more asteroids were discovered in this region, it eventually became clear that these objects were simply the biggest members of a very large population,” he added. “Today, we know of over a million asteroids — so many that we call that region the ‘asteroid belt’ — and nobody considers them planets.”

But whether Pluto is a planet — and again, right now, it’s not — comes down to how we decide to define the word “planet” in scientific terms. But the tools we use to view the cosmos, like high-powered space telescopes, are getting better all the time. Every few years, it seems like we can see farther and clearer into space.

Using these tools to discover new celestial objects was actually what got Pluto booted from its status as a planet in the first place. Here’s what happened.

A planet no more

In 2005, three astronomers discovered a distant, Pluto-sized celestial body and nicknamed it Xena, after the warrior princess from TV. The IAU official named it Eris, after the ancient Greek god of chaos. It’s a fitting name, as chaos ensued.

Because Eris is roughly the same size as Pluto and shares many characteristics, Eris’s discovery set off a fierce debate around what objects in space should be considered a planet. Eventually, this led the IAU to set out conditions that a celestial body must satisfy to be classified as a planet in 2006.

Image of the dwarf planet Eris (also known as 2003 UB313 or Xena) that was taken using the Samuel Oschin Telescope at the Palomar Observatory. Screenshot by CNET

According to the astronomers of the IAU, a celestial object needs to do three things to be considered a planet. First, it must orbit a star. So, if it’s a planet in our neck of the woods, it has to orbit the sun.

Second, the object has to be big. If the object is big enough, it will have sufficient gravity to force it into a sphere. So, planets have to be a big ball. No flat planets allowed.

Third, the planet also needs to be so large that it cleared anything else of similar size from its orbit. Obviously, moons and asteroids can be nearby, just not other planets.

The IAU then set three categories for celestial bodies in our solar system: planets, dwarf planets and small solar system bodies. Dwarf planets have the same attributes as planets in this context, except they do not meet the third criterion: They have not cleared out the neighborhood around their orbits. Also, dwarf planets can’t be satellites.

The third category, small solar system bodies, is everything else orbiting the sun that’s not a planet or a dwarf planet. Again, satellites don’t count here.

“These definitions are somewhat arbitrary, and people still like to debate them,” Gerdes says. “But one thing is certain: There’s no way to define a ‘planet’ that includes Pluto without also adding other objects like Eris, Sedna, Makemake and Ceres to the list.”

So, unless we add more planets to the list, Pluto probably won’t be reclassified as a planet.

“Modern science provides much more knowledge than the simple fact that objects orbiting the sun appear to move with respect to the background of fixed stars,” the IAU president at the time, Ron Ekers, wrote in August 2006.

“For example, recent new discoveries have been made of objects in the outer regions of our solar system that have sizes comparable to and larger than Pluto. These discoveries have rightfully called into question whether or not they should be considered as new ‘planets,’” he added.
